descriptions.ns.life.plant-observation: Trace the veins in a leaf, peek at the roots under a green onion, and see what a microscope reveals inside an onion cell.
descriptions.ns.life.animal-observation: Watch a duck paddle, a silkworm change inside its cocoon, and a dragonfly leave its old skin behind. Then follow barn swallows across a map.
descriptions.ns.life.human-body: Bend an elbow, take a bite of a steamed bun, and follow a breath. Find out how oxygen from the air reaches a leg.
descriptions.ns.life.local-ecology: Find neighbors in a tree's shade, at a pond, and in a patch of flowering grass. See what a bird's menu can tell you about a food web.
descriptions.ns.life.orchard-fruits: Look for a star inside an apple, a fruit on the outside of a strawberry, and the path from a strand of corn silk to a kernel.
descriptions.ns.life.bird-feathers-beaks: Look closely at a wing feather, a hummingbird at a flower, and a finch cracking a seed. How much can you learn from a bird's shape?
descriptions.ns.life.forest-layers: Look up into the canopy and down at the moss. A hole in a tree, a pool beside a log, and a seedling's perch all have stories to tell.
descriptions.ns.life.marine-animals: Watch a fish turn and a sea turtle come up for air. Look underneath a sea star and listen for the echo a dolphin uses to find prey.
descriptions.ns.life.body-senses: Feel the ridges in a piece of cloth, follow a ring through the ear, and discover how your body keeps track of a hand you can't see.
descriptions.ns.life.seasonal-notebook: Follow a bud as it opens and mark the days when flowers and insects appear. Even an empty square on the calendar has a story.
descriptions.ns.matter.everyday-materials: Sort a set of spoons, pick a roof for a paper house, and peek between the layers of a milk carton to find out what each material does.
descriptions.ns.matter.water-and-air: Tip an upside-down cup to let bubbles out. Follow water as it melts, evaporates, and gathers in drops on a cold cup or a blade of grass.
descriptions.ns.matter.mixtures-and-separation: Where does salt go in water? Why does oil come back to the top? Follow sand through a funnel and colors up a strip of paper.
descriptions.ns.matter.material-changes: Compare torn paper, rusty nails, and a potter's fired cup. Then use two scale readings to track material that comes or goes.
descriptions.ns.matter.minerals-and-metals: Meet the grains in granite and the graphite in a pencil. Read a mineral hardness scale and trace a metal spoon's protective surface.
descriptions.ns.matter.fibers-in-paper-and-cloth: Follow a fiber into a sheet of paper and a strand of yarn through a knitted hat. A towel loop, a wet paper edge, and a clothing label offer more clues.
descriptions.ns.matter.glass-ceramics-and-concrete: Follow window glass across a pool of liquid tin, look beneath the glaze on a porcelain jar, and find out why fresh concrete needs moisture.
descriptions.ns.matter.polymer-structures: Draw a long molecular chain, watch a rubber band spring back, and decode a number on the bottom of a plastic bottle.
descriptions.ns.matter.water-treatment: Find out what sinks, what dissolves, and what can stick to a carbon filter. Follow water through a treatment plant and into a distiller.
descriptions.ns.matter.reuse-and-recycling: A loose strap can be mended, old glass can go into new bottles, and part of an old road can go into a new one. Try designing a pencil box for its next use.
descriptions.ns-physics-force: Watch a sheet of paper bend, a toy car slow down, and a little boat settle deeper in the water. Each change gives a clue about a force at work.
descriptions.ns-physics-light: Trace light from a lamp to a shadow, around the corners of a periscope, and through water and glass to see how it reaches your eyes.
descriptions.ns-physics-sound: A ruler hums, a drum thumps, and two paper cups carry a whisper. Follow vibrations through string, air, and water, and listen for the sounds that bounce back.
descriptions.ns-physics-heat: Why does a metal spoon feel cool? How does a cup sleeve help water stay warm? Follow energy from warmer places to cooler ones and see what a thermometer can tell you.
descriptions.ns-physics-machines: A door handle, a ramp, and a pulley change how a push or pull gets a job done. Compare the force you use with the distance your hand travels.
descriptions.ns-physics-balance-pressure: Balance a model seesaw, picture a block tipping over, and explore how snowshoes, suction cups, and pistons spread or transmit a push.
descriptions.ns-physics-lenses: Follow the light from a tiny letter to an eye, a screen, or a camera. Discover how magnifiers, glasses, and microscopes bring details into view.
descriptions.ns-physics-musical-sound: Listen for what changes as a guitar string tightens, a pipe gets longer, or two notes sound together. Look inside the instruments for the parts that vibrate.
descriptions.ns-physics-electromagnetism: A comb lifts paper, a switch lights a bulb, and a current turns a compass needle. Explore electric charge, circuits, motors, and generators through familiar objects and exhibit models.
descriptions.ns-physics-energy: Follow the energy in a rolling ball, a swinging pendulum, a spring, and a pair of warming hands. Lifting a box of books offers a way to measure work and power.
descriptions.ns-earth-album-weather-notebook: Watch a flag, read a thermometer, and follow clouds and fog through the day. Then open the longer weather record to see what years of observations can tell us about a place.
descriptions.ns-earth-album-landscape-traces: Sandstone pillars, deep gullies, coastal mud, and moving ice hold clues to the work of water, wind, and glaciers across China.
descriptions.ns-earth-album-earth-moon-sun: Sketch the bright edge of the Moon and trace a stick's shadow. Use pictures and models to explore moon phases, day and night, and the seasons.
descriptions.ns-earth-album-space-evidence: Follow weather satellites, telescopes, rovers, and sample missions as they send observations, messages, lunar soil, and pieces of an asteroid back to Earth.
descriptions.ns-earth-album-water-paths: Trace water as a puddle shrinks, a leaf loses moisture, and a well fills from spaces in rock. Discover the many paths linking land, ocean, and air.
descriptions.ns-earth-album-rock-records: A sparkling grain, a rounded hole, a striped cliff, and a fossil leaf each tell part of a rock's history. Read those clues from the surface down to the crystals inside.
descriptions.ns-earth-album-natural-resources: Explore soil layers, freshwater, copper minerals, coal, underground heat, and wind. Discover where these resources come from and what makes them useful.
descriptions.ns-earth-album-weather-evidence: From dew and snow crystals to rainfall totals and a sea breeze, connect weather you can observe with measurements and forecasts you can use.
descriptions.ns-earth-album-night-sky: Start with a few lights in a window frame. Find the North Star, track Mars, and explore the Milky Way and the distances that astronomers measure in light-years.
descriptions.ns-earth-album-space-station: See an orbital sunrise, follow a robotic arm, and trace the paths of power, water, and heat aboard the International Space Station.

ns-g1-leaves.title: Two Leaf Portraits
ns-g1-leaves.markdown:
In Lucy's photo album, the ginkgo leaf opened wide like a folding fan. The willow leaf was long and narrow. Lucy covered the photos to give her little brother a guessing game. With her green pencil she drew the top of a fan and a little boat with two pointed ends. Her brother leaned in. “There's the fan. Where's the handle?”

She had left out the slender stalk at the bottom. Both leaves had a stalk. Both had fine lines, too. Those lines are called veins. On the ginkgo leaf they spread out from the handle of the fan. The willow leaf had one long vein down the middle, with smaller veins branching off to the sides.

Lucy covered the photos again. “Ginkgo!” her brother called, pointing at the little fan. He ran a finger up the leaf stalk. Where a vein split in two, he spread two fingers and followed both branches.

ns-life-roots.title: The Whiskers Under a Green Onion
ns-life-roots.markdown:
The green onions on the windowsill leaned toward the window. Whenever Ben drew them, he started at the rim of the pot. Below that he drew just the pot. One day Mom brought home a bunch of green onions with the roots still on. A whole tassel of thin roots hung from each white base. Some had little branches. “All that fits in our pot?” Ben drew a spray of long and short lines.

The dandelion in his book had different whiskers. One thick root stood out, with smaller roots branching off its sides. That main root is called a taproot. The green onion had a bunch of roots of about the same thickness. Together they form a fibrous root system. Ben could draw the two with quite different pencil strokes.

Roots hold a plant in the soil and take in water and the minerals dissolved in it. Ben made a little paper window in the pot in his drawing. When his sister lifted the flap, she found the other half of the picture underground.

ns-life-dandelion.title: What Flies With a Dandelion Parachute?
ns-life-dandelion.markdown:
“What's hanging from that tiny parachute?” Lucy leaned closer to the photo. A long, thin brown speck dangled below a tuft of white fluff. She turned back one picture. The dandelion was still a white ball, and now she could make out all the little parachutes packed together.

She turned back even farther. What looked like one round yellow flower was a crowd of tiny flowers. When the fruits are ripe, each little dry fruit has its own tuft of white hairs. A seed is tucked inside the fruit. Gather all those tufts together and you see a white puffball. A breeze can carry the fruits off one by one, each hanging from its tuft.

Lucy told the picture's story again. “The white hairs make the parachute. The fruit hangs underneath. The seed rides inside the fruit.” The wind could carry it, but the photo caught just one part of the flight. She left the next page blank. Would that little fruit land in a crack between stones or in the grass?

ns-life-leaf-veins.title: Where Do the Lines in a Leaf Go?
ns-life-leaf-veins.markdown:
Lucy traced a line on a photo of a corn leaf. Her pencil headed toward the tip as if it were following a long running track. On a maple leaf the track soon forked. A thick vein split into thin ones, which branched again. The lines made different patterns. Inside both kinds of veins were tiny passageways that carried things the plant needed.

Water taken up by the roots travels through the stem to the leaves. Passageways inside the leaf veins carry it farther into each leaf. In the light, a leaf uses water and carbon dioxide from the air to make sugar. Another set of passageways can carry sugar to the stem, the roots, or a growing part of the plant.

Her classmate had a blue pencil and a red one. A blue arrow followed the water from the leaf stalk into the blade. Where should the red arrow point? He found a new leaf that was still growing and drew the arrow toward it from an older leaf that made sugar. He could trace the veins right on the photo. A plant diagram helped him fill in what traveled through them.

ns-g5-onion-cells.title: A Closer Look at an Onion
ns-g5-onion-cells.markdown:
Long bricks lay in rows across the screen, with a dark seam here and a lighter seam there. The teacher was showing a micrograph, a picture taken through a microscope. It showed the thin surface layer of one of the fleshy leaves inside an onion bulb. The caption said 100×. Lucy traced the edges of a single “brick” with her finger. She had outlined one cell. Where neighboring cells meet, there are cell walls.

In the next picture, labeled 1,000×, a big round shape filled the center. Someone read the English label and asked where its line ended. The round shape was the nucleus. The line reached inside it to an even smaller structure, the nucleolus. A moment ago the class had been picking out whole cells. Now they were looking inside one.

Lucy's classmate zoomed in until the round shape filled half the screen. The nucleus in the onion stayed the same size. A scale bar shows how much real length a line in a picture represents. If the picture gets bigger, its scale bar gets bigger with it, so you can still work out an actual length. These two pictures had no scale bars. Lucy put her ruler away. She could still name three things she had found. A cell, a nucleus, and a nucleolus.

ns-life-autumn-leaf.title: The Yellow in a Ginkgo Leaf
ns-life-autumn-leaf.markdown:
In Ben's September photo, the ginkgo was green from top to bottom. In October, some branches on that same tree were green and some already showed yellow. He set the photos side by side. He almost wrote, “Yellow first appears in October.” Then he looked again. What he knew was which colors the camera had picked up on each date.

Green leaves contain chlorophyll. It gives them much of their green color and helps plants use light to make sugar. They can also contain pigments that look yellow or orange. When there's plenty of chlorophyll, green is usually the color you see. In fall, chlorophyll gradually breaks down in many trees that shed their leaves. Yellow pigments that were there all along become easier to see. Some red leaves have a different story. Certain red pigments can form in fall.

Ben found another photo from the same week. The ginkgo next door was still green. Even two sides of one tree can turn at different times. Days grow shorter and nights longer in fall. Temperature and the condition of the tree can affect its colors, too. Ben picked three branches on the right that reminded him of antlers. In a few days he would come back to the same spot.

This time he wrote, “When I photographed the yellow leaves in October, that branch on the right still had a few green ones.” To find out whether yellow pigment was in the leaves in September, he turned to his plant book. The camera had kept a record of what he saw.

ns-life-duck-feet.title: A Duck's Little Fans
ns-life-duck-feet.markdown:
A mallard waddled down the path. From her side of the railing, Ruby caught it lifting one foot. Its three front toes looked like the ribs of a fan. Thin skin stretched between them and spread out when the toes did. That skin is called webbing. The Mandarin word for it is pronounced pǔ.

At the water's edge the duck began to float. It swam past a rock and on toward some water plants. Its back looked steady. Underwater its feet were busy. With the toes spread, each wide webbed foot could push water backward and help the duck move forward.

Ruby drew the duck swimming to the right. Her little brother added an arrow for the water, pointing right, too. She showed him the paddling motion. “The foot pushes the water back behind the duck.” He turned his little arrow around. One arrow went forward with the duck. The other went back with the water.

ns-g2-animal-homes.title: Whose Nest Is in the Branches?
ns-g2-animal-homes.markdown:
A little bowl woven from grass, with blue-green eggs inside! The photo caught Owen's eye. On the left the bowl rested against a tree trunk. At the lower right a branch helped hold it up. The photographer had found an American robin's nest. Stems of different thicknesses stuck out around its cup-shaped rim.

American robins often nest on branches that reach out sideways, with leaves nearby. A robin shapes grass and small twigs into a cup, strengthens it with mud, and lines the inside with fine, dry grass. Some robins build under the eaves of a roof. You can find the same kind of bird nesting in different places.

Owen covered the bottom of the photo with his hand. The nest seemed to hang in midair. He lifted his hand, and there was the branch holding it up again. He could trace the fine grass with his finger. He had learned about the mud by reading bird scientists' accounts of how robins build.

ns-g3-silkworm.title: Before the Silkworm Moth Appears
ns-g3-silkworm.markdown:
Four picture cards, four dates. On April 9, a few eggs sat on a mulberry leaf. On May 2, a silkworm was eating a leaf. The May 18 picture showed just an oval white cocoon. In early June, a moth rested beside an empty cocoon. The teacher had made up the dates for the puzzle. Jamie picked up the third card. “Where's the pupa?”

A silkworm hatches from an egg as a larva that eats mulberry leaves. When it has grown enough, the larva spins silk around itself to make a cocoon. Then, inside the cocoon, it changes into a pupa. The pupa continues to develop. An adult moth emerges from the pupa and makes its way out of the cocoon. Jamie added a little cutaway drawing to the third card. The silk cocoon went on the outside, the pupa on the inside.

With the zoo's description, he could put the stages in order. Egg, larva, pupa, adult. The diagram alongside showed the cocoon separately so he could recognize its shape. He put the cards away and explained the tricky part in his own words. “It's the same little animal. When the larva becomes a pupa, there's silk around it.”

ns-life-dragonfly.title: An Empty Shell on a Water Plant
ns-life-dragonfly.markdown:
Lily was watching a dragonfly film in class. In one scene, four wings flashed in the sun as a dragonfly rested on a water plant. Then the camera went underwater. A short, stocky insect clung to a stem. Where were the wings it could fly with? Lily thought the film had switched to a different animal. Then she saw the caption. “Dragonfly nymph.”

A dragonfly starts life in an egg. After it hatches, the nymph lives in water. It hunts small animals and sheds its outer covering as it grows. When it's ready to become an adult, it often climbs onto a plant sticking out of the water. The adult comes out of that last old skin, and its wings slowly unfold. The empty skin, complete with legs and the outline of a body, may stay on the stem for a while.

Lily liked pausing the film right there. The empty shell had legs and a back, as if a little insect were still sitting there waiting. She ran the film backward to see the nymph climb out of the water. She let it play forward. The wings opened, the dragonfly flew, and its last old skin stayed on the stem.

ns-life-butterfly-sun.title: When a Butterfly Basks
ns-life-butterfly-sun.markdown:
Ethan paused the garden videos to look at two butterflies. One held its wings open. The other's wings were folded. They were both in bright spots. “Could the one with its wings open be feeling cold?” He put a little question mark beside his guess.

The temperature of a butterfly's body depends partly on its surroundings. Some butterflies spread their wings or turn toward the sun to absorb more warmth. When it gets too hot, a butterfly may move into shade or turn so that less sunlight hits its body and wings. A change of spot or a change of posture can make a difference.

When Ethan watched again, he noticed the clips had been taken at different times. One leaf was closer to the shade of a tree. “One open, one folded” could go straight into his notes. To investigate whether the first butterfly was warming up, he'd like to watch the same butterfly move from shade into sunlight. How would it hold its wings? What were the temperature and wind like? A pair of spread wings by itself gave him no reading of the butterfly's body temperature.

ns-life-swallow-migration.title: Why Do Barn Swallows Fly So Far?
ns-life-swallow-migration.markdown:
In summer, swallows often skimmed the tips of the grass above a school field. A friend in North America wrote to Owen. Where did those barn swallows go in winter? Owen opened the Cornell Lab of Ornithology's range map and read the key. Much of North America had the color for breeding areas. Large parts of Central and South America had the color for places where the birds spend the nonbreeding season.

Barn swallows often catch insects in flight. In places with a cold season, there are usually fewer flying insects to catch than there are in warm weather. Migrating lets birds reach places with more suitable conditions as the seasons change. Many North American barn swallows fly south after breeding, spend the winter in Central or South America, and later fly back to their breeding grounds. They need places to feed and rest along the way, too.

Owen had drawn a route through the colors, marking three cities where one swallow might have stopped. At the third city he put down his pencil. The map showed where barn swallows generally turn up at different times of year. For the journey of one particular bird, he'd need records that tracked that same bird. He erased all three city names and tucked the map into his letter.

ns-life-elbow.title: A Wave From the Elbow
ns-life-elbow.markdown:
Max waved at Grandma by the window. He kept his upper arm against his side and bent his arm just a little. Up came his hand, from his waist to his face. Where did his arm bend? Follow it down from the shoulder. Between the upper arm and the forearm is a joint called the elbow.

He relaxed his arm and gently bent it again. A little bump rose on the front of his upper arm. A muscle there tightens and works with other muscles to pull on the bones and lift his forearm. To straighten his arm, muscles on the back of his upper arm can pull on the bones of his forearm.

He showed Grandma two little figures he had drawn. Both had their upper arms down. One had a hand by its waist and the other had a hand by its face. With a little dot, Grandma showed where to find the elbow in each drawing. Max waved again. He could almost see the forearms in the picture waving back.

ns-life-pupil.title: The Little Opening in Your Eye
ns-life-pupil.markdown:
At the theater, Miles walked through a bright lobby and into the dark seating area. For a moment he couldn't make out his seat number. He stood still and waited. Soon he could see the chairs along the aisle. Why did it take a little while to see when the light changed?

His science book had two close-ups of an eye. The black circle in the middle is the pupil, a little opening that lets light in. The first part of its Mandarin name sounds like tóng. Around it is a colored ring called the iris. In bright light, the iris makes the pupil smaller, so less light gets in. In dim light, the pupil can get bigger and let in more light.

Miles remembered the seat numbers slowly coming into view. A wider pupil had let in more light. The part at the back of his eyes that senses light had also needed time to adjust. On the back of his ticket, he drew the same eye twice, with a small black circle in one and a bigger black circle in the other. His sister picked out the one for the dark theater right away.

ns-life-food-mouth.title: Digestion Begins With a Bite of Steamed Bun
ns-life-food-mouth.markdown:
Mia took a little bite of a steamed bun and chewed. A moment ago it had been one piece. Now it was damp and crumbly. “I bet your body starts digesting it when it gets to your stomach,” said her classmate. Mia lifted the tip of her tongue. The bits of bun had already mixed with saliva in her mouth.

Two jobs were already under way. Her teeth broke the food into smaller pieces, her tongue moved them around, and saliva moistened them. Some foods, including steamed buns, contain starch. Saliva contains a substance that helps break starch down. Between chewing and the work of saliva, digestion had already begun.

When Mia swallowed, the food went down her esophagus to her stomach. There it would be churned with digestive juices before moving on to the small intestine. Digestion would continue there, and most nutrients would be absorbed there, too. Mia could feel the bun getting soft and wet. To find out how her saliva had begun breaking down starch, she'd have to read a little farther into the story inside her body.

ns-g4-breath-route.title: Follow a Breath
ns-g4-breath-route.markdown:
Daisy drew a map of the body, with a nose at the top and a pair of lungs below it. Her blue pencil traveled down from a nostril and stopped at the chest. How could one path reach two lungs? In a diagram of the airways, she found the fork. It looked like a branch on a tree.

When you breathe in through your nose, air passes through the nasal cavity. This space warms and moistens the air a little and traps some dust. Air continues through the throat, past the voice box, and down the windpipe. The windpipe splits into two large tubes called bronchi, one for each lung. The tubes branch into smaller and smaller airways that lead to tiny air sacs called alveoli. That's where gases pass between the air and the body.

Daisy said each name as her finger moved along. Just past the windpipe she picked one side of the fork and kept going.

**Follow the air**  Nasal cavity → throat (pharynx) → voice box (larynx) → windpipe (trachea) → left and right bronchi → smaller airways → alveoli

The smell of smoke drifted through the window. Daisy and Dad moved somewhere with fresh air. She had just drawn the route that smoke could take along with a breath. She set her pencil back on the page and followed one narrow airway all the way to a cluster of air sacs.

ns-life-heart-loop.title: Where Does the Heart Send Blood?
ns-life-heart-loop.markdown:
Max had already drawn the path air takes to the lungs. His sister pointed to the lower leg on his map. “My leg needs oxygen, too. Does it have a tube all the way from my nose?” Max checked his body diagram. He moved his pencil to the tiny blood vessels alongside the air sacs in the lungs.

When a breath reaches the air sacs, some oxygen crosses a very thin barrier into the blood. The heart sends blood returning from the lungs out to the rest of the body. When the blood reaches tiny vessels in places such as a leg, some of its oxygen moves into the tissues that need it. The blood can also carry away carbon dioxide the tissues produce. Back in the lungs, some of that carbon dioxide crosses into the air sacs and leaves with a breath out.

Max drew two loops in red. One ran from the heart to the lungs and back to the heart. The other went from the heart to the rest of the body and back. “So what should we draw going to the leg?” his sister asked. Max knew where to put the blood vessel now. Air goes through airways to the air sacs. Oxygen passes into the blood there, and the blood carries it the rest of the way.

ns-life-sweat.title: Why a Breeze Feels Cool on Sweaty Skin
ns-life-sweat.markdown:
“My forehead's still sweaty. How did that breeze cool it so fast?” In the breezy hallway, Natalie thought of the table she'd wiped that morning. The damp patch near the window had dried first. She'd also wiped that part first. The table alone couldn't tell her how much difference the moving air had made.

Evaporation could explain that cool feeling. Sweat glands bring sweat to the surface of the skin. Most of sweat is water. For liquid water to become water vapor and spread into the air, it has to take in heat. As sweat evaporates, it carries some heat away from the skin. In humid air, sweat often evaporates more slowly. Quite a lot of sweat may stay on the skin. The amount you see gives you only part of the story about how much heat has gone.

Natalie thought of a different question. Suppose she laid out two cloths at the same time. They'd be the same size and equally wet, with just one facing a breeze. Which would dry first? Those cloths could help her picture how water leaves a surface. Skin has sweat glands and blood vessels whose blood flow can change. To explain the chill she felt in the hall, she'd need both the cloth comparison and what she knew about her body.

ns-life-tree-shade.title: Where the Tree's Shadow Falls
ns-life-tree-shade.markdown:
Two benches stood beside the school field. One was under a tree. Shadows of leaves made light and dark patches across its back. The other bench stood farther away, all in the sun. Grace and Dad crossed the bright ground and stepped into the shade. It felt cooler there.

Grace looked up. Leaves crowded the branches overhead. They blocked some of the sunlight. The bench and the ground beneath the tree got less direct sun and often stayed cooler. In gaps between the leaves, little patches of sunlight made it all the way to the ground.

That afternoon, sunlight reached the legs of the shady bench. “The bench hasn't moved,” Grace said. “Where did that shady spot go?” She looked up again. The sun was in a different part of the sky, and the tree cast its shadow in a different place. Dad opened his book. This time, a little leaf shadow landed right on the page.

ns-life-pond-neighbors.title: Who Lives Where in a Pond?
ns-life-pond-neighbors.markdown:
The teacher brought in a picture of a pond. Grace drew two lines. One ran along the surface of the water. The other sloped down from the bank and followed the pond bottom. She had three picture cards left to place. One showed a tall cattail, one showed floating duckweed, and one showed a fish.

Cattails often grow in shallow water near the shore. Their roots reach into the mud, and their leaves rise above the water. Duckweed floats at the surface, with tiny roots that can dangle in the water. A little fish can swim here and there. Some little fish shelter among water plants. Even in one pond, the depth, the light, and the places to hide change from spot to spot.

Grace put the duckweed at the surface. She placed the cattail so it stretched from the mud up above the water. When she came to the fish, she put the glue away. For now it was hiding in the plants. One swish of its tail and it might be off to the other side of the pond. She'd found the card that could move house.

ns-life-flower-visitors.title: A Bee Drops In on an Apple Blossom
ns-life-flower-visitors.markdown:
In the first video clip, a bee backed out of an apple blossom with a little yellow dust on its body. In the next clip, a bee landed on another blossom. “It brought the pollen over,” Grace began. Her classmate rewound the video. “Can you tell if that's the same bee?”

Bees visit flowers for nectar and pollen. A bee brushing against an anther, the flower part that makes pollen, may get quite a dusting. When it lands again, a few grains may touch the stigma of another apple blossom. Moving pollen from an anther to a stigma is called pollination. In many flowering plants, fertilization follows before the ovules can develop into seeds. Some butterflies and flies pollinate flowers, too.

Grace drew a dotted line between her two blossoms for the path one pollen grain might have taken. She could point out a visiting bee in each clip. To see exactly what it left on the stigma, she'd love a close-up that stayed with the bee the whole way.

ns-life-fallen-leaves.title: Where Does a Fallen Leaf Go?
ns-life-fallen-leaves.markdown:
The class looked at two close-up photos of fallen leaves. In the first you could follow one leaf's edge all the way around and trace a thick vein down the middle. In the second there were holes everywhere. One leaf had fallen to pieces, its fine veins broken. Grace wondered where the rest of those leaves had gone.

Wind might have carried little pieces behind a rock. Small animals nibble and shred fallen leaves, leaving gaps. Decomposers such as fungi gradually break down the organic matter in a leaf. Some nutrients return to the soil, where roots can take them up again. As living things use this material in respiration, some of the carbon goes back into the air as carbon dioxide.

In the album Grace picked out a leaf with veins like a fish skeleton. A speckled rock beside it would help her find the same spot a few days later. For today she wrote, “A piece is missing from the edge.” As for what had visited the leaf, that hole was keeping its secret.

ns-life-grassland-count.title: Four Flybys. How Many Butterflies?
ns-life-grassland-count.markdown:
There were two patches of grass outside the school hall. Patch A had short grass. A few little flowers grew in Patch B. The teacher made up two records for Grace to read. At 9 a.m., someone watched Patch A for three minutes and saw a butterfly fly past once. At 11 a.m., someone watched Patch B for ten minutes and counted four flybys. Maybe butterflies liked the flowers in Patch B better, Grace guessed.

She laid a ruler across the first lines of the cards. The observations started two hours apart and lasted different lengths of time. Besides, two of the four flybys might have been one butterfly coming back. The cards counted passes. To work out how many butterflies had visited, she'd need a way to recognize a repeat visitor.

Grace found two matching clipboards. Next time two classmates could start and finish together, watching the same size area in each patch. They could mark each landing on a flower and count flights overhead separately. The flowers, wind, and sunlight could still change. They could jot those down, too, for clues when they compared their numbers.

She gave the Patch B card a new heading. “Four butterfly flybys in ten minutes.” That would be accurate even if the same butterfly made all four trips.

ns-g6-school-food-web.title: Who Eats What in a Patch of Grass?
ns-g6-school-food-web.markdown:
At the edge of a grassy patch, Grace saw a grasshopper jump and a bird drop down. She had just drawn a line between their two circles when her friend asked, “Did you actually see the bird eat it?” Grace held her pencil still. A clump of tall grass had hidden the bird's beak.

In class the teacher brought out feeding records from open grassy places in North America. Some grasshoppers eat plants in the grass family. The Cornell Lab of Ornithology lists grasshoppers among the animals that eastern bluebirds catch. Those records let Grace draw an example food chain. Each arrow points from the food to the animal that eats it. Matter and energy in the food can move in that direction.

**An example food chain**  Grass → plant-eating grasshopper → eastern bluebird

The records also listed beetles, caterpillars, and fruit as bluebird foods. Grace wrote “caterpillar” and “fruit” on separate slips of paper and drew an arrow from each to the bluebird. Several feeding paths could meet at a single bird. The bird would need food in the grass and might perch on a nearby branch. Places to feed and rest could both be part of its habitat.

She turned back to the schoolyard page. There was still space for an arrow beside the bird. For now she marked where it landed. To fill in its meal, she'd have to see what it carried in its beak. Looking up what that species eats in her area could give her more clues, too.

ns-life-apple-star.title: The Star Inside an Apple
ns-life-apple-star.markdown:
Grandma brought in a plate of apples. On the table were two photos. One showed an apple sliced from top to bottom, with a fine line running down below the stem. In the other, a star seemed to hide right in the middle of the flesh. It took Eli a moment to see that both photos showed apples. The second apple had been cut across its middle.

In the points of the star were little chambers. Dark apple seeds lay in some of them. The flesh went around the outside, with the core in the middle. Eli had expected one seed in every point. When he enlarged the picture, he could see two seeds in one place and what looked like an empty space in another. He left those spaces blank in his drawing.

His sister picked up the pencil to put a black dot in every point. “Wait!” Eli slid the photo over. “I can see two in this room, and that one's empty.” They colored the flesh pale yellow and put dark brown dots wherever they could see a seed. Now their star looked like the one in this particular apple.

ns-life-pea-pod.title: Peas in a Long Green Pocket
ns-life-pea-pod.markdown:
Owen watched Grandma Bennett shelling peas. A line of bumps ran along a closed pod. He counted four and guessed there must be four peas inside. Grandma opened it. He counted the peas one by one from end to end. Tucked near the point was one tiny pea he had missed from the outside.

After a pea flower fades, a part of the flower called the ovary grows into a pod. The pod is the pea plant's fruit. The peas lined up inside it are seeds. Green peas for the table are picked early. Pods left to ripen on the plant gradually dry out. Some split along the edges and release their seeds.

Grandma handed him a second pod. “I'm just guessing this time!” He counted the bumps and made his guess. Then he opened the pod and counted back from the pointed end, all the way down to the tiniest pea.

ns-life-strawberry-dots.title: The Specks on a Strawberry
ns-life-strawberry-dots.markdown:
There were strawberries on the fruit tray at the snack counter. Avery colored a patch of red and dotted it with specks. Her classmate guessed her drawing at once. “Strawberries have all these seeds on the outside,” she said. Her teacher handed her an enlarged cutaway drawing. What could she find inside one of those specks?

Most of the soft red part grows from the flower's base, the part that holds the other flower parts. Its name is the receptacle. As a strawberry grows, that base gets bigger and softer. Each little dot on its surface is actually a tiny dry fruit with a seed inside. Avery drew one dot very large. She outlined the tiny fruit, then added a smaller dot inside for the seed.

She had a riddle for her classmate. “What holds a whole crowd of little fruits on the outside?” Her classmate pointed at the whole strawberry. Avery touched the tip of her pencil to one speck. Each little ovary in the flower had grown into its own dry fruit. The swollen flower base held them all up together.

ns-life-peach-stone.title: What's Inside a Peach Pit?
ns-life-peach-stone.markdown:
After lunch the class saw a cutaway drawing of a peach. In the bright flesh sat a darker, wrinkly shape. Henry wrote “peach pit” on the board. Where should he write “seed”? He was about to label the whole hard lump.

The diagram showed three layers of the fruit wall. The outside layer is thin. Some peaches even have fuzz there. The thick middle layer is the juicy part we usually eat. The innermost layer becomes the hard shell of the pit. The seed is tucked inside that shell. When Henry enlarged the diagram, he could see the separate shape inside. He had taken the two for one.

Apple seeds lie in little chambers in the core. A peach seed has another hiding place. Henry asked his classmate to guide him through the picture. A finger moved from thin skin to juicy flesh to hard shell. A pause, then one more step inward. There was the seed.

ns-life-coconut-float.title: Can a Coconut Float Ashore?
ns-life-coconut-float.markdown:
In an island photo book, Riley spotted a brown coconut resting on a beach. It still had its thick outer covering. It looked different from the round shells he'd seen at the market. Someone in his group thought the tide might have brought it there. Could a fruit really travel by water? And where might a new palm begin to grow?

A thick layer of fibers wraps around a whole coconut fruit. The fruit can float with its seed tucked inside. If the water carries the coconut ashore, that's one part of the journey. The seed still has to be alive. It needs a place with enough moisture and the right temperature for a chance to sprout.

Riley drew a curving line on his map and labeled it “one possible route by sea.” There were footprints in the picture, too. Someone might have carried that coconut onto the beach. The book helped him see how coconuts can spread by water. A photo of one at rest left the route it had taken a mystery.

ns-life-corn-silks.title: Follow a Strand of Corn Silk
ns-life-corn-silks.markdown:
At the top of a corn plant in a summer field photo stood a spray of pale branches. Lower down, a green husk wrapped around an ear, with a tuft of fine silk sticking out. At first Theo put just one label under the photo. “Corn.” A diagram from his teacher showed where the flowers were. Now he could see two places to look on that one plant.

The male flowers at the top release pollen. Wind can carry a pollen grain onto a silk sticking out of the ear. Each strand leads to the ovary of a female flower. Inside that ovary is an ovule. When pollen lands on a silk ready to receive it, it can grow a pollen tube down the length of the silk. After fertilization, the ovary can grow into a corn kernel, and the ovule inside develops into the seed.

Theo drew from the pollen's landing spot all the way to the inside of a kernel. Beside the silk he wrote “the path.” Beside the ovary he wrote “a kernel can grow here.” In the photo the silks overlapped in a tangle. To match each ripe kernel to the strand it once had, he'd need a record of that same ear from flowering through kernel growth.

ns-life-wing-feather.title: Two Sides of a Wing Feather
ns-life-wing-feather.markdown:
The bird opened its wing. At the tip, Alice could see long feathers spreading like an open fan. She picked the outermost feather to draw. She ran a line from its base toward its tip. Now she could see that there was plenty of room on one side of the line and only a narrow strip on the other.

That line followed the shaft. Many fine branches grow out on either side of the shaft. They hook together to make the flat surface of a feather, called the vane. Some long feathers near the outer part of the wing help the bird fly. Spread out, they give the wing a wide surface. Toward the tip of a feather, its shape changes, too. A pencil can follow that curving edge slowly.

Alice covered the other feathers with a piece of paper while she carefully finished this one. She slid the paper over, and the edge of the next feather appeared. When the bird folded its wing, the row of long feathers tucked neatly one over another. The fan had closed.

ns-life-woodpecker-bark.title: What's the Woodpecker Looking For?
ns-life-woodpecker-bark.markdown:
Tap, tap. Jack heard the sound on a video. A small woodpecker gripped the bark with both feet and braced its tail against the tree trunk. It pecked once and dipped its beak toward a crack. The caption identified a North American bird called a downy woodpecker. Jack thought tapping meant it was looking for food. Would the clip show him a meal?

Downy woodpeckers eat insects on the bark and hidden underneath it. The pointed beak can chip open a spot, and a long, slender tongue can reach into a crack for food. On the video, the bird slipped around the back of the tree. The camera caught its beak approaching the crack. Its tongue and any insect stayed out of sight.

Tap! Jack wrote down the sound he'd heard and the way the beak moved toward the crack. He was still curious about that mouthful behind the tree. A woodpecker can also drum to signal to other birds, or peck to make a hole. Next time he heard tapping overhead, he would look up to see what went with the sound.

ns-life-bird-fluff.title: How Did That Bird Get So Round?
ns-life-bird-fluff.markdown:
The bird on the branch had puffed up! Violet sat inside the window, sketching it while a phone recorded. She had just finished the thin line of its back when the bird shook itself and fluffed its feathers. Its head pointed the same way and its feet stayed put. Now the curve of its belly almost touched the twig beside it.

Soft, fluffy down close to a bird's body traps a layer of air. When the outer feathers puff up, more air can stay next to the body without moving around much. Heat escapes more slowly. Something Violet couldn't see was tucked inside that extra ring of fluff.

She wound the video back. There was her thin line of a back, then a round ball, with just one shake of the feathers in between. Her classmate had thought she'd drawn two different birds that day.

ns-life-two-beaks.title: One Beak Reaches In, Another Cracks a Seed
ns-life-two-beaks.markdown:
Finn chose two close-ups from some bird guides. A long, slender beak reached into the opening of a tube-shaped flower. A short, thick beak gripped a seed on a table. He set the pictures one above the other in class. What could each bird do with that shape of beak?

When a hummingbird visits a long, tube-shaped flower, its slender beak can reach toward the nectar inside. Its tongue reaches in to feed. Some finches that eat hard seeds have short, sturdy beaks that can crush seed coats. Finn paused the video and drew a line on each picture. One line followed the hummingbird's beak into the flower. The other went to the spot where the finch gripped its seed.

The hummingbird pulled its beak out and drew its tongue back in. In the other scene, a little piece of seed coat fell from the finch's beak. Finn gave each drawing an action. The teacher only had to say “reach inside” or “crack it open,” and everyone knew which picture went with the words.

ns-life-owl-feather-sound.title: A Barn Owl Flies Over the Grass
ns-life-owl-feather-sound.markdown:
Oliver watched a video of a barn owl gliding over grass. Its Mandarin name ends in xiāo, a word for owl. He could just hear the soft beats of its wings. In a clip of a different bird the wings sounded much louder. Both sounds came out of the same speaker. Had the microphone been the same distance from each bird? He left the volume where it was and turned to a close-up of a feather.

Many owls have special edges on their flight feathers. Some have a row of fine, toothlike points along the front edge and a soft fringe along the back. These features, along with soft parts of the feather surface, help reduce the sound of flight. Oliver sketched the enlarged feather edge and used different colors for the fine teeth and the soft fringe. His search for a sound had taken him right to the wing.

He could see the teeth in the close-up and hear what the microphone had picked up in each video. The second microphone had been closer to the bird, and the background was quieter. To compare how much sound the flying birds made, he would want similar flights under similar conditions, recorded from the same distance. Watching the barn owl again, he wanted one more close look at that smooth-looking wingtip.

ns-life-finch-population.title: The Finches That Survived a Drought
ns-life-finch-population.markdown:
Noah found Daphne Major on a map of the Galápagos Islands. Scientists studying ground finches there had lived through a severe drought. When they measured the survivors, those birds had thicker beaks on average than the group before the drought. Noah studied two model beaks, one thick and one thin. Could cracking hard seeds somehow have made an individual bird's beak grow thicker?

Even before the drought, birds of the same species had beaks of different thicknesses. Many of the seeds left during that drought were large and hard. Larger birds with larger beaks could crack those seeds more easily. A greater share of those birds survived. The mix of birds in the group had changed between the scientists' two sets of measurements.

Noah made up numbers for a card game. He started with ten birds, five with thick beaks and five with thin ones. He kept four thick-beaked birds and one thin-beaked bird and spread them out. Before, half the birds had thick beaks. Now four out of five did. Every beak on the cards looked exactly as he'd drawn it. His cards could explain a change in the average. For the actual numbers on the island, he'd need the scientists' records.

ns-life-forest-roof.title: A Roof of Leaves
ns-life-forest-roof.markdown:
Zoe stood at the entrance to a forest trail. At first she saw a row of trunks. Higher up, big leaves and little leaves crowded the branches. In places they met overhead like a roof. She tilted the phone up to take a picture. The treetops filled the top of the frame, leaving only a short stretch of gray trail below.

Under the tall trees, Zoe found plants that reached her waist and others that hugged the ground. On her picture she drew three lines to mark the treetops, the low plants, and the forest floor. Leaves and branches grow at different heights. Up high, the leafy canopy catches some of the sunlight. Plants that grow well in dimmer light can live underneath it.

Her brother hunted for the highest treetop in the picture, walking his finger up a thick trunk. Zoe had him look down, too. Low leaves grew right beside the trail. With one of them looking up and the other looking down, they finally took in the whole little patch of forest.

ns-life-moss-mat.title: A Green Blanket on a Rock
ns-life-moss-mat.markdown:
In a forest photo, a thin patch of green lay over one side of a rock like the corner of a little blanket. “Did the rock grow leaves?” Emma asked her teacher. The teacher enlarged the picture. The blanket was made up of tiny tips packed close together. Some curled up a little at the edges.

This is what moss looks like when many little plants grow together. Mosses can grow on soil, on bark, or on the surface of a rock. They generally stay low. Even a thin patch can cover quite a bit of stone. Some mosses like damp places. Shade and small cracks in a rock can help moisture linger, so a damp forest is a good place to spot them.

Emma drew the rock in two colors, gray underneath for the stone and green on top for the moss. A few days later she recognized a patch of green like it in a photo of tree bark. She gave her first picture a name. “A Little Green Blanket With a Rock to Rest On.”

ns-life-standing-dead-tree.title: A Bird Slips Inside a Tree
ns-life-standing-dead-tree.markdown:
The tree in the photo had lost its leaves long ago, and patches of bark had fallen away. Ruby's eye went straight to a round hole partway up the trunk. She circled it, then found another higher up. The two openings were different sizes. Nobody poked a head out in that first photo.

A dead tree that stays standing can offer room to all sorts of forest animals. Some birds peck holes where the wood has softened. Later, another animal may use an old hole for shelter, to get out of bad weather, or to make a nest. Even after the leaves are gone, the branches make perches and the holes make places to tuck inside.

Later photos of the same opening showed a bird. In the first, its feet rested on the rim. In the next, it slipped inside. Ruby put the two pictures together and told what she had seen happen. Would the bird spend the night there? Might it build a nest or sit on eggs? The camera had only seen as far as the entrance. That's where she ended her story for the day.

ns-life-stream-wood.title: A Pool for Young Salmon
ns-life-stream-wood.markdown:
In a picture from NOAA, the U.S. ocean and weather agency, young salmon swam in a shallow pool. Trees and shrubs cast shade from the bank, and a log lay across the water. Leo had looked only for fish at first. When he read about the calm pool in the caption, he went back to find the log.

Young salmon live in some streams in the northwestern United States. Shade from trees keeps some sunlight off the water. Large pieces of fallen wood change how the current moves nearby. In some spots they help form pools where the current flows more gently. Young fish can rest there and may find cover beside the wood.

Leo marked a slow spot in his drawing with a short arrow. His teacher asked what the length of the arrow meant. He laughed. All he meant was, “A fish could rest here.” To say how far the water actually traveled in a second, he'd need a current measurement. If the water level rose or fell, the flow beside that very same log could change.

ns-life-nurse-log.title: A Tree Grows on a Fallen Log
ns-life-nurse-log.markdown:
In a nature film, the camera passed over a fallen tree. Several seedlings grew in a row on its rough, damp bark. Charlie paused the film and drew the first seedling, right where it stood on the trunk. Another photo showed tall trees with roots raised high off the ground. There was a gap under the roots, as if they had grown across a little bridge.

In the temperate rain forest of Olympic National Park in the United States, fallen wood slowly decomposes. A seed that lands on a log can sometimes sprout and grow there. The wood holds moisture and gives a seedling a start a little above the forest floor. As the young tree grows, its roots can reach the ground on either side. Many years later, when the old log has crumbled away, the roots may still stand like a raised frame.

Charlie pictured three moments over the years. First, young roots rested on a log. Later, the roots reached the soil. At last the old wood had decayed, leaving a space underneath. Together the pictures told a story that could happen in a forest. To see how tall those particular seedlings in the film grew, he'd have to find their log again.

ns-life-canopy-gap.title: A Skylight in the Forest
ns-life-canopy-gap.markdown:
Two overhead photos at the science museum showed the same forest. The winding path appeared in both. In the second photo, a large patch of high treetops was gone to the left of the bend. Now you could see low plants in the opening. Oscar started to write, “The young trees must be growing faster.” His friend wanted a picture from down on the forest floor.

Sunlight that the canopy once blocked can now reach seedlings in the opening. Some kinds of trees may grow faster while that light lasts. But the middle of the gap and its edges get sun at different times. Moisture and the plants growing nearby also affect whether a seedling can survive there.

Oscar marked three places on his trail map. One was under the canopy, one at the edge of the gap, and one in the middle. To find where more seedlings grew, he could count them in patches of equal size. To find how fast one grew, he'd have to recognize that same seedling and measure its growth over time. He changed the caption on his second photo to a question. “There's an opening in the treetops. What's happening to the seedlings below?”

ns-life-fish-fins.title: Watch a Fish Make a Turn
ns-life-fish-fins.markdown:
A fish swam from left to right past the aquarium window. Emma followed its path with a finger near the glass. Its tail swung from side to side. Little flaps on either side of its belly were moving, too. It slowed down beside a rock, and something about the way it moved changed.

The parts that help a fish swim and adjust its position are its fins. When many fish swim fast, the back of the body and the tail fin swing from side to side, helping drive them forward. Fins along the sides can help, too. In some fish, their movements change as the fish turns or slows. Fish have different ways of swimming. When you're drawing one, take a look at which parts are moving.

Emma drew her fish twice. First it was to the left of the rock, then to the right. In the second picture its tail happened to be swinging the other way. She showed her little brother. Back and forth went the tail, and around the rock went the fish, leaving an invisible curve behind it.

ns-life-turtle-surface.title: A Sea Turtle Comes Up for Air
ns-life-turtle-surface.markdown:
In the slow-motion film, a green sea turtle paddled past some seagrass and swam up at a slant. Charlie drew its path. At first his line ran underwater. At the end it curved up to the surface. The turtle's mouth was still at the waterline, but its two little nostrils were out in the air.

Green sea turtles live in the ocean and use their front flippers like paddles. They have lungs. Once a turtle brings its nostrils above the surface, it can breathe air. After swimming underwater for a while, it will come up to breathe again. In the pictures, sometimes only part of the head showed. The rest of the turtle was still underwater.

Charlie asked his little sister to swim the path on the paper with her finger. She started below the blue line. At the top she tapped the nostrils in the drawing, then swam back down to the seagrass. “It swims down here,” she said, “and gets its air up there.”

ns-life-seastar-tube-feet.title: A Sea Star's Tube Feet
ns-life-seastar-tube-feet.markdown:
Tyler watched an aquarium video. A sea star rested beside a fine line on the glass. A little later, several of its arms had crossed the line. In a close-up he could see the side of the sea star pressed against the tank glass. Rows of little bumps ran along its arms.

Those bumps are tube feet. A tube foot can reach out, attach, and pull back in. A system of water-filled tubes inside the sea star helps its tube feet extend and retract. Many feet working together let the animal creep slowly along a surface. With its underside against the glass, you can see some of those feet reach ahead and attach.

Tyler saved two clips for his classmate. In the close-up a tube foot reached out, stuck to the glass, and pulled back. In the wide shot, the line on the glass stayed still, giving them something to compare the sea star's position against. To tell how many centimeters it had moved, they'd also need to know what a length in the picture measured in the tank. Tyler gave the ending six words. “It moved right across that line.”

ns-life-octopus-camouflage.title: The Octopus Beside the Rock
ns-life-octopus-camouflage.markdown:
In the aquarium film, dark spots dotted a corner of a pale gray rock. Liam searched the scene for a long time before he spotted a round eye. An arm lifted away from the rock and out swam a whole octopus. Its colors and pattern of light and dark looked different now.

A giant Pacific octopus can change color. It can also raise little bumps in its skin, making it look rougher and more like the rocks around it. Changes like these sometimes make the animal hard to pick out against the sea floor. Liam drew the same spot twice. In one drawing he gave the octopus spots close to the color of the rock. In the other, its spots stood out more.

He showed his classmate the first frame of the film. That octopus was hard to find beside the gray rock. Then one arm stirred. “There's the eye!” his classmate called. They went back a frame and traced the faint outline from the eye. To tell how well its colors matched its surroundings, they needed to leave the rock in the picture, too.

ns-life-dolphin-echo.title: How Does a Dolphin Hear a Fish Ahead?
ns-life-dolphin-echo.markdown:
One recording at the exhibit sounded like a few quick knocks. The other was more like a long whistle. Isaac read that dolphins can make many sounds. One way they find prey is called echolocation. The guide asked him to imagine a school of fish. How could a dolphin find them by sound?

A bottlenose dolphin can send out a series of short clicks. Sound travels through the water. When it reaches a fish, some sound bounces back. The returning echo helps the dolphin tell roughly how far away an object is and in which direction. Echoes are especially handy in dim water. Sometimes dolphins also listen quietly for sounds the prey itself makes.

Isaac traced the path on the exhibit panel, from dolphin to fish and from fish back to dolphin. If the fish swam farther away, both parts of the trip would get longer. In the same water the dolphin would have a longer wait for its echo. His sister tapped a finger on the table. “How long would it take to hear this one come back?”

ns-life-coral-partners.title: The Little Partners Inside a Coral
ns-life-coral-partners.markdown:
Penny opened a close-up photo of coral. A ring of tentacles reached into the water like flower petals, which was why she'd put it in her plant album. The exhibit label said the coral polyps were animals. She took a closer look at the opening in the middle. A polyp uses its tentacles to take small bits of food from the water. Many reef-building corals have lots of polyps living joined together.

Many reef-building coral polyps have tiny algae living inside them. The algae use light to make food, and some of what they make goes to the coral. The coral gives the algae a place to live and supplies materials they can use. That partnership helps explain why many reef-building corals do well in shallow, sunlit seas. Other corals live deeper. Conditions there are different, and so may be the way they get food.

Penny moved the photo to her animal album. Beside it she drew one polyp enlarged, with tentacles around its mouth and tiny dots inside for the algae. “Could you actually see those dots in the photo?” her family asked. She pointed to her note in the corner. A diagram had shown her where the algae go. What she could see in the photo were the tentacles reaching out into the water.

ns-life-skin-touch.title: Two Scraps of Cloth, Two Different Feels
ns-life-skin-touch.markdown:
Grandma wanted to make a little cushion for a chair. Two pieces of cloth lay on the table, nearly the same color. Jordan ran a finger gently over one, then the other. His finger slid smoothly across the first. On the second he could feel raised lines, like little ridges with furrows in between.

Inside the skin of a fingertip are structures that sense touch. As a fingertip passes over a ridge, the pressure on the skin changes. Signals travel along nerves to the brain. That helps you tell where you were touched and what a surface feels like. With enough light, your eyes can help you find the pattern in the cloth, too.

Jordan decided to use both fabrics. The smooth piece went in the middle of the cushion, the ridged piece around the rim. Grandma slid her fingertip from the center until she felt those little ridges. She had found the border. Jordan had made a pattern you could read with your hand.

ns-life-ear-sound.title: Follow the Sound of a Bell
ns-life-ear-sound.markdown:
The school bell rang. Nora looked at her ear in a mirror. She could see its curved outer rim and sketch its outline with a pencil. How had the ringing traveled inside? At the opening of the ear, her pencil stopped.

The part you can see is the outer flap of the ear. It guides sound into the ear canal. Sound waves travel down the canal and set a thin membrane called the eardrum vibrating. The eardrum passes the vibrations to tiny bones deeper inside, and from there the vibrations reach the inner ear. The inner ear turns them into signals. The hearing nerve carries those signals to the brain. That's how Nora heard the ring.

In her picture book she followed the canal all the way to the eardrum. On her drawing, she added a little drumhead at the end of the line. The next time the bell rang, her pencil tip traveled that path again. At the eardrum she gave the page a tiny tap.

ns-life-taste-aroma.title: The Sweetness and Scent of an Apple
ns-life-taste-aroma.markdown:
There were slices of apple on the table and a ripe pear on the windowsill. Noah noticed a fruity scent as he came into the room. When he ate a piece of apple, he tasted a little sweetness and a little sourness. He could also describe a whole flavor as “apple” or “pear.” Where were all those clues coming from?

Taste buds on the tongue and in other parts of the mouth help us sense basic tastes, including sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and savory, also called umami. Chewing also releases aromas. At the back of your mouth there's a passage to your nose. Aromas from the food can reach the nose that way. Nerves carry signals about smell and taste to the brain. Together they shape the flavor of a bite.

Noah gave his apple two descriptions. His tongue picked up sweet with a little sour. His nose picked up the scent of ripe apple. His sister took a bite and added a third. “There's a crunch, too!” The scent, the sweetness, and that crisp crunch all belonged to the bite they'd just taken.

ns-life-inner-ear-balance.title: When the Bus Turns a Corner
ns-life-inner-ear-balance.markdown:
The bus rounded a corner, and Chloe felt herself lean a little to one side in her seat. A tree that had been straight ahead appeared beside her window. At home she drew the turn and added two clues. One came from the changing view outside. The other was what she'd felt in her seat.

Your eyes can see the scenery move past. Part of the inner ear senses movements of the head, too. The semicircular canals are curved tubes. When you turn your head, fluid inside them shifts relative to the tubes. This bends sensing structures, which signal the change to your brain. Other structures in the inner ear help you sense changes in speed along a straight line and the tilt of your head. Your brain combines these signals with information from your eyes and other parts of your body to help you balance.

Chloe put an eye symbol beside the tree in her picture. Beside her head she drew a curved line to remind herself that her inner ear had sent a message about the turn. Even with a billboard blocking her view, she could feel her body press against one side of the seat. Her brain had several places to look for news of that corner.

ns-life-limb-position.title: How Do You Know Where Your Hands Are?
ns-life-limb-position.markdown:
At rehearsal the teacher asked everyone to look at the screen and put both hands behind their backs. Caleb could still tell roughly whether his hands were together or apart. His fingers brushing his clothes gave him one kind of feeling. Knowing that his elbow was bent and his arm was behind him seemed like a different message.

Muscles and tendons contain structures that sense changes. When an arm lifts or bends, those structures send signals about changes in position and tension. Your brain gathers clues from many parts of the body. You get a sense of where your arms and legs are. It's called proprioception. It helps you walk and adjust a step while your eyes are looking ahead.

Caleb moved his hands a little farther apart until his fingers cleared his clothes. He still had a sense of how far he'd moved his arms. Touching the cloth had given him a clue through his skin. His muscles and tendons kept sending their own signals. At the next rehearsal he could keep his eyes on the conductor.

ns-life-knee-reflex.title: Why Does a Knee Give a Little Kick?
ns-life-knee-reflex.markdown:
In a health-class video, a doctor asked a patient to relax one leg, then tapped just below the knee with a little reflex hammer. The patient was still looking at a chart on the wall when the lower leg swung forward. Felix replayed the clip. Very little time passed between the tap and the kick.

That tap briefly stretches the muscle at the front of the thigh. Structures in the muscle sense the stretch. A signal travels along a sensory nerve to the spinal cord. Connections there can produce a quick response. A signal goes back along a motor nerve to the muscle at the front of the thigh. The muscle contracts and the lower leg swings. An automatic response like this is called a reflex.

Felix paused the clip just as the lower leg began to rise. Slow motion showed which movement happened first. To follow the nerve signals under the skin, he needed the body diagram. “Message to the spinal cord, instruction back to the muscle,” he read. If a doctor checked that reflex at his next checkup, he'd know what the doctor was looking for.

ns-life-winter-tree.title: Which Tree Still Has Leaves in Winter?
ns-life-winter-tree.markdown:
On the way home one winter day, Grandpa took a picture of two trees for Owen. He could see a whole patch of sky through the branches on the left. The tree on the right looked thick with long, needlelike leaves. Snow rested on both trees, but Owen could tell at a glance which one still looked green.

Where winters are cold, many deciduous trees shed their leaves in fall. Buds stay on their branches. Some pines still carry plenty of needles in winter. Old needles fall, too, while other needles keep growing. From a distance the treetop stays green. Owen leaned closer to the photo and picked out a few fine needles at the end of a branch.

On his winter page he left a big patch of sky around the branches on the left and filled in the treetop on the right. Grandpa helped him write the date. In spring they'd take this same path past the same two trees to see what showed up first on their branches.

ns-life-spring-tree-bud.title: The Little Point at the Tip of a Twig
ns-life-spring-tree-bud.markdown:
It was March. Nina found last month's photo of the branch outside the window. At the very end of the bare twig was a little brown point. Nina asked Dad to take another photo from the same window. Now the point had a bit of green on it. A fork in the branch helped her line up the same spot in both pictures.

Buds can grow at the tip of a twig or along its sides. Some hold leaves that will unfold. Other buds can produce flowers. As many trees begin growing new leaves in spring, the buds swell. The little scales on the outside part, revealing the new growth. If the photo shows just a speck of green, a few more pictures over time can show what that particular bud produces.

A little later, small leaves did open from the green-tipped bud. Nina put the third photo last and tapped the same fork in each picture. Even with new leaves on the twig, that bend in the branch still marked the spot where she'd seen the little brown point.

ns-life-first-flower-record.title: Which Day Did the Flowers Open?
ns-life-first-flower-record.markdown:
On Monday, Grandma photographed a stem in the flower bed. It held only buds. On Friday, Evelyn photographed the same stem. This time two flowers were open. She had just written “flowers opened Friday” on the calendar when Grandma moved the pencil to the squares in between. “What about these days?”

Nobody had gone to look on Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday. The flowers might have opened today. They might already have been open on Wednesday. On Monday's square Evelyn wrote, “Looked. Only buds.” On Friday's she wrote, “First time I saw open flowers.” She put a little question mark in each of the three squares between.

Her classmate read Wednesday's square as “no open flowers.” Evelyn rested her pencil on the question mark. “If I'd gone that day and seen every bud closed, I'd have written ‘none open.’ The question mark means I never went to look.” She handed him the calendar. Which days could he actually match to photographs?

ns-life-spring-pool.title: The Little Pool That Was Dry by September
ns-life-spring-pool.markdown:
In September's woodland photo, a flat patch beside the trail was covered with leaves. In the next picture Jamie recognized the same trees, but now a shallow pool filled that low spot. The album showed the newest photos first. When he checked the dates, he found that the watery scene came from spring.

In some hollows in the woods, rain or melting snow gathers in a pool. When the weather turns drier, the water gradually disappears. These seasonal pools give certain frogs and salamanders a place to lay eggs. The eggs and the newly hatched young can develop in water. How long the pool lasts matters to them.

Jamie put the spring photo first and the September photo second. He kept the tree beside the trail in both pictures. Now it was easy to find the place where the waterline had been. When would that patch fill with water next year? The album still had to wait for next year's rain and snow.

ns-life-two-year-phenology.title: Did the Flowers Really Open Earlier This Year?
ns-life-two-year-phenology.markdown:
Last year's photo from April 6 showed open flowers. This year's, from April 3, showed open flowers, too. “Three days earlier?” Nancy was about to write it down when she went looking for last year's page for April 3. It was blank.

She used a strip of paper for each year. A solid dot meant she'd seen an open flower. An empty circle meant she'd seen only buds. With only the April 6 photo, last year's flowers might have opened long before that date. Suppose she found a clear photo from April 5 showing that all the buds were still closed. Then she could narrow the first opening down to the interval between those two observations.

Nancy added one word beside each date. “Seen.” To compare the years, she'd watch the same kind of plant in the same flower bed, agree on how far the petals must unfold to count as open, and go back on several days in a row. If she looked and all the buds were closed, she could write “none open.” If the light was too dim to tell, a question mark would do. Someone else could read a calendar like that, too.

ns-life-overlap-calendar.title: Which Flowering Days Also Had Insects?
ns-life-overlap-calendar.markdown:
Grace's teacher made up two sets of dates, counting the first and last day of each stretch. In the first set, flowers were open April 4 through 10. Insects that visit flowers were seen every day from April 7 through 12. In the second set, the flowers were open April 1 through 6. The insects appeared on the same days as before. When did the flowers and the insects have a chance to meet?

Grace colored the dates with two pencils. In the first set, four squares had both colors. April 7, 8, 9, and 10. In the second, the two colors never overlapped. If flowers bloom or insects become active at different times of year, they can have more days in common, or fewer. Many flowers offer nectar or pollen, and some visiting insects help pollinate them. That's why scientists watch both sets of dates.

Grace covered everything before April 7 and after April 10 with her fingers. Four shared squares still showed in the first set, and none in the second. A shared square meant that both had been seen that day. To tell whether a particular insect had pollinated a particular flower, she would need to see where it landed and whether it brought pollen to the stigma. Her little calendar window held a good question. She'd have to look among the flowers for the answer.

ns-g1-object-features.title: Three Spoons, Two Baskets
ns-g1-object-features.markdown:
Tessa helped put the spoons away. One large wooden spoon, one large steel spoon, one small steel spoon. There were two baskets on the table. She stacked the shiny steel spoons in one. The wooden spoon had the other basket all to itself.

“Why do the big one and the little one go together?” her brother asked. Tessa let him feel the wooden spoon. Then she showed him the labels for the other two. Both were made of stainless steel. This time she'd sorted by material. Wood and stainless steel were the materials. All three things made from them were spoons.

She laid the spoons out again and tried sorting by size. The bowls of the big wooden spoon and the big steel spoon were about the same size. The little steel spoon's bowl was smaller. This time the big spoons went together. One steel spoon had found a new partner because Tessa had picked a different way to sort.

Her brother came back with a pair of wooden chopsticks. Before Tessa could reach for them, he set them next to the wooden spoon. “I know this game! We're sorting by what they're made of.” A spoon could change partners, and chopsticks could find a partner, too. It helped to know the rule before clearing the table.

ns-g2-paper-plastic.title: Which Roof Will Keep the Rain Out?
ns-g2-paper-plastic.markdown:
A little paper house needed a roof. On the table lay a piece of ordinary drawing paper and a smooth sheet of plastic from a clean folder. Both were big enough to cover the house. Which would keep out a short shower?

The builder tried out both roof materials. The pieces lay flat. A drop of clean water landed on the paper and an equal-sized drop landed on the plastic. After the same wait, the water on the paper had spread, and the paper looked darker. There was water on the plastic, too. When that drop was wiped away, there was no wet mark underneath.

The shape of a drop is one clue. Whether water has soaked into the material is another. The drawing paper had gotten damp and would soak up some rain. The builder chose the unbroken plastic sheet for the roof and overlapped two pieces where they met. Rain takes only a little gap to find its way into a house.

A piece of waxed paper was still on the table. The builder picked it up and decided to try a drop first. It was paper, too, with a different surface to investigate.

ns-mm-corrugated-board.title: Little Waves in a Cardboard Box
ns-mm-corrugated-board.markdown:
Open a shipping box and look at an edge where the cardboard already shows. A flat sheet of paper runs along the top. Another runs along the bottom. Between them, a third sheet bends up, down, up, down, like a row of little waves. This kind of board is called corrugated cardboard.

At the opening of a cookie box you may find an edge made from a single flat piece of paperboard. In the shipping box, the waves hold the two flat faces apart. They are glued to the faces where they touch. A modest amount of paper makes a thick wall that resists bending. Flat board has a job of its own in the cookie box. A little folded tab can hold the top closed.

Try sketching each edge from the side. Which drawing needs spaces inside? Which needs just a thick line? How strong a full box will be depends on the board's thickness, the paper it's made from, and the direction of the push. The little waves at the opening give you a look at how the walls are built.

ns-mm-window-material.title: Which Window Lets You Read the Words?
ns-mm-window-material.markdown:
A card in the classroom had big letters on it. Through a clear, colorless sheet of plastic, each letter had a sharp outline. Behind a milky plastic sheet, the letters looked fuzzy even though light still came through. A thick piece of cardboard hid the whole card.

The clear sample is transparent. Light passes through and you can see details on the other side. The milky sample is translucent. It lets light through, but scatters the light in different directions, blurring letters held a little way behind it. The opaque cardboard blocks visible light. The side facing you can look bright on all three samples because light is shining on that side. The test is whether light from behind a sample reaches you and how sharply you see the letters.

Ivy had two windows to put in her model house. From the study she wanted to see a little tree outside. Clear plastic would do. In the bathroom she wanted daylight, with the towels on the shelf hard to see from outside. She chose the milky sheet. She held the same letter card the same distance behind each window. Words through one, a patch of light through the other. Her house had its windows.

ns-mm-plastic-family.title: A Floppy Bag and a Stiff Lunch Box
ns-mm-plastic-family.markdown:
Jacob folded a bag into his pocket and set his lunch box on the table. The bag flopped over. The box stood up by itself. Both were plastic. How could one fold so easily while the other held its shape?

There were two clues to follow. The first was the material. Many plastics are made of molecules shaped like long chains. The kinds of chains, the way they're arranged, and the other ingredients mixed in all affect the material. Sheets made from different plastics may bend differently.

The second clue was thickness and shape. Picture two flat pieces of the same plastic, equally long and wide, one thin and one thick. Give them a gentle bend. The thick one is generally harder to bend. A lunch box also has sides and corners that help hold it up. With just the box and the bag, several things change together. It's hard to tell which change matters most.

Jacob thought of two better pieces for a comparison. He would look for two flat strips of the same plastic with matching lengths and widths and different thicknesses. He'd support them in the same places and bend them gently with the same force. Even with the bag and lunch box put away, he could investigate just what thickness does.

ns-mm-milk-carton.title: What's a Milk Carton Made Of?
ns-mm-milk-carton.markdown:
A spotted cow was printed on Tessa's milk carton. The carton looked a lot like a cardboard cookie box. Ordinary cardboard gets soggy in milk.
