Why hadn't the milk softened all four of that little cow's legs? In the maker's cutaway drawing of this carton, Tessa found a thin line right against the milk.

The drawing showed several materials. A thicker layer of paperboard supported the sides. Thin layers of plastic helped hold the liquid in and seal the seams. Some cartons designed to keep milk at room temperature before opening also have a thin layer of aluminum to block light and keep oxygen out. Joined together, the layers make a container that holds its shape.

A peaked carton in the refrigerator and a shelf-stable carton can both look like paper from the outside. Their layers may differ. Some have no aluminum layer. For a particular carton, its packaging information or the maker's diagram can tell you more. When you read the storage instructions, pay attention to what applies before opening and what applies afterward.

Tessa drew one corner in close-up. The thin inner line helped keep the water in. The thick middle layer held the spotted cow on its feet. Whether to draw any aluminum depended on that model of carton. Next time at the shelf, she knew which words she wanted to find. “After opening.”

ns-g4-air-cup.title: What's in an Upside-Down Cup?
ns-g4-air-cup.markdown:
Oscar held an empty plastic cup upside down. He waited. No water dripped out. Dad said there was still something inside. It made no sound and Oscar couldn't see it. How could they tell it was there? They brought over a shallow basin of water and turned the clear cup upside down above it.

Dad lowered the cup straight into the water, opening first. Looking from the side, Oscar saw that the water level inside the cup was lower than the level in the basin. A large space above it stayed dry. The cup had been full of air. Trapped for the moment under the water, the air took up space that the water couldn't fill.

Dad tilted the cup a little, keeping the rim underwater. A string of bubbles rose from the higher edge. The gas in those bubbles had been air inside the cup. As air got out, water went in and the level inside rose. Same cup, same basin of water. Dad had changed the angle of the opening.

Back at the table, Oscar tipped out the water. Now he knew what would take its place. Air all around the cup came in through the opening. The cup looked just as “empty” as when he started.

ns-mm-liquid-shape.title: A Cup of Water Moves House
ns-mm-liquid-shape.markdown:
Grace poured water from a narrow cup into a wide container. It had stood tall in the cup. In the container it made a shallow layer. Was there less water, or had its shape changed?

On a tray, set two clear plastic containers, one narrow at the top and one with a wide base. Check the marks on the narrow cup and remember which mark the water reaches. Pour slowly into the wide container and set it level. The water spreads across the bottom and takes the shape of the sides. Once the water settles, its top surface is almost flat.

Grace poured it back into the narrow cup. With no spills, it came close to the original mark. A few droplets still clung to the wide container. She drew the tall column and the shallow layer on the same page and wrote the same amount beside them. Different measuring cups can measure the same amount, too, as long as their markings are accurate and use the same units. Pouring back into the first cup was a handy check.

She thought of her ice tray. Move a cube of ice from the narrow cup to the wide container before it melts, and its four corners stay right where they belong. Liquid water spreads to fit its new home. Ice brings its shape along.

ns-g3-ice-water.title: What's Left When an Ice Cube Melts?
ns-g3-ice-water.markdown:
On a tray sits a shallow, nonslip plastic dish. A fresh ice cube has corners that are easy to see. Wait at the table and you may notice a ring of water against the bottom of the cube. The cube shrinks and the puddle grows. When the last piece melts, only liquid water is left in the dish.

Morgan meant to draw just a square of ice in her first frame. By the time she picked up her pencil, its edges were already wet. She drew the thin line of water. After a while the dish held a much smaller lump of ice with water all the way around it. That was her second frame.

Ice is water in its solid state. The water that flows in the dish is liquid. When ice takes in heat from its surroundings at the right temperature, it can turn into liquid water. This change is called melting. When solid and liquid are in the dish together, part of the ice has melted and part is still solid.

That evening, what went into the ice tray was liquid water. In the freezer it gave off heat. When it got cold enough to form ice, it changed from liquid to solid. That's freezing. Morgan said the two words to Dad. “Melting” brought back that thin wet line in the dish. “Freezing” brought to mind a little cube she could lift out.

ns-mm-evaporation.title: Where Did the Wet Ring Go?
ns-mm-evaporation.markdown:
A cup left a wet ring on a smooth tray. Wyatt turned to fetch a cloth. When he looked back, only half the ring was left. The tray didn't soak up water. No trail of water ran off onto the table. Where had the missing half gone?

On the same smooth, nonabsorbent tray, put two small, equal amounts of water. Gently spread one out with a clean plastic spoon and leave the other as a bead. Leave both in the same place at the same room temperature and check every few minutes. The spread-out water and the bead expose different amounts of surface to the air. The spread-out patch often disappears first. If they disappear at about the same time, record the times you actually see.

When liquid water changes to gas at its surface, that's evaporation. The invisible water vapor mixes with the air. Water can evaporate at room temperature. How much surface is exposed, how humid the air is, and whether the air is moving can all affect the drying time. In a picture of boiling water, vapor bubbles form inside the liquid, too. The bead on the table quietly shrinks from the surface.

A bead's bright glint can also disappear quickly on absorbent paper. Lift the sheet and there's a wet patch underneath. Water first works into spaces between the paper fibers and can evaporate later. Wyatt put the cloth away. When he checked the tray again, the last shiny half circle had gone.

ns-g5-cold-cup.title: Where Do the Drops on a Cold Cup Come From?
ns-g5-cold-cup.markdown:
Jordan took a cup of cold water out of the refrigerator and wiped its sides dry. She'd read just a little of her book when she touched the cup and felt water again. She watched a drop slide down the outside. If it was leaking from the inside, what would happen with a cup of room-temperature water?

She and Dad chose two matching clear plastic cups with lids. They put chilled water in one and the same amount of room-temperature water in the other. They closed the lids, dried both cups on the outside, and set them together on the same tray. After two or three minutes, they looked from the side. On this try, tiny drops covered the outside of the cold cup where the water lay against the wall. The other cup still felt dry.

Invisible water vapor was already in the surrounding air. The cold cup cooled the air right beside it. When the cup wall got colder than the dew point of that air, some water vapor turned to liquid droplets on the wall. This is condensation. The little drops grew. Two met and slid down the cup together.

Jordan was still thinking about a leak. They put a lid on an empty cup that was dry inside and out. They chilled it, took it out, wiped the outside, and set it back on the tray. If drops formed outside this cup, there was no liquid water inside to leak. Here was a way water could reach a cup from the air. Very dry air or a cup that warms up quickly may leave few drops to see. Jordan left a space in her notes for whatever she actually found.

On the way to school the next morning, bright drops hung from blades of grass. Grass can cool during the night, and water vapor from the air can condense on it as dew. Last night's cold cup had shown her one way a drop could arrive on a leaf.

ns-mm-fog-and-dew.title: Dew on the Grass, Fog by the Hills
ns-mm-fog-and-dew.markdown:
Early in the morning your shoe brushes the grass and picks up a drop of dew. At the foot of a hill, a bank of fog still hangs in the air. One drop rests on a leaf. Countless others float. Where did the water come from? Air contains invisible water vapor. When damp air cools enough, some of its vapor can condense into little liquid droplets.

Dew clings to the grass. On a suitable night a blade cools, chilling the thin layer of damp air next to it, and drops can grow on its surface. Fog also contains tiny droplets. They hang in the air close to the ground. Together they scatter light, making the foot of the hill look white. Both fog near the ground and clouds higher up can contain liquid droplets. Clouds can also contain ice crystals. To fall as rain, cloud droplets must grow larger.

Think back to the water on a cold cup. A cup wall and a blade of grass both give drops something to cling to. Fog droplets are spread through the air. A cup on a table shows one step, condensation. Out in the weather, water can also evaporate, travel with the air, form clouds or fog, and eventually return to the ground as precipitation.

A weather notebook has two sets of imaginary readings. Both places start at 18°C. At A the dew point is 16°C. At B it's 10°C. The dew point is the temperature at which air reaches saturation as it cools, assuming its water vapor stays the same and its pressure changes very little. Cool both places to 15°C. A has passed its original dew point, so condensation is possible. B is still 5°C above its original dew point. To know whether fog will form by the hill, you'd need to consider the air close to the ground and tiny particles there, too. One look at a white hillside won't give you those two sets of readings.

ns-mm-salt-dissolves.title: Where Did the Salt Grains Go?
ns-mm-salt-dissolves.markdown:
One last grain of salt glinted at the bottom of the cup on the left. Its tiny white outline disappeared. Jane put down her spoon. The cup on the right had held plain water all along. Now she could read the words on the wall through either cup. How would she remember which one held salt?

When salt dissolves, the particles that make up the salt leave the crystal and spread through the water. They're too small to see. Once the salt is evenly distributed, the mixture is salt water. A mixture with the same composition throughout, like this salt water, is called a solution. The substance the salt dissolves in is the solvent. Here, that's water.

Picture a pinch of clean, coarse sand. Stir it into water and the grains can swirl about for a bit. Give them time and most gather at the bottom. The grains of sand are still easy to spot. The particles of dissolved salt are far too small to pick out by eye.

Jane had stuck a label on the left cup before she added the salt. Even if someone turned the pair of cups halfway around, the label would travel with its cup. Her two lines of notes began with “I put salt in this cup.” They ended with “I can no longer see white grains at the bottom.”

ns-mm-saturation.title: How Much Sugar Can Water Dissolve?
ns-mm-saturation.markdown:
Sophie put a small spoonful of sugar into a cup of water and stirred gently. Soon she couldn't find a grain at the bottom. She wondered what would happen if she kept adding sugar to the same cup. Could it go on dissolving forever?

For a given amount of water at a fixed temperature, there's a limit to how much sugar it can dissolve. Imagine adding it a spoonful at a time and waiting for each spoonful to dissolve. Eventually some of the added sugar stays at the bottom. When the limit is reached, the liquid is a saturated sugar solution. The sugar already dissolved in it and the grains you can still see can be there together.

Sophie made up two records. Cups A and B each held 100 milliliters of water at the same temperature. Each got the same spoonful of sugar, with grains of about the same size. Cup A was stirred gently. Its grains disappeared in 20 seconds. Cup B sat still. Its grains took 60 seconds to disappear. In these records the sugar dissolved faster in A. Both cups eventually dissolved this spoonful. How close either one had come to its limit was still an open question.

Now picture Cup C. A white layer covers the bottom just after the sugar goes in. To find out whether the solution is saturated, it needs time to mix thoroughly and settle at the same temperature. Are grains still there then? Sophie drew a clock beside the cup and left a space for each view, one just after adding the sugar and one after waiting long enough.

ns-mm-oil-water.title: The Oil Drops Float Back Up
ns-mm-oil-water.markdown:
A spoonful of cooking oil covers part of the water in a clear cup. A gentle swirl with a spoon breaks the oil into little drops. Some spin down into the water. After a while, the cup has two layers again, one on top and one underneath.

Most everyday cooking oils and water hardly dissolve in each other. Stirring scatters the oil as droplets. When the cup stands still, small drops can meet and form larger ones. Common cooking oils weigh less than the same volume of water. Gradually the oil gathers on top and the water stays below. You can show what you see by drawing the boundary between the layers.

Compare a freshly stirred cup of clear salt water. After the same wait, it usually still looks like one even layer. Oil and water give you a clue to a way of separating them. In the kitchen you can sometimes skim some oil off the surface with a spoon. Near the boundary your spoon may pick up a little water, too.

Hazel had two photos to put in order. One showed scattered droplets and the other showed a nearly continuous layer of oil on top. If she knew the cup had been stirred once and then left still, she could make a good guess from the pictures. What if someone had stirred it again? She checked the times the camera had recorded.

ns-mm-filter-paper.title: The Sand Stays on the Filter. What About the Salt?
ns-mm-filter-paper.markdown:
Two funnels stood on the table, each lined with ordinary filter paper. Jane had water with coarse sand for the funnel on the left. On the right she had water with salt already dissolved in it. If she looked just at the two cups below the funnels, she guessed the liquid in both might look clear.

Coarse sand stayed on the paper in the left funnel. Water flowed through its tiny pores. The grains were too big to fit. Salt water flowed into the cup on the right. The particles of dissolved salt were small enough to travel through ordinary filter paper with the water. No pile of salt grains collected on the paper the way the sand did. The liquid dripping into the cup still contained salt.

Suppose one cup contained both coarse sand and dissolved salt. Filtering could take out the sand first. To recover the salt, the water could be allowed to evaporate under suitable conditions. Mainly water would leave the surface. The dissolved salt would stay in the dish and could form crystals as the water level went down.

Jane drew a little pile of dots for the sand on the left filter. For the liquid collected on the right she wrote “salt water.” Her friend could read the letters right through the cup, so she turned the label toward him. The paper had caught the coarse sand. The dissolved salt had gone on into the cup with the water.

ns-mm-salt-pans.title: Little Squares in a Salt Field
ns-mm-salt-pans.markdown:
In a photograph of the Yinggehai salt works in Ledong on Hainan Island, long banks divide the water into pools. Turn to reporter Liu Sunmou's close-up. What looked like a patch of white is full of tiny square edges. The camera caught grains of salt that had already formed. Where did the little squares come from?

Seawater already contains dissolved salts. In the shallow pools, water evaporates from the surface. A cup of what's left can contain more salt than a cup did at the start. Salt workers call this concentrated salty water brine. When the brine reaches its limit for dissolved table salt and conditions continue to change, some of the salt can come out as solid crystals. The square corners are one sign of crystal growth. Other substances also dissolve in seawater, and some impurities may be mixed in with the coarse salt that's harvested.

One photo shows reflections on the water. The close-up shows the edges of crystals. Invisible water vapor doesn't show up in either one. Tell that part of the story out loud. First came seawater, then brine that grew more concentrated as water evaporated, and finally salt crystals big enough to see.

ns-mm-ink-chromatography.title: Blue and Yellow in a Single Ink Dot
ns-mm-ink-chromatography.markdown:
Tina's classmate thought two dark markers would make exactly the same color. Tina put a dot from each marker on its own strip of white coffee-filter paper. At first the dots looked much alike. Then water worked its way up from the bottom and through each dot. On one strip, two different colors stretched out from the ink.

Use two white coffee-filter strips of equal width and put an ink dot near the bottom of each. Let the bottom edge touch a little clean water in a plastic cup, with the ink dot above the waterline. As water moves up the paper and past the dot, it carries dyes that dissolve in water. Different dyes travel with the water or cling to the paper to different degrees. Colors can separate at different places along the strip. This way of separating parts of a mixture is called paper chromatography.

A blue band here and a yellow band there. Tina could describe what had happened with that marker. The second marker left only one dark band. Some dyes might have traveled about the same distance, or some might have stayed close to the starting spot. Beside the second strip she wrote, “One band separated this time.” She capped the markers. They still had a few secrets left.

ns-mm-paper-pieces.title: Is Torn Paper Still Paper?
ns-mm-paper-pieces.markdown:
Morgan tore a sheet of wrapping paper into pieces and arranged them in the shape of a house. A scrap could still take a fold or a crayon mark, just as the big sheet had. At a torn edge, the fine paper fibers were sometimes easier to see than at the neat edge of the original sheet.

Two things helped describe the change. The size and the edges were different. One large sheet had become several small pieces. The material was still the same kind of paper. Tearing mainly changed its shape. That's a physical change. Ice melting is another physical change. In that case what changes is its state.

Morgan tried fitting the pieces back together. The roof matched up and the walls lined up, but a seam marked each tear. She liked her little house too much to take it apart. She drew a window on a leftover corner. The sheet of wrapping paper had a new shape, and even the corner pieces were made of the paper she'd started with.

She gave her classmate a puzzle. With only one scrap in his hand, what could he match to the big sheet? He found a bit of the original pattern first. Along the tear he also found a few fine fibers.

ns-g6-rust.title: Where Do the Reddish Brown Patches on Iron Come From?
ns-g6-rust.markdown:
Cover the second photo and look at the far left of the first. Gray iron nails stand in water with air above it. The water looks pretty clear. How does the same set look several weeks later? Uncover the second photo. The water on the left now looks orange-brown, and brown marks cover parts of the nails. The nails in the group beside it still look gray. The captions identify the same groups in the before and after photos. Morgan kept her eye on the far-left tube.

Over time, iron exposed to water and oxygen can form rust. Rust contains substances made from iron and oxygen, among other elements. Its properties differ from those of the original metal. For example, the rusty coating is often loose enough to flake off. The formation of new substances makes rusting a chemical change.

“A reddish brown patch has appeared here” is a clue you can read from the photo. To explain it as rust, you need to know the starting material, how long it was there, and the conditions around it. Comparisons and information about rust help, too. Imagine sticking reddish brown paper to a sound iron box. Its color would change. Peel the paper off and the original iron is underneath.

Morgan wrote two sentences for the pictures. She read the first to her little brother and asked him to point to the spot on the left that had changed from clear to orange-brown. Her second sentence explained how water and oxygen take part in rusting. That one took the captions and the science reading together. The captions didn't say whether the nails originally had a metal coating, so the entry for that detail stayed blank.

ns-mm-copper-patina.title: The Statue's Green Coat
ns-mm-copper-patina.markdown:
From a distance, the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor looks pale green. Its skin is made of copper sheet. Fresh copper often has a reddish brown color. What happened to the outside of the statue?

After many years outdoors, the copper surface has reacted with substances in the air and with moisture. A layer of new, copper-containing substances has formed. Such a layer often looks bluish green and is called a patina. Most of the green you see on the statue comes from its patina. The copper sheet is still there underneath.

Copper patina and iron rust are both examples of chemical changes at a metal surface. The statue's patina can cling tightly and slow further corrosion of the copper. Iron rust is usually looser, and the iron beneath it can keep rusting. To explain the color or coating on a particular sculpture, check its material and its surroundings. A green surface gives you a starting clue.

Draw one fold of the Statue of Liberty's robe in close-up. Color the outside green, with copper sheet below it. A layer of reddish brown rust on ordinary iron often loosens and flakes away. The statue has worn its homegrown green coat for years, and that coat helps shelter the copper from the weather.

ns-mm-ceramic-firing.title: From a Clay Cup to a Ceramic Cup
ns-mm-ceramic-firing.markdown:
Two cups appeared in pictures from a potter's workshop. One label read “air-dried clay cup.” The other read “fired ceramic cup.” Both had a rim and a base. Holly wondered what would happen if water touched them.

After a potter shapes a cup from wet clay, it needs time to dry. Some of its water leaves. Dried clay that hasn't been fired can often soften again in water, and the potter may be able to use it again. In a potter's kiln, the clay undergoes high-temperature firing. Its clay minerals change. Tiny particles bond more tightly together, and some kinds of clay form a little glassy material. Getting the fired cup wet won't turn it back into the original soft clay.

One way to compare the two steps is to consider how the cups respond to water. Another is to look at what changed inside. Drying mainly takes water away. Firing changes the structure of the clay and can produce new substances. Both cups can keep their shape, but their materials now have different properties. Some ceramics still contain small pores and can absorb water. The type of ceramic and the way its surface was finished matter.

For the first photo Holly chose the caption “water has left the clay.” For the fired cup she wrote “the minerals and the structure have changed.” The rims still looked much the same in the pictures. The next part of the story lay inside the cup walls.

ns-mm-aluminum-reuse.title: An Aluminum Can's Next Stop
ns-mm-aluminum-reuse.markdown:
An empty drink can lands in a recycling bin. At a plant it may join other old cans on the way to becoming a roll of thin, silvery metal for new cans. Its old shape, color, and printed design will be hard to find again. Where might the aluminum from its body turn up?

At the recycling plant, aluminum cans are sorted out from other scrap. Coatings and some unwanted material are removed, and the metal is recovered. In an industrial furnace, metal from many cans can melt into a liquid. As it cools, the liquid becomes solid again. Suitable metal can be rolled into thin sheets to make new things. A can body and its lid often use different aluminum alloys. An alloy combines a metal with other elements. To match the needs of the new product, the plant checks and adjusts what the metal contains.

Follow three shapes along the route. A can body, liquid metal, and a roll of metal sheet. During melting and solidifying, the metal changes state. The full recycling trip includes sorting and further processing, and some material is lost along the way. How much usable new metal comes from a given number of cans is something the plant must measure.

Kai put two words on the route map, four characters in Chinese. “Melting. Solidifying.” They fit right where the metal turned liquid and then cooled to a solid. People still had to sort the scrap, check the alloys, and roll the sheet before someone could hold another lightweight can.

ns-mm-mass-and-boundaries.title: The Missing Three Grams
ns-mm-mass-and-boundaries.markdown:
Josephine read two imaginary scale records. In one, a dish and the water in it weighed 40 grams at first. After standing for a while, together they weighed 37 grams. In another, a piece of iron started at 10 grams. After it rusted, the iron and its attached rust weighed more than 10 grams. One reading went down. The other went up. Where should she look for an explanation?

She drew a circle around what the scale included. In the first example it included the dish and the water still inside it. If nothing spilled and the dish stayed in place, 40 minus 37 left three grams that evaporation into the air could explain. In the second example the scale included the iron and any rust on it. Oxygen and other material from outside the original piece took part in rusting. If all the flakes stayed on, the reading could increase.

In ordinary chemical reactions, atoms rearrange to form new substances. A drawing could use two colors of dots for iron and oxygen atoms. The same dots would appear in new combinations after the change. When all the starting materials and all the products are accounted for, the total mass stays the same.

Josephine added two arrows at the scale. One followed water out into the air. The other followed material from the surroundings into the rust. In the first problem she'd worked out a loss of three grams. For the second, all she had was “more than ten grams.” She put her pencil down to wait for another reading.

ns-mm-granite-grains.title: The Grains in a Granite Wall
ns-mm-granite-grains.markdown:
From a distance the granite wall by the station looked as flat and gray as a sheet of paper. Up close, the stone was full of grains. Some looked white or pink. Some caught the light like glass. Others were black. In a photo, the children circled three spots on the very same slab.

A rock can contain several minerals. Quartz, feldspar, and mica are found in many granites. Quartz grains in granite may look grayish white and let some light through. Feldspar is sometimes white or pink. Some mica shows up in thin flakes. Grain size and color vary from slab to slab. Appearance gives you a start. To identify a mineral, scientists also use information about properties such as crystal shape, luster, and hardness.

The children asked the collection's keeper about three dark specks and got a close-up with mineral names on it. They picked a grain labeled quartz and looked to see whether a nearby quartz grain was exactly the same color. Circling three places told them they'd picked three grains. Finding out how many kinds of minerals made up that whole stone would take the labels and more clues about the grains themselves.

ns-mm-mineral-hardness.title: Can Quartz Leave a Scratch on Calcite?
ns-mm-mineral-hardness.markdown:
Two pale minerals shared a display case. One label said “calcite” and the other said “quartz.” In a photo they looked a bit alike. Their hardness numbers were quite different. Calcite was 3 and quartz was 7. What could those numbers tell a visitor?

Mineral scientists compare resistance to scratching by seeing whether one mineral can leave a scratch on another. The Mohs hardness scale puts familiar reference minerals in order. Quartz ranks above calcite. Under suitable test conditions, quartz can scratch calcite. On paper you can show this with an arrow from the mineral that can make the scratch toward the softer one.

The display also listed gypsum at 2 and apatite at 5. From easiest to hardest to scratch, the four minerals line up as gypsum, calcite, apatite, and quartz. Could Quinn divide 7 by 3 and say exactly how many times harder quartz was? The numbers give an order. The steps between them can differ in size. Quinn rubbed out the decimal and left each photo with its rank, 7 or 3.

ns-mm-graphite-pencil.title: What Makes a Pencil's Black Line?
ns-mm-graphite-pencil.markdown:
Summer had drawn a tree. A gray-black trunk now ran across the paper, and her pencil point looked a little rounder. As the point moved over the page, tiny bits of its core stayed behind.

The core of an ordinary black pencil is often made with graphite and clay. Graphite is a mineral made of carbon. Its atoms are arranged in layers that can slide past one another fairly easily. A thin trace of graphite left on the paper makes a visible line. The wooden barrel protects the core and gives your hand a place to hold it.

Summer tried an HB and a 2B from the same brand. She drew a little with each on the same paper, pressing about equally hard. In the same line of pencils, the 2B is usually softer and makes a dark mark more easily. She used the 2B for shade under the tree and switched back to the HB for fine twigs. The Chinese name for a pencil has two characters, and one of them means “lead.” Graphite made the marks on her paper.

ns-mm-bauxite-aluminium.title: From Bauxite to a Sheet of Aluminum
ns-mm-bauxite-aluminium.markdown:
At one end of the exhibit sat a piece of bauxite, reddish brown with little hollows on its surface. At the other end lay a silvery sheet of aluminum. The ore and the sheet looked so different. Why did they share a display card?

Bauxite contains several minerals that include the element aluminum. It's an important source of that metal. Industry first extracts aluminum oxide from the bauxite. Aluminum oxide is usually a white solid, with aluminum and oxygen chemically combined. At a smelter, electrical energy helps separate out the aluminum as a metal. Leo made room between the ore and the sheet in his drawing for the white substance that comes between them.

Once the metal is available, it can be rolled into a thin sheet. Rolling changes its shape. Going from aluminum oxide to metallic aluminum changes what the substance is made of. All three samples contained the element aluminum. Reddish brown, white, silvery. Now each had a place in the story.

ns-mm-brass-bronze.title: What Goes Into Brass and Bronze?
ns-mm-brass-bronze.markdown:
The display held a bronze mirror and a brass handle. The back of the mirror was dark. The handle was a brighter yellow. According to the labels, copper was a main ingredient in both. Combine copper with other elements and the name and properties of the material can change with the mix.

An alloy contains two or more elements, at least one of them a metal. Common brasses contain mainly copper and zinc. Traditional tin bronze uses copper and tin. A craftsperson may use other ingredients, too. The choice of ingredients and their amounts can affect hardness, color, and how easily the material can be shaped. A surface can also change color after long exposure to air.

The guide gave out three little labels. On the first, Ivy read “copper, zinc.” She matched it to brass. The second said “copper, tin.” That went with tin bronze. The third said only “yellowish.” She paused. Even a change in the display lighting might affect the color she saw. She turned to the page listing the materials in that particular object.

ns-mm-stainless-steel.title: A Steel Spoon's Invisible Shield
ns-mm-stainless-steel.markdown:
A washed stainless steel spoon gleamed as it dried on the rack. In a book Grace saw a piece of ordinary iron speckled with rust. Both materials had a metallic shine, yet their surfaces could change in quite different ways.

Stainless steel contains enough of the element chromium for a very thin, chromium-rich protective film to form on its surface in air. The film is too thin to see. It slows the attack on the metal beneath it. Under suitable conditions, a damaged spot in the film can even form again. These surface properties help make stainless steel a good choice for tableware and sinks.

Grace drew a slice through the spoon much larger than life. She added a fine line at its outer edge for the invisible film. On the drawing of the iron, she showed loose bits flaking off a layer of rust. Even some stainless steels can corrode in harsh surroundings, such as salty ones. Next time she spotted a shiny spoon, she'd remember the little film she could never see in its shine.

ns-mm-paper-fibers.title: What Holds a Sheet of Paper Together?
ns-mm-paper-fibers.markdown:
A scrap of handmade paper lay on the table. Held up to ordinary room light, parts of it showed faint lines, one crossing another. Leah looked at a smooth sheet of printer paper. The lines were much harder to see there. She could lift either sheet in one piece. What held all those fine strands together?

Most paper is made mainly of fibers from plants. To make paper, fibers are mixed with water to form pulp. A papermaking screen lets the water drain away and leaves a thin, wet mat of fibers behind. The fibers lie close together. As the sheet dries, bonds form between them, holding the sheet together. Fillers and other materials may be added to modern papers, giving them different colors and smoother or rougher finishes.

Leah found a single strand sticking up at an edge of the paper. Both ends disappeared into the other fibers. She imagined being small enough to walk across the page, stepping from one crossing fiber to the next. All those places where fibers overlapped and joined helped make the thin sheet in her hand.

ns-mm-woven-knitted.title: A Woven Shirt and a Knitted Hat
ns-mm-woven-knitted.markdown:
On the cuff of a shirt, two sets of yarn crossed one another. In a close-up, Stella could see which thread went over and which went under. The pattern on a knitted hat looked like rows of little braids. She placed the pictures together and traced a single color of yarn to see where each path went.

In woven cloth, one set of threads runs lengthwise. These are the warp. The weft threads cross them, row by row. In a close-up of knitting, yarn curves into loops that interlock with other loops. When you pull a knitted hat over your head, the loops can change shape a little. Two fabrics made from the very same yarn can look different and stretch differently depending on how the yarn is arranged.

On graph paper, Stella drew a red line over a blue line, then under the next blue one. A tiny patch of woven cloth took shape. In the hat picture she followed the blue yarn, meeting another loop drawn through each loop. She already knew what to call this second drawing.

ns-mm-towel-loops.title: The Little Loops on a Towel
ns-mm-towel-loops.markdown:
Fold a clean cotton handkerchief and look at its smooth surface. Now look at a cotton towel. Short loops rise out of the fabric, turn, and go back in. Someone wiping a table might choose the towel. Someone wrapping a pair of glasses might like a piece of smooth cloth. Both fabrics are cotton, and each has its uses.

In many towels, some of the yarn stands out from the surface in loops. The extra yarn brings more fibers into contact with water, with spaces between the loops as well. Water readily wets cotton fibers, and this looped structure is often used to soak water up. A towel can be thicker and heavier than a little handkerchief and may contain more yarn. To investigate the loops themselves, look for samples close in size and made from the same kind of yarn. Keep track of any differences in thickness and weight.

Eva's brother said the towel soaked up more. “Our towel's much thicker, too,” she pointed out. To judge what the loops contributed, they'd need to pay attention to how much cotton yarn went into each cloth. She followed a thread in the pictures. In the handkerchief it stayed close to the cloth. In the towel it rose, curved over the top of a loop, and dived back in.

ns-mm-paper-wicking.title: How Does Water Climb a Paper Towel?
ns-mm-paper-wicking.markdown:
The lower end of a paper towel touched water in a shallow dish. At first only its foot was wet. After a while, the paper higher up began to darken. The water in the dish was still at about the same level. The wet edge on the towel had climbed above it.

Tiny spaces run between the paper fibers. Water is attracted to fibers it can wet, and water molecules also attract one another. Together these attractions can draw water into narrow passages in the paper. The movement of a liquid through narrow spaces in this way is called capillary action. The wet edge may be wavy because those passages vary across the sheet.

Grace and Dad stood a strip of paper towel and a smooth plastic strip in the same shallow dish. The bottom of each just touched the clean water. The wet patch on the paper crept above the waterline. The bottom of the plastic got wet, too, but it showed little of that broad, climbing patch. Grace drew two lines beside her picture of the towel. One marked the water in the dish. The other marked how high the wet paper reached after a while.

ns-mm-fiber-label.title: Read the Label Inside a Hat
ns-mm-fiber-label.markdown:
Two blue hats felt just as soft in the hand. The fiber label on one said “100% cotton.” The other said “60% cotton, 40% polyester.” Looking at the hats side by side, which label listed one kind of fiber, and which listed two?

Cotton fibers grow on the cotton plant. Polyesters are a family of synthetic fibers. The familiar textile fiber called dílún in Chinese is one kind of polyester. Manufacturers can blend different fibers and spin them into yarn, or they can use different yarns together in one fabric. That lets them combine a range of properties. How soft, absorbent, or easy to wrinkle the finished fabric is also depends on the arrangement of the yarns, the way the cloth is made, and how it is finished.

Nancy took the label on the second hat. Did this line describe the outside or the lining? If it described the outside, then in every 100 grams of fiber there, 60 grams were cotton and 40 were polyester. The amounts added up to 100 grams. If the lining had its own line, she'd read that one separately. Two soft blue hats, each with a little label that named its fibers.

ns-mm-newsprint-yellow.title: The Yellow Edge of an Old Newspaper
ns-mm-newsprint-yellow.markdown:
An old newspaper lay folded at the bottom of a drawer. Unfolded, it had a yellowish border. The part tucked inside the fold looked paler. Both places were on the same sheet. What had happened to the paper while it was folded up?

Many newspapers are made from wood pulp. Along with fibers, the paper may contain other material from the wood, including lignin. The composition of the paper, its exposure to light and air, and the temperature and humidity in storage can all affect how quickly it ages. Some components take on a yellow-brown color as they age. Some reactions shorten chains in the fibers, and the paper gradually loses strength.

Grandma remembered the paper had stayed folded. She couldn't quite remember how long it had sat by a window or when she'd put it away. Clara pointed to two spots in the photo, one inside the fold and one on the exposed edge. The colors on that single sheet really did differ. Its missing history in the light was the part she most wanted to ask Grandma about.

ns-mm-glass-from-sand.title: From Grains of Sand to Window Glass
ns-mm-glass-from-sand.markdown:
A little bottle in a display case held sand used to make glass. Beside it stood a flat pane of clear window glass. The sand could pour out of the bottle grain by grain. The pane formed one smooth sheet. Several factory steps lay between the two exhibits.

Sand containing silica, or silicon dioxide, is a main ingredient in many kinds of everyday glass. Glassmakers add other ingredients to help the batch melt and give the finished glass properties people need. In the factory's hot equipment the ingredients form molten glass. It is shaped and cooled into a solid. Different kinds of glass call for different mixes of raw materials.

Stacy searched the pane for the old outlines of the grains. The display label told her that the atoms in a quartz crystal repeat in a regular pattern. In ordinary window glass that pattern doesn't repeat over long distances. She shifted her head and looked through the pane. There, quite by chance, was the little bottle of sand. Melting, shaping, and cooling had given its neighbor in the display a very different form.

ns-mm-window-flat-glass.title: How Does a Windowpane Get So Flat?
ns-mm-window-flat-glass.markdown:
A big classroom window lets daylight in and gives a clear view of a faraway building. To make a pane like that, the factory needs a large sheet with two smooth, flat sides. Leveling a whole surface after the glass has hardened would take much more work.

Many modern factories make flat glass by floating it. Molten glass spreads in a continuous ribbon on a bath of liquid tin. The tin provides a level surface, and the glass spreads out on its own. After the long ribbon leaves the tin bath, it cools gradually. Once formed and cooled, the glass is cut to the sizes needed for different uses.

At first Julian saw only the glass ribbon in the cutaway factory drawing. Looking again, he found the shiny layer of liquid tin underneath. His finger traveled along the ribbon and lifted just where the glass left the bath. He looked at the crisp outline of the building outside. One side of that smooth windowpane had once rested on a level pool of liquid metal.

ns-mm-safety-glass.title: Two Ways Safety Glass Can Break
ns-mm-safety-glass.markdown:
In a factory guide, two pictures showed broken safety glass. In the picture on the left, many small pieces lay apart. The picture on the right had a web of cracks, yet a large area still held together. The two labels read “tempered glass” and “laminated glass.”

A special factory treatment leaves the surface of tempered glass under compression. This helps it resist some forces. When fully tempered glass breaks, it usually breaks into many small pieces. Laminated glass has a layer of material sandwiched between two or more sheets of glass. If the glass cracks, many pieces can stick to that middle layer and stay in place. Some products combine the two approaches.

Casey explained the difference to her family with drawings. In one, she showed little pieces spread apart. In the other, many cracked pieces still held on to the layer in the middle. Both designs can reduce certain injuries. Broken pieces can still cut. At a counter, an intact pane gives few clues to how it was made. Casey and her family found the line about construction in the product information.

ns-mm-pottery-porcelain.title: The Outside of a Flowerpot and a Bowl
ns-mm-pottery-porcelain.markdown:
The outside of a flowerpot looked a little rough. A white porcelain bowl at home felt smooth. Annie checked the labels. One said “unglazed earthenware.” The other said “glazed white porcelain.” Both pieces had been fired by potters. Would they soak up water in the same way?

The body of some earthenware contains tiny pores. Water can enter those spaces in an unglazed flowerpot. Many porcelains have a dense body after firing, making it harder for water to enter. A glaze is a thin, glassy layer left on a piece by firing. It can smooth the surface and help keep water out. Some pieces have glaze only on the inside. Others are glazed on the outside as well.

Annie drew a section of the unglazed pot and dotted the wall with tiny pores. She drew the bowl with a fine, shiny rim to show the glaze. Comparing just these two pieces by touch left a question. How much of the difference came from the clay body, and how much from the glaze? A pair with the same clay body, one glazed and the other plain, would give her a clearer look at what the glaze did.

ns-mm-blue-white-porcelain.title: Where Are the Blue Flowers on the Jar?
ns-mm-blue-white-porcelain.markdown:
A porcelain jar from Jingdezhen belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art. The museum's photo is black and white. You can see curling stems and lotus flowers going around the jar. How did Jenna know the design was blue? The material record described cobalt blue beneath the glaze. She read the four characters of the Chinese description slowly. The first two meant “under the glaze.” Now she knew where to look.

To make this kind of blue-and-white porcelain, a potter first paints a design in pigment containing cobalt onto the clay body. A coating of glaze goes over it. After firing, light passes through the glaze and the blue pattern shows underneath. A pencil tracing the wall from outside in would reach the glaze first, then the painted design. Around and around the jar went the lotus flowers, all the way back to where they began.

In her notebook Jenna drew a little slice of the jar wall. She put the white porcelain body on the inside, the clear glaze on the outside, and a blue line between them. To find the position of the design on a different blue-flowered bowl, she'd look for that bowl's own label.

ns-mm-cement-concrete.title: How Does a Concrete Path Get Hard?
ns-mm-cement-concrete.markdown:
Two material diagrams stood beside a path. In the first, a bag of gray powder was labeled “cement.” The second showed hardened concrete. In the cutaway you could see fine sand and pieces of stone of different sizes. Both diagrams looked gray, but the materials lists told quite different stories.

Cement is a binding material in many kinds of concrete. When cement, water, sand, and stone are mixed, the cement and water form a paste that coats the sand and stone. Some ingredients in the cement react chemically with water. New solid material forms and gradually binds the grains and stones together. These reactions are called hydration. On a construction site, workers often manage the moisture in freshly placed concrete so hydration can continue.

The new concrete beside the road was curing. Sometimes the workers needed to keep it moist. Josephine had thought they were waiting for the road to “dry.” Then she remembered the page about hydration. The cement needs water for the reactions that bind sand and stone into a strong mass. A dry-looking path may have lost moisture at the surface. Hardening on the inside follows its own timetable.

ns-mm-polymer-chain.title: A Long Chain Inside Plastic
ns-mm-polymer-chain.markdown:
Ivy drew a string of circles. Each circle stood for one small repeating part. A circle in the middle had a neighbor on either side. At either end, the last circle had just one neighbor along that chain. Her drawing was a model of the tiny parts and connections within a molecule. The circles were pencil marks standing in for structures far too small to see in a plastic bottle.

Scientists call large molecules made of repeating parts polymers. Take polyethylene. Its model can show many similar units linked one after another. The real material has many long chains. Some bend and some sprout short branches. The units can differ from one kind of plastic to another. Chain length, shape, arrangement, and other ingredients in a material all help determine whether it's flexible or clear.

Ivy drew several chains on one page, one curving in an arc and another with a small branch. They all came from the same pencil. In real life, changing the polymer or mixing in different ingredients can make bags and boxes floppier or stiffer. Under a label that said only “plastic,” she'd like to add the kind of material this particular object used.

ns-mm-rubber-forms.title: How Does a Rubber Band Spring Back?
ns-mm-rubber-forms.markdown:
A diagram showed a rubber band lying loose. Beside it, a magnified model showed the long chains inside as a tangle of curving lines. A second drawing showed the same band gently stretched. Many of those curves now reached farther in the direction of the pull.

Long chains in rubber tend to coil. As a piece of rubber stretches a little, many chains straighten out along the pull. Let go, and many return to a more coiled arrangement. The whole object moves back toward its earlier size and shape. In some rubbers, links between chains help keep them from sliding far past one another. Different rubber mixes can recover their shape to different degrees.

Ivy added a third frame for the moment after the band was released. She marked the same chain in blue in every frame. In the middle picture it was more stretched out than in the first. In the last it curled again, with room for a different set of bends. The rubber band she could see returned close to its original shape. Her winding blue lines were a model of what might explain that springy return.

ns-mm-foam-cells.title: Why Is Packing Foam Full of Tiny Pockets?
ns-mm-foam-cells.markdown:
A new item often comes with a pad of foam in its box. Enlarge a photo of an already broken foam sample and you'll see small spaces throughout it. In another close-up, the cross section of a solid plastic board looks much more continuous. Both materials can form blocks. Inside, they look quite different.

Foam often consists of a connected solid framework with many pores. Those pores usually hold gas. Some connect to one another, and some have thin solid walls between them. Compare a foam block and a solid block made from the same kind of solid material and occupying the same volume. Gas fills much of the space in the foam block, so the foam block usually has less mass. Some packing foams can compress a little, cushioning what's inside the box.

Eva colored a solid block blue in her drawing. In a second block of the same size, she left many small spaces. “Is there anything in here?” her little sister asked. Eva chose a circle and wrote “gas.” With gas taking up part of that same space, less solid material was needed. Weighing equal-volume samples made from the same solid would give them something to check their idea against.

ns-mm-natural-synthetic-rubber.title: Two Kinds of Rubber in a Tire
ns-mm-natural-synthetic-rubber.markdown:
A sign at the tire shop showed a rubber tree and a roll of factory-made rubber. Eva guessed that both materials could go into a tire. Both were called rubber. Where did each one come from?

Natural rubber usually comes from the milky liquid, or latex, of rubber trees. Synthetic rubber is made by chemical processes in factories and comes in many varieties. Both kinds contain large molecules shaped like long chains. Manufacturers blend different rubbers and other ingredients for particular jobs. The tread meets the road. Other materials in the tire give it support or help hold in air. Different jobs call for different mixes.

Eva traced two routes on the display. One started with latex from a tree. The other started with synthetic rubber from a factory. The routes could meet in a single tire. To find out which kinds were used in which layers, and how much of each, she'd need the materials diagram for that tire. Once the wheel began to turn, the tree and the factory would both have a part in its journey.

ns-mm-thermoplastic-network.title: Can This Plastic Be Shaped Again?
ns-mm-thermoplastic-network.markdown:
In materials class, Ethan studied two factory diagrams. The first showed plastic being made into parts. Clean scraps of the same kind of plastic later went back into the equipment to be shaped again. In the second, a factory needed a different way to handle a hardened resin part. One diagram was labeled “thermoplastic” and the other “thermoset.”

Many thermoplastics soften when heated to a suitable temperature and set into shape again as they cool. A factory can use this property to reshape suitable scraps. When a thermosetting resin cures, its long molecules link together into a strong network. Once the part has set, heating it again generally won't make it flow into a new shape. Too much heat can break the material down.

Ethan had planned to label the two samples “hard” and “soft.” Then he remembered that the part in the first picture could be hard once it had cooled. He looked past how the pieces felt and found the factory record that said the first material could soften and be shaped again at the right temperature. Sorting at a recycling plant sometimes takes knowing both what a material has been through and how it will behave next.

ns-mm-plastic-resin-code.title: A 1 and a 2 on the Bottom of a Bottle
ns-mm-plastic-resin-code.markdown:
Look at the bottoms of two clean, empty containers. One has a 1 beside the three letters PET. The other has a 2 and the letters HDPE. Both containers can hold things. The numbers tell you something about two different plastics.

Some plastic products carry resin identification codes. Code 1 is used for polyethylene terephthalate, or PET, a plastic common in clear drink bottles. Code 2 is used for high-density polyethylene, or HDPE, which you may find in opaque bottles for household products. The code gives an initial clue to which kind of plastic makes up the main part of a container.

As soon as Grace recognized PET, her brother held up the bottle and headed for the recycling bin. She drew him over to read the sign first. The number identified the resin in the bottle. The local collection instructions said what the site accepted and how to handle bottles and caps. If the cap had a different number, she'd give the cap and the bottle separate lines in her notes. They might have separate destinations.

ns-mm-water-settling.title: What Settles at the Bottom of Cloudy Water?
ns-mm-water-settling.markdown:
A guide gave Nancy three drawings to arrange in time order. Each showed the same cup of cloudy water sitting still. In the first, gray dots filled it from top to bottom. In the second, a dark band had gathered at the bottom. In the third, the band was thicker and the water above it looked clearer.

Some solid particles suspended in water slowly fall and collect at the bottom of the container. This is called settling. How quickly they fall depends on their size, shape, and material. Very fine particles can stay in the water for a long time. Even if the upper layer looks clearer, it may still hold things too small to see.

Nancy drew an arrow in the air from a gray dot halfway up the cup down to the bottom. The kinds of particles that settle easily also collect at the bottom of a settling tank in a water treatment plant. As for the clearer water above them, it still had other stages of treatment ahead. She was ready to follow it to the next one.

ns-mm-water-clearness.title: Two Cups of Clear Water
ns-mm-water-clearness.markdown:
Nancy could read the same card with black letters through either cup of clear water. Yet the water-sample reports gave two different readings. She nudged the cups aside to find which dissolved substance had been measured and which units the reports used.

Many tiny particles suspended in water can make it cloudy. Other substances dissolve, spreading evenly throughout water that may still look clear. The letter card shows how easily you can see through a sample. Finding out which substances are present or how much of one substance it contains takes a measurement with instruments and methods suited to the question.

Here are some made-up readings. Sample A has 20 milligrams of one dissolved substance per liter. Sample B has 100 milligrams of the same substance per liter. Comparing a liter of each, B contains five times as much of that substance as A. The black letters behind the cups looked equally sharp. The report showed the difference. To learn what else was in each sample, Nancy would read the entries for the other substances, too.

ns-mm-hard-water.title: Where Does the White Ring in a Kettle Come From?
ns-mm-hard-water.markdown:
One photo showed a white ring of deposits inside a kettle. The kettle in another photo looked cleaner. Clara checked the water reports for the two places. One had a higher reading for “hardness.” Water has its own meaning for that word. In a rock, hardness describes a different property.

Water hardness mainly reflects the amount of dissolved calcium and magnesium ions. When hard water is heated in a kettle, solids such as calcium carbonate can be left behind. Over time they can build up into a layer of white scale. How often a kettle is used and how often it's cleaned help determine how thick the layer gets.

If two local water reports use the same units, Clara can compare the readings on their hardness lines. A lower reading generally means less of the dissolved calcium and magnesium that contribute to hardness. Other dissolved substances have their own entries. This time she read the reports first, then went back to look at the white ring in the photo.

ns-mm-gac-adsorption.title: When Water Flows Past a Grain of Carbon
ns-mm-gac-adsorption.markdown:
At a drinking-water exhibit, an enlarged picture showed a black grain full of tiny pores. The label called this porous material activated carbon. In the plant diagram, some substances in the water stayed on the carbon surfaces as the water flowed past.

The walls inside a pore count as surfaces, too. Add up all the pore walls in all the little grains, and there's a great deal of space for substances to stick. When some of the material dissolved in water sticks to the carbon surface, that's called adsorption. Ordinary filter paper catches sand grains that are bigger than its pores. Adsorption depends on how the carbon surface interacts with a substance in the water. Plants select materials and conditions to fit what they're trying to remove.

Jane drew a slice through one carbon grain, with several pores reaching deep inside. Her blue pencil went in through an opening and traced the walls. Her finger turned corner after corner on its way back out. “One tiny grain, and all those places to stick!” Whether a particular substance will stay there is something the plant has to consider when it chooses a treatment for it.

ns-mm-waterworks-steps.title: What Happens in the Tanks at a Water Plant?
ns-mm-waterworks-steps.markdown:
A long map stretched across the wall at the water plant exhibit. Water entered at one end, passed through tanks drawn side by side, and flowed off the other end. Someone thought the tanks just moved the water from place to place. The names beside them told a different story. Each stage had a job.

Many plants that treat surface water first gather fine particles into larger clumps and give them time to sink. The water passes through a filter that catches some remaining particles. A plant also uses steps such as disinfection to control harmful microorganisms. Engineers choose and arrange the stages to suit the incoming water, the equipment, and the standards for the water supply. The treated water is checked before it leaves.

Nancy gave three places on the map action words. At the settling tank she wrote “sink.” At the filter she wrote “catch.” At the disinfection stage she wrote “control germs.” Her eyes could follow the path from one tank to the next. To find out whether the finished water met the supply standards, she turned to the test results. That was the last stop on her map.

ns-mm-desalination-distillation.title: How Can Fresh Water Come From Salt Water?
ns-mm-desalination-distillation.markdown:
Two diagrams started with salt water. In one, sunlight fell on a grid of shallow salt ponds. The other showed desalination equipment, with a route for water vapor and a place to collect liquid water. In both diagrams, some of the water changed from liquid to vapor.

In a distiller, some liquid water becomes water vapor. The dissolved salt stays behind and the remaining salt water gets more concentrated. The vapor travels to another part of the equipment, cools, and condenses into liquid water for collection. At the salt ponds, the main crop is salt. Water vapor escapes into the air. Both methods make use of water's ability to change state. Follow the product being collected and the two routes end in different places.

Nancy used two little baskets as collection symbols. She placed one by the pile of salt crystals on the pond diagram and the other at the outlet for condensed water on the distiller. “We collect the salt that stays here and the water that condenses over there,” she told her classmate. If that water is going to people's faucets, it still needs any treatment and water-quality checks required for the local supply.

ns-mm-reuse-and-repair.title: A Book Bag Gets a Second Chance
ns-mm-reuse-and-repair.markdown:
The strap on Bella's book bag had come loose, but the bag itself was sound. She hated to throw it away. She'd picked out the blue checked cloth inside it herself. Grandma looked at the strap and offered to sew it back on. Bella had another idea, too. The bag could hold markers on her desk. She could enjoy the blue checks every day, even without using the strap.

A repair can let the same bag go on doing its original job. Changing its use gives the still-intact bag a different job. Sending the cloth for material recycling is another possibility. It may be sorted or processed and become material for something new. Whether that route is available depends on what the local program accepts, what the fabric contains, and the condition it's in.

Bella needed to carry her books to school the next day, so she asked Grandma to sew up the strap first. When she no longer needed it for books, the bag could still hold markers beside her desk. As for the recycling route, she opened the community guide to the two-character Chinese word to check first. It meant “fabric.”

ns-mm-recycling-collection.title: Which Bin Takes the Paper Box?
ns-mm-recycling-collection.markdown:
On the table were pictures of clean packages. A brown paperboard box, a clear drink bottle, an empty metal can. All three had held something. At a sorting site, their materials could send them along different routes.

Paper boxes, plastic bottles, and metal cans can go through different processes. Collected paper is processed as paper, metals are sorted by type and use, and plastics come in many varieties. Labels mixed in with the materials or leftover liquid can sometimes affect sorting and processing. A collection site lists both the items it takes and the condition they should be in.

Tessa was about to give two paper boxes the same collection label. Her brother turned the pictures over. One box had a clean bottom. The other had soaked up grease. Tessa went back to the local sign. Beside the list of materials were the conditions for accepting them. She left a space on each card to describe the actual box in the picture.

ns-mm-recycled-paper-shorter.title: How Long Are the Fibers in Old Paper?
ns-mm-recycled-paper-shorter.markdown:
Hand a clean piece of scrap paper to a paper mill and its next job may be as a fresh sheet. The mill can separate its fibers again, remove some unwanted material, and form the fibers into new paper. Draw the process in a circle and you might picture the same fibers taking trip after trip.

Each trip involves recovering the fibers, cleaning them, and forming a new sheet. With repeated processing, some fibers get shorter or reach the end of their usable life. Longer fibers help make a strong sheet. Depending on the paper's purpose, a mill can mix longer fibers or some fresh fibers into the pulp. Some recycled products need strength. Others can use a larger share of short fibers.

Clara had just drawn a second loop around her recycling circle when Dad asked, “How many trips can a fiber make?” She looked at the long and short lines in her drawing of the pulp. It depended on the fibers in the old paper, how much was lost in processing, and the strength the next sheet needed. She gave the circle a fork. Some fibers carried on into paper. Others left the loop during sorting and processing.

ns-mm-glass-cullet-color.title: Why Sort Glass Bottles by Color?
ns-mm-glass-cullet-color.markdown:
In a glass factory photo, piles of raw material lay side by side. One was almost colorless, one greenish, one brown. These were pieces of used glass that had been broken and sorted at the plant. On the table, three pictures of finished bottles showed much the same three colors.

A factory can add suitable pieces of used glass to its new raw materials and melt them together. Color in the old glass can affect the color of the new glass. To make clear, colorless glass, workers carefully select material with a suitable color and composition. Glass for bottles, heat-resistant dishes, and windows may have different recipes. The types also need to be sorted to meet the plant's requirements.

For a batch of colorless bottles, a glassmaker looks for pieces with the right color and composition. One dark green piece would stand out in the photo. A piece of colorless heat-resistant dishware mixed in with colorless bottle glass might be much harder to spot. Grace was looking at pictures from a factory. For bottles and jars from her own home, she'd follow the local collection site's list of accepted types.

ns-mm-reclaimed-asphalt.title: Can an Old Road Go Into a New One?
ns-mm-reclaimed-asphalt.markdown:
In one roadwork photo a machine had left dark, broken-up material behind. Another photo showed a finished road. The project put the pictures side by side because some material from the old pavement could be processed and used in a fresh layer of road.

In typical asphalt pavement, sand and rock in different sizes form the aggregate. Asphalt binder holds those pieces together. Specialized equipment mills off old pavement. Road engineers sort it by size and test it. Reclaimed material contains aggregate as well as some of the old binder. The expected traffic and weather, along with the properties of the reclaimed material, help determine how much can go into the new mix and how much new material it needs.

Leo noticed that the new road looked dark, too. Could he tell from its shade how much old pavement had gone in? The construction records had a better clue. They listed the amounts of the different parts of the new mix. The two photos showed a possible destination for old pavement. For the amount actually used, he ran his finger down the numbers.

ns-mm-recycling-material-choices.title: A Little Window in a Pencil Box
ns-mm-recycling-material-choices.markdown:
Ivy wanted a clear window in a storage box so she could see the markers inside. The box body was one kind of plastic and the window a different material. In her first design the two were glued firmly together. For her second drawing she kept both materials and both sizes exactly the same. She gave the window a fastening that could be undone.

When a factory needs material of a fairly uniform composition, it usually has to remove other materials mixed in with it. A designer can help by choosing materials that are easy to identify or making certain parts easy to separate. A box made of two materials, for instance, could have a removable clear panel, if its construction allows that. A label could identify each part. Engineers also have to consider the box's original job. Its new fastening still has to protect what's inside.

Ivy pointed to the two designs for her classmate. At the end of the box's life, a removable window would help each material go its own way. While the box held markers, though, that window had to stay secure and its edges had to fit snugly. She left two boxes to check beside her new design. “Stays together in use” and “comes apart when it's worn out.”

ns-g1-push-pull.title: A Paper Bridge Between Two Hands
ns-g1-push-pull.markdown:
A little paper bridge stood on Charlie's desk. He held one end in each hand. There was a space under the arch. A moment ago, this had been a flat strip of paper! He slowly moved his hands apart. The bridge got lower. One more gentle pull, and the strip was straight again.

When Charlie pushed his hands toward each other, the ends of the paper moved closer together. The middle bent up. When he pulled the ends apart, the bend straightened out. A push is a force. A pull is a force, too. A force can change the shape of a piece of paper.

Charlie let go. The strip he had bent gently lay almost flat. He picked up another piece of paper, one he had folded. Even after he opened it and took his hands away, he could still feel a little ridge along the fold.

ns-g2-magnet-paper.title: How Does a Magnet Hold Up a Drawing?
ns-g2-magnet-paper.markdown:
Molly's drawing hung on a steel message board. A flat, flexible magnet held down one corner. The paper came between the magnet and the steel. Molly held her hand under the picture while Dad tried the same magnet on a wooden cabinet door. When he let go, the drawing fell right into her hand.

The steel board contains iron, which the magnet attracts. The pull is still strong enough through one thin sheet of paper to press the drawing against the board. Friction between the paper and the board helps keep the drawing from sliding down. On the wooden door, the magnet couldn't press the paper against the wood that way.

What if Molly tried to hang a thick pad of drawings on the board? The magnet would be farther from the steel, so its pull would be weaker. The stack of paper would also be heavier. Molly picked out her favorite drawing and hung up that one sheet.

ns-g3-motion-track.title: Which Toy Car Goes Faster?
ns-g3-motion-track.markdown:
“The blue car won!” Zack called. Then he noticed something. When the red car had started, the blue car was already close to the finish. His big brother played the video again. Two lines on a strip of paper marked a distance of exactly one meter. Zack decided to time each car separately.

He started the clock as the front of the blue car crossed the first line. When its front crossed the second line, he stopped the clock. Two seconds. He timed the red car the same way. It took three seconds to go one meter. The blue car covered the same distance in less time, so its average speed over that meter was higher.

They raced the cars again. Zack kept the times from both runs and replayed the video. The blue car actually slowed down near the finish. The stopwatch gave him a time for the whole meter. To find out where the car went fastest, he would have to time shorter parts of the run.

ns-g5-friction.title: Pulling a Block Across Two Surfaces
ns-g5-friction.markdown:
The pointer on the spring scale moved while the wooden block was still sitting on the table. Emma pulled a little harder. The block began to slide. As she pulled it steadily across the level tabletop, the scale showed a little less force than it had just before the block started moving.

“Which number should I write down?” Her teacher asked her to watch the part where the block slid smoothly. When it moved in a straight line at almost constant speed, her forward pull and the backward force of sliding friction were nearly equal. The scale could then tell her roughly how much friction the tabletop exerted on the block.

For the second surface, Emma spread a cloth flat on the table. She used the same block, kept the same side down, and pulled as nearly horizontally as she could. If the block suddenly sped up, she set that reading aside. A few readings from steady slides on each surface would give her something to compare.

ns-physics-force-buoyancy.title: One More Block in the Boat
ns-physics-force-buoyancy.markdown:
Emma floated an empty lunch container in a shallow basin of water, open side up. From the side, she could see the water just touching a stripe on her little boat. Dad gently set a toy block in the middle. The boat bobbed a couple of times. Now the water reached a higher stripe.

Emma held out a finger to compare the marks. “The boat went down a little!” As the container settled deeper, it pushed more water out of the way. The water pushed up on it with a greater force. That upward push is called the buoyant force. Once the boat floated steadily again, the push balanced the weight of the container and the block together.

Dad took the block out. The boat floated higher, and the stripe that had been underwater showed again. If the blocks were piled at one end, the boat might tip. The best time to see how deep it sits is when it's level and floating steadily.

ns-physics-force-inertia.title: The Truck Stops and the Paper Keeps Sliding
ns-physics-force-inertia.markdown:
A toy truck rolled across a level tabletop with a ball of paper in its bed. Thump! The front of the truck hit a soft cloth bumper and stopped. The paper slid all the way to the front of the truck bed. Had something given the paper another push?

The truck and the paper had both been moving forward. The bumper pushed back on the truck, slowing it down quickly. The paper didn't hit the bumper. Friction from the truck bed slowed the paper, too, but there wasn't time for the paper to stop along with the truck. Seen from the table, the paper kept moving forward. Seen from the truck bed, it slid toward the front edge.

An object tends to keep moving the way it was moving. This tendency is called inertia. Imagine taping the paper firmly to the truck bed before the ride. When the truck slowed, the tape could pull back on the paper and help it slow down with the truck.

ns-physics-light-shadow.title: Which Side Gets the Shadow?
ns-physics-light-shadow.markdown:
A paper figure reached one arm toward the edge of the table. A thin shadow arm stretched across the tabletop. Daisy turned the figure around. The shadow arm changed shape. The lamp was still on the left, though, and the shadow still stretched to the right of the figure.

Light from the lamp traveled toward the tabletop. Through an even stretch of air, you can picture its path as a straight line. The paper figure blocked some of the light that would have reached the table. That darker patch was its shadow. Light reflected from other places in the room could still reach the patch, so the shadow could look gray.

Daisy left the figure where it stood and moved the lamp to the right. Now the light came from the right, and the patch where the figure blocked it lay on the left. The paper toes hadn't budged. The shadow at their feet had switched sides.

ns-physics-light-mirror.title: A Turning Mirror Moves a Spot of Light
ns-physics-light-mirror.markdown:
A beam of light struck a little mirror, and a bright spot shone on a white screen nearby. Riley gave the exhibit's knob a gentle turn. The spot slid across the screen. She checked the lamp. It was in the same place. Behind the knob, she saw what had turned. It was the mirror.

The light still followed the same path from the lamp to the mirror. Some of the light that struck the mirror reflected off it. The direction it took depended on the tilt of the mirror. Even a slight turn sent the reflected light in a new direction. It reached a different part of the white screen.

Riley slowly turned the knob back. The spot retraced its path. She marked the two places where it had shone. Starting at either mark, she could trace the beam back to the same little mirror.

ns-physics-light-diffuse.title: A Word You Can Read from Either Side
ns-physics-light-diffuse.markdown:
Near a window lay a mirror and a sheet of white paper with a word penciled on it. From the left, Hugo saw the window frame in the mirror. From the right, he saw the bookshelf. Yet from either place he could read the Chinese character for “spring” on the paper.

When light reflected by the window frame hits a smooth mirror, the mirror reflects it in a particular direction. Hugo could see the frame when his eyes were in the path of that reflected light. On the other side of the table, it was light from the bookshelf that reached him by way of the mirror.

Paper feels smooth, but its surface has tiny bumps. Light striking it reflects in many directions. This is called diffuse reflection. Some light from the paper reached Hugo's eyes on either side of the table. The pencil marks usually reflected less light into his eyes than the white paper did. That made the gray strokes stand out.

ns-g6-periscope.title: A Swallow in the Periscope
ns-g6-periscope.markdown:
A picture of a swallow was hidden behind a piece of cardboard. From her seat at the table, Hannah could see only the cardboard wall. Her teacher handed her a periscope. She looked into the lower opening. First she spotted the bird's two long tail feathers. Then the whole swallow came into view.

Follow the light, starting at the picture. The room lights shone on the card. Some light reflected from it passed above the cardboard wall and entered the top of the periscope. A slanted mirror reflected the light down the tube. At the bottom, a second slanted mirror sent it through the lower opening to Hannah's eyes. The swallow stayed on its card while the light made both turns.

Hannah turned the upper opening toward the bookshelf. Now a row of book spines appeared in the mirror. To find the swallow again, she had to point that opening back toward the card.

ns-physics-light-refraction.title: Why Does a Chopstick Look Bent in Water?
ns-physics-light-refraction.markdown:
Jamie leaned a straight chopstick inside a clear cup half full of water. Looking down through the opening at an angle, she saw what looked like a kink. The part above the water and the part below seemed to meet at an odd angle. She took the chopstick out and looked along its length. It was straight.

Light reflected by the underwater part traveled through water first. At the surface it crossed at an angle into air. The light changed direction where the two materials met. This change is called refraction. When the light reaches your eye, the underwater part appears to lie along a straight line back from the direction the light came in. That puts it in a different place from its actual position.

Jamie moved to the other side of the cup, and the bend looked different again. The chopstick was resting in the very same spot. Her new view caught a different set of light rays coming through the water's surface.

ns-physics-light-spectrum.title: How Can White Light Make a Ribbon of Color?
ns-physics-light-spectrum.markdown:
White light went into a prism. On the other side, a ribbon of color appeared on a white screen. Red ran into orange, then yellow and green. At the far end were shades of blue and violet. Lola wanted to mark where each color ended. She kept looking for a good place to draw a line. Each color faded gently into the next.

The white beam at the exhibit already contained light of many colors. As the light entered the glass prism at an angle and came out through another face, its path bent. In this ordinary glass, violet light bent more than red light did. The colors reached different parts of the screen. This spreading of white light into colors is called dispersion.
