A staff member blocked the lamp. The entire ribbon vanished. When the light shone through again, the colors reappeared in the same places. All along, the screen was white. It was the light that supplied the colors.

ns-g4-sound-ruler.title: The Ruler That Hums
ns-g4-sound-ruler.markdown:
A low buzz came from the edge of the desk. Laura held down one end of a bendy plastic ruler. She gave the tip sticking out over the edge a gentle pluck. Down it went, then up, then down again. That back-and-forth motion is a vibration. As the vibrations grew smaller, the buzz faded away.

She slid the ruler a little farther onto the desk, held it tight, and plucked again. The buzz sounded higher. The shorter overhanging part took less time to go back and forth once. The number of vibrations in one second is called frequency. Within the range of sounds people can hear, a faster vibration usually makes a higher-pitched sound.

This time Laura kept the length the same and plucked more gently. The buzz was quieter. Its pitch sounded much the same. If she wanted to copy those sounds for her desk partner, she had two things to get right. How high did the buzz sound? How loud was it?

ns-physics-sound-medium.title: How Do Paper Cups Carry a Message?
ns-physics-sound-medium.markdown:
“Little bear,” Ryan whispered into a paper cup. Across the table, his big sister held up another cup. “I heard you!” she said. A cotton string stretched between the bottoms of the cups. When they let it go slack, the same words were harder to make out.

Ryan's voice made the air in his cup vibrate. The air set the bottom of the cup vibrating, too. With the string pulled straight, those vibrations could travel along it to the bottom of the other cup. That set the air in his sister's cup vibrating, and she heard “little bear.” A loose string usually does a poorer job of carrying the vibrations from one cup to the other.

His sister could also hear a little of his voice coming straight through the air. She stayed in the same seat while Ryan spoke at about the same volume each time. Comparing how clearly she could hear the words that way helped her tell what difference the string made.

ns-physics-sound-amplitude.title: Why Was the Second Drumbeat Louder?
ns-physics-sound-amplitude.markdown:
Thump. THUMP! The teacher tapped a hand drum lightly, then tapped the same spot a little harder. Josephine listened from the same chair. The second tap sounded much louder.

The drumhead dipped where the teacher tapped it, then sprang back. The greatest distance it moved from its resting position is called the amplitude of the vibration. With a harder tap, the drumhead usually moved farther back and forth. The air around it vibrated more strongly, too. To the same listener sitting in the same spot, the second beat would usually sound louder.

Josephine moved a few steps away and asked for another tap just as hard. Sound spreads out as it travels. Farther away, a drumbeat often sounds quieter. How loud a drum sounds also depends on how far your ears are from it. If music feels too loud, turn down the volume or move farther from the source.

ns-physics-sound-echo.title: A “Hey!” from the Wall
ns-physics-sound-echo.markdown:
“Heeey!” The voice on the recording stopped. After a short pause came another, quieter “Heeey!” Ella played it twice. Even the ends of the two calls sounded alike. There had been only one caller, standing in an open space facing a distant wall.

The shout spread out from the caller. Some of the sound waves that reached the wall reflected back. Sound takes time to travel through air. The caller heard the shout first, then heard it again after it had traveled to the wall and back. With enough time between the two sounds, the second one can be heard as a distinct echo.

The program played another recording, this one made closer to the wall. Sound had a shorter trip to the wall and a shorter trip back. Ella was still waiting for the second “hey.” The sounds had arrived so close together that her ears could hardly pick them apart.

ns-physics-sound-room.title: Drawing the Curtains Shortens the Ring of a Room
ns-physics-sound-room.markdown:
“Turn to page two.” In the nearly empty classroom, Rosie could still hear a trace of “two” after the teacher had finished speaking. She gave a light clap. The clap had a little tail of sound that slowly faded, too.

Sound from a clap spreads in all directions. Some reflects from the walls, the floor, and the desks. Some bounces several more times. These sound waves take paths of different lengths, so they reach your ears at slightly different times. When lots of reflected sounds arrive close together, a word can seem to hang in the air after the speaker stops. That lingering sound is called reverberation.

The teacher drew the thick curtains, returned to the front of the room, and read the sentence again. This time the tail was shorter. The curtains absorbed some of the sound energy, leaving less to bounce around the room. Rosie heard exactly which page to turn to.

ns-physics-sound-wave.title: One Note, Two Wavelengths
ns-physics-sound-wave.markdown:
Two pictures of a sound wave froze at the very same instant on the exhibit screen. The picture on the left showed sound in air. The one on the right showed it in water. Both had the same distance scale. Ruth found a place where the particles were bunched close together and then found the next such bunch. In water, the two bunches were much farther apart.

The pictures showed a steady note traveling from air into water. The wave repeated in the water at the same frequency as the source vibrated. In the time it took to make one vibration, sound traveled farther in water than in air. The distance from one bunch to the next is the wavelength. The same note had a longer wavelength in water.

Ruth fixed a probe at one spot and restarted the animation. With a ruler on a still picture, she could measure the distance between neighboring bunches. With a clock and the probe, she could count how many bunches passed that spot in one second. One measurement told her a length. The other told her how often the pattern repeated.

ns-physics-heat-temperature.title: When the Thermometer Reading Settles Down
ns-physics-heat-temperature.markdown:
Twenty-one, twenty-two... Olivia had her pencil ready, but the thermometer's numbers were still climbing. The water on the table was at room temperature. The thermometer probe had just come out of a cooler cabinet. As soon as she put it in the water, the reading started to rise.

The thermometer was displaying the temperature of its own probe. That probe was cooler than the water. When they came into contact, energy flowed from the warmer water to the probe. As its temperature got closer to the temperature of the water around it, the numbers on the screen began to settle down.

Following the directions, Olivia kept the sensing part under the water and clear of the sides and bottom of the cup. Once the reading steadied near 24, she wrote down 24 degrees Celsius. The climb from 21 to 24 degrees had shown the probe gradually reaching the water's temperature.

ns-physics-heat-conduction.title: Why Does a Metal Spoon Feel Cooler?
ns-physics-heat-conduction.markdown:
A wooden spoon and a metal spoon had spent the night side by side on the table. Zane touched the wood with a fingertip and then touched the metal. “How come this one feels like it just came out of the fridge?” The room temperature had been steady all night. The two dry spoons were actually close to the same temperature.

Zane's finger was warmer than either spoon. When he touched the metal, heat flowed from his skin into the place he touched, then quickly spread farther into the metal. His fingertip lost heat quickly and felt cool. Wood conducts heat more slowly. When the same finger touched the wood, heat usually left his skin more slowly.

Zane spotted another spoon with a metal bowl and a wooden handle. Now he could see how the choice of handle material affected the speed at which heat traveled along it. To find the actual starting temperatures of the two spoons on the table, he would need a suitable thermometer.

ns-physics-heat-convection.title: How Does Air Move Around a Room?
ns-physics-heat-convection.markdown:
In the model room, a radiator stood low on the left and a cool wall stood on the right. Josephine followed the red arrows up from the radiator and the blue arrows down beside the wall. Her finger continued along the floor. There she was, back at the radiator!

Air near the radiator warms and expands. A pocket of this warm air weighs less than an equal-sized pocket of the cooler air around it, so it tends to rise. Nearby air moves in to take its place. Along the cool wall, air cools and becomes denser, so it may sink. As air moves, it carries energy from place to place. This way of transferring heat is called convection.

Back in her classroom, Josephine found a window open a crack and people coming through the door. The loop of arrows in the model showed one simple pattern. A breeze, a row of desks, and an open door can give the air in a real room a much more complicated trip.

ns-physics-heat-radiation.title: A Patch of Sunlight by the Window
ns-physics-heat-radiation.markdown:
A patch of sunlight fell across Dylan's book. As he turned a page, the back of his hand moved into the light. By the time he had read a few lines, his hand felt warm. He shifted it into the shadow of the window frame. After a little while it felt cooler again.

Light from the Sun carried energy across the vast stretch of nearly empty space between the Sun and Earth, then through the window to his hand. His skin absorbed some of that energy and could grow warmer. Energy traveling by electromagnetic waves is called radiation. Both the visible light in sunshine and invisible infrared radiation carry energy.

The frame blocked the direct sunlight. Some light still reflected into the shadow from the rest of the room, but less solar energy reached his hand there. In the sunny patch, his hand had warmed up without touching the window at all.

ns-g6-heat-loss.title: Can a Sleeve Help Water Stay Warm?
ns-g6-heat-loss.markdown:
Two cups of water started at 34 degrees Celsius. Grandpa slipped a thick cloth sleeve around one cup. Liam put lids on both. The cups were alike, held equal amounts of water, and stood together in the same room. Every five minutes Liam took a temperature reading.

At first, the two readings were close. After a while, the cup without the sleeve gave a slightly lower reading. The room was cooler than the water. Heat flowed out through each cup wall, and the surrounding air could carry it away. The thick cloth and the air caught inside it conducted heat slowly. The extra layer slowed the flow of heat out of the cup.

The water in the sleeve was cooling, too. Liam followed both rows of readings from beginning to end to see which cup had cooled faster. Given enough time in a room that stays at the same temperature, the water in both cups would get closer and closer to room temperature.

ns-physics-heat-equilibrium.title: How Warm Will the Mixed Water Be?
ns-physics-heat-equilibrium.markdown:
One cup of water was at 32 degrees Celsius and another was at 24. Adam's sister had used a scale to measure equal masses of water. He watched her pour both portions into a larger cup, gently stir them together, and use a thermometer to check the result. The reading settled close to 28 degrees Celsius.

As the two portions mixed, energy passed from the warmer water to the cooler water. By the time the mixture was the same temperature throughout, the warmer portion had cooled and the cooler portion had warmed. If very little heat goes into the cup or the surroundings, mixing equal masses of water gives a temperature close to halfway between the two starting temperatures.

“What if we put in an extra portion of warm water next time?” Adam moved his finger a little way along the scale from 28 toward 32. With the same amount of cooler water and a larger share of warmer water, the mixture would end up closer to the warmer water's starting temperature.

ns-physics-machines-lever.title: Where Is the Easiest Place to Push a Door?
ns-physics-machines-lever.markdown:
Wendy put her hand close to the hinges and pushed straight against the face of the door. The door moved just a little. She brought it back to its starting position, moved her hand near the handle, and pushed in the same direction. This time the door swung open easily.

A door turns around a line through its hinges. Imagine three dots on the door, one next to that line, one in the middle of the door, and one on the handle. Give the same push squarely against the door at each dot. The farther the dot is from the hinge line, the greater the turning effect. Near the handle, a smaller force will give the same turning effect.

When the door swings through a certain angle, each dot follows its own path. The dot near the hinges moves only a little. The handle sweeps a long arc above the floor. The easiest place for Wendy to push is also the place where her hand travels farthest.

ns-physics-machines-ramp.title: Two Ramps to the Same Platform
ns-physics-machines-ramp.markdown:
Two ramps led up to the same low platform. One was short and steep. The gentler one stretched all the way to the edge of the exhibit. Lucy slowly pulled the same model cart up each ramp. The gentle slope took a lighter pull, but the cart had farther to travel.

The height of the platform was fixed. On the steep ramp, even a short trip along the board lifted the cart quite a bit. The gentler slope spread that same rise over a longer path. If the wheels roll freely and both ramps offer little resistance, keeping the cart moving steadily takes less force on the gentler slope.

Lucy held a paper ruler upright to measure how high the cart had climbed. Then she laid it along the boards to measure how far the cart had traveled. The two upright measurements matched. Along the longer board, her finger passed many more marks on the ruler.

ns-physics-machines-fixed-pulley.title: The Rope Comes Down and the Flag Goes Up
ns-physics-machines-fixed-pulley.markdown:
The flag climbed higher and higher as the person raising it pulled the rope down. Luke looked up. At the very top of the tall flagpole, the rope turned a corner. Later, a small model gave him a closer look at that corner.

At the top sits a little wheel that can turn. Its axle stays attached to the pole. This is a fixed pulley. The rope runs around the rim of the wheel, with the flag on one side and a length of rope to pull on the other. Pull one side down a certain distance, and the other side carries the flag up about the same distance.

With a light rope and a wheel that turns easily, the force needed to raise the flag slowly is about the same as the force needed to lift it straight up. The wheel changes the direction of the pull. Someone standing on the ground can pull down and send the flag up the pole.

ns-physics-machines-moving-pulley.title: A Pulley That Rides with the Basket
ns-physics-machines-moving-pulley.markdown:
A pulley was fastened to a small basket, so the wheel could rise and fall with the basket. One end of a rope was fixed high above it. The rope ran down under the wheel, then back up to a free end. A guide pulled the free end upward. The basket rose one mark on a scale. The children saw her hand travel two marks.

On either side of the wheel, a vertical stretch of rope pulled up. Picture a fixed line drawn across both stretches of rope, well above the wheel. As the basket rises one mark, the stretch of rope from the wheel up to that line gets shorter by one mark on each side. The guide has to pull two marks' worth of rope at the free end. A wheel that moves along with the basket is called a movable pulley.

Together, the two sides of the rope support both the wheel and the basket. With a light rope and a freely turning wheel, the tension is nearly the same on both sides during a slow, steady lift. Each side supports about half the total weight. The guide gets a lighter pull, and her hand travels farther than the basket.

ns-physics-machines-axle.title: One Turn of a Wheel and Axle
ns-physics-machines-axle.markdown:
Abby turned a large disk slowly through one full turn. Her hand went around a big circle at the rim. A little axle at the center also made one full turn. It wound up only a short length of string, so the cloth bag at the end rose just a little.

The disk and the axle are fastened together. This simple machine is called a wheel and axle. The rim of the disk lies far from the center, so it travels farther in one turn than the edge of the small axle does. A push along the direction the rim is moving can turn the axle and slowly lift the bag with a relatively small force.

Abby put one white dot on the rim of the disk and another at the edge of the axle. After half a turn, each dot was exactly opposite its starting point. They had turned through the same angle. One dot had traveled around a large half-circle and the other around a small one.

ns-physics-machines-mechanical-work.title: Why Pull More Rope to Use Less Force?
ns-physics-machines-mechanical-work.markdown:
Two little baskets on the exhibit weighed the same. One hand lifted a basket directly. The other raised a basket using a movable pulley. Both baskets rose slowly by 10 centimeters. The hand using the pulley needed less force and pulled a longer length of rope.

Picture an ideal setup. A basket weighs 4 newtons. Lifting it directly takes a force of 4 newtons through 10 centimeters. On the movable pulley, two vertical stretches of rope support the load. With a very light rope and wheel and very little friction, the hand can apply 2 newtons through 20 centimeters. Half the force goes with twice the distance.

In physics, when a constant force acts in the direction an object moves, you can multiply the force by the distance to find the work done by that force. The two calculations here give the same amount of work. A real pulley has some friction as it turns, so the hand has to pull a little harder.

ns-physics-balance-pressure-seesaw.title: Where Should the Heavier Block Go on a Seesaw?
ns-physics-balance-pressure-seesaw.markdown:
The tabletop seesaw started out level. Two identical wooden blocks sat on the second mark from the pivot, one on each side. The teacher replaced the block on the left with a heavier one. Down went the left end. Could the heavier block stay on the left and still let the board balance?

The teacher held the board level, slid the heavy block a little closer to the pivot, and let go to check. The block weighed just as much as before. Closer to the pivot, though, its weight had a smaller turning effect. At just the right spot, the two weights tried to turn the board equally strongly in opposite directions. The board stayed level.

Now the blocks were different distances from the pivot. The lighter block sat farther out, and the heavier block sat closer in. Moving the light block one more mark to the right would increase its turning effect. This time the right end would go down first.

ns-physics-balance-pressure-stable-box.title: Will a Tall Block Tip Over?
ns-physics-balance-pressure-stable-box.markdown:
Lying on the table, the long rectangular block looked like a bench. Standing on end, it looked like a tower. Stacy gently tilted it, keeping one bottom edge against the table. When the block started out lying flat, it had to tilt quite a way before it would topple.

Imagine the block's weight acting at a single point called its center of gravity. This solid block is made of the same material throughout, so the point is right in the middle. Picture a line going straight down from that point as the block tilts slowly. While the line falls inside the block's original footprint, letting go allows gravity to settle it back down. Once the line passes beyond the bottom edge that's holding it up, gravity tips the block the rest of the way over.

Lying flat, the block has a lower center of gravity and a wider base in the direction of the tilt. Stacy drew the vertical line in sketches of both positions. Now she could see how much farther the same block could lean in one position before it fell.

ns-physics-balance-pressure-wide-foot.title: Why Are Snowshoes So Wide?
ns-physics-balance-pressure-wide-foot.markdown:
In the old photograph, a pair of snowshoes stretched far beyond the edges of ordinary shoes. Webbing filled each frame. Every step left a broad print. Hope thought such big shoes must feel clumsy. Then she noticed the deep marks ordinary shoes had left in the soft snow nearby.

The same person standing on the same kind of snow pushes down with about the same total force. A wider area of contact spreads that force over more snow. Dividing the total downward force by the area it acts on gives the average pressure. Snowshoes reduce that pressure, so the person usually sinks less deeply.

Wide boards under the feet of a table can help in much the same way. If the same things stay on the tabletop, the ground supports about the same total weight. With boards underneath, a wider patch of ground carries the force, and the feet may leave shallower marks.

ns-physics-balance-pressure-water-pressu.title: How Does Water Pressure Change with Depth?
ns-physics-balance-pressure-water-pressu.markdown:
A probe just a finger's width below the surface gave a small reading on the screen. The guide lowered it slowly into the tank, and the number grew. She stopped, then moved the probe sideways at the same depth. Once the water was still, the reading was almost exactly what it had been before the sideways move.

The deeper you go in still water, the taller the column of water above you. Its weight makes the pressure increase with depth. You can feel pressure from the side, too. Water pushes straight against the side of the tank, at a right angle to its wall. Water pressure at two spots at the same depth is equal if the water has the same density and the air pressure at the surface is the same.

The tank next to this one had a lower bottom. To find the same water pressure in that tank, the guide would measure the same distance down from its surface. Counting marks up from the bottom could lead her to a different depth.

ns-physics-balance-pressure-suction.title: Why Did the Suction Cup Come Loose?
ns-physics-balance-pressure-suction.markdown:
Dad pressed a soft suction cup flat against a bathroom tile. Some air escaped around the edge. When he let go, the cup sprang back a little while the rim stayed tight against the tile. How could that little cup hold its place on the wall?

As the cup sprang back, the space under it grew. The small amount of air trapped in that space had a lower pressure than the air outside. Outside air pressed the cup firmly against the tile. Friction between the cup and the wall could then help support the downward weight on its hook. A smooth, flat tile gives the rim a good chance to seal.

One day, a corner of the rim lifted. Air slipped in through the gap, and the difference between the inside and outside pressures gradually shrank. With less force pressing the cup against the wall, the hook slid down. A tiny opening at the rim had changed the pressure under the whole cup.

ns-physics-balance-pressure-hydraulic.title: A Small Piston and a Large One
ns-physics-balance-pressure-hydraulic.markdown:
At a clear exhibit, a tube joined two liquid-filled cylinders, one narrow and one wide. Each cylinder had a piston, a part that fit across its opening and could slide up and down. The guide slowly pushed the small piston down. A board resting on the big piston rose a little.

An extra push on the small piston increased the pressure of the liquid beneath it. That increase in pressure was transmitted throughout the enclosed liquid. The larger piston had a wider face. The same increase in pressure, acting over a greater area, gave it a greater extra push upward.

Now look at how far each piston moved. Almost exactly the amount of liquid pushed out of the narrow cylinder entered the wider one. The wide cylinder had a larger cross-sectional area, so the same amount of liquid lifted its piston only a little. The marks beside the small piston showed a longer trip than the marks beside the large one.

ns-physics-lenses-magnifier.title: Pencil Strokes Under a Magnifying Glass
ns-physics-lenses-magnifier.markdown:
The Chinese character for “small” looked surprisingly big inside the frame. Nell moved the plastic magnifier aside. The writing on the card was as tiny as ever. She held the lens above the card again and could make out fine pencil marks along the edges of the strokes.

The lens was thick in the middle and thin at the edges. It was a convex lens. Light spread out from every point on the writing. Some of it changed direction as it passed through the lens and entered her eye. With the lettering close enough to the lens, tracing that incoming light backward made it look as though it came from a larger, upright character.

A sheet of white paper placed where the big character seemed to be couldn't catch that enlarged image. The light reaching Nell's eye had passed through the lens. Extending those rays backward in her imagination placed the image on the same side as the card. When she looked through the lens again, the great big “small” was clear as ever.

ns-physics-lenses-screen-image.title: Why Is the Writing on the Screen Upside Down?
ns-physics-lenses-screen-image.markdown:
A character gradually came into focus on a white paper screen. Cameron tilted his head and recognized it. It was the Chinese character for “up,” upside down! The brightly lit card still stood at the far end of the table. A lens stood between the card and the screen.

It was a convex lens. With the card far enough from it, light reflected from one point at the top of the character came together lower down on the other side of the lens. Light from a point at the bottom came together higher up. Light from many points met at different places on the screen and formed an upside-down image.

The teacher moved the screen back a little. Light that had come together was already spreading apart again. Each point now covered a little patch on the screen, making the edges of the strokes look fuzzy. Back in its old position, the screen caught a sharp image of “up” again. That was where the light actually came together.

ns-physics-lenses-focus.title: Which Number Is in Focus?
ns-physics-lenses-focus.markdown:
The box in front had the Chinese character for “one,” a single horizontal stroke. The box behind it said “two,” with two strokes. Adam's brother focused his camera on the front box and took a picture. Adam could see tiny pencil marks along the “one.” Behind it, the two strokes blurred together. His brother focused on the back box and took another picture. Now “two” was sharp and “one” was fuzzy.

Inside the camera is a surface called a sensor that records incoming light. When rays from one point on a letter pass through the lens and meet right on the sensor, that point looks sharp. Light from boxes at different distances usually comes together at different distances behind the lens. With the front box in focus, each point on the back box could spread into a small blurry spot on the sensor.

Adam put the boxes side by side, equally far from the camera. His brother kept the same settings and focused on that row. Light from both numbers could now meet close to the sensor. Both numbers came out sharp in the same picture.

ns-physics-lenses-aperture.title: The Opening Inside a Camera Lens
ns-physics-lenses-aperture.markdown:
Several thin, overlapping blades surrounded a hole inside the model lens. When Bridget turned a dial, the hole widened or narrowed. Photographers call that opening the aperture. Its size affects how much of a scene looks sharp in the photograph.

Two pictures at the exhibit showed a model boat in front and boxes with writing behind it. The boat, the boxes, and the camera had stayed in the same places. Both times the photographer focused on the bow. With a wide aperture, the bow looked sharp and the writing looked fuzzy. Narrowing the opening a little narrowed the bundles of light from the boxes. They spread into smaller spots on the sensor. A greater range of distances in front of the camera now looked reasonably sharp. That range is called the depth of field.

The smaller opening did something else, too. Less light could pass through in the same amount of time. Bridget found the aperture and exposure time listed under each photograph. Now she could see why photographers often consider the two settings together.

ns-physics-lenses-glasses.title: Glasses Bring the Bus Stop Sign into Focus
ns-physics-lenses-glasses.markdown:
Harry took off his glasses. He could still read the booklet in his hand, but the writing on the distant bus stop sign looked blurry. With his glasses back on, he could pick out the individual strokes again.

At the back of the eye is a light-sensitive layer called the retina. Imagine a model of a nearsighted eye looking at one bright point far away. When the eye is relaxed and looking into the distance, light from that point comes together in front of the retina. By the time it reaches the retina, it has begun to spread out again. A point becomes a little patch, and the fine strokes of a letter can run together.

Glasses for nearsightedness use diverging lenses. They spread the light slightly before it enters the eye. The eye then brings the light back together. With lenses that suit Harry's eyes, the light from the sign comes together on his retinas, and the faraway writing looks much clearer.

ns-physics-lenses-microscope.title: Two Lenses in a Microscope
ns-physics-lenses-microscope.markdown:
The teacher set a tiny printed letter under the microscope. Looking through the eyepiece, Summer could see the sharp bend in one stroke as clearly as a corner on a big road sign. She looked up. There were lenses at the other end of the tube, close to the sample. What was each set of lenses doing?

In this ordinary compound light microscope, the lens set nearest the sample is called the objective. Light from the sample passes through the objective to form an enlarged image inside the tube. That image is what the eyepiece looks at. The eyepiece, close to Summer's eye, acts like a magnifying glass. It makes that first image look even larger.

Summer traced the route from the bottom of the tube to the top. First came the sample. Then came the image made by the objective. Finally the light passed through the eyepiece into her eye. With both sets of lenses working together, the lighting set properly, and the microscope in focus, she could see the fine detail in that little corner.

ns-physics-musical-sound-guitar-tension.title: A Higher Note on the Same Guitar String
ns-physics-musical-sound-guitar-tension.markdown:
The music teacher plucked a guitar string, listened, and turned a tuning peg. The next note sounded a little higher. Melody watched the teacher's fingers closely. She kept plucking the same open string, with no finger pressing it against the fingerboard.

The string is free to vibrate between the bridge and a piece near the head of the guitar called the nut. As the teacher tuned the string, this stretch stayed almost exactly the same length. The string itself grew tighter. Waves traveled back and forth along it faster, so it vibrated more times each second. The note went up in pitch.

The teacher loosened the string a little on purpose and plucked it once more. This time Melody could hear the note go down. To predict how high a string will sound, she would need to know how tightly it was stretched as well as how much of it could vibrate.

ns-physics-musical-sound-xylophone-rest.title: The Soft Supports Under a Xylophone Bar
ns-physics-musical-sound-xylophone-rest.markdown:
The wooden bars of the xylophone looked as if they lay flat on their frame. Claire bent down for a closer look. Each bar rested on soft cord near its ends, leaving a long space underneath the middle. The teacher gently tapped one bar in the center. A clear note rang on after the tap.

As a bar bends back and forth, some parts move more than others. In the vibration that produces its lowest note, the center moves quite a bit. Near either end is a spot that moves very little. These spots are called nodes. With the soft supports near the nodes, the frame interferes very little with this vibration, so the note can ring for a while.

The teacher struck the same bar again. While it rang, she lightly touched its center with a finger. The sound quickly died away. Now Claire could see why the maker had left all that space under the middle. It gave the moving part of the bar room to vibrate.

ns-physics-musical-sound-pipe-length.title: Which Pipe Plays the Lower Note?
ns-physics-musical-sound-pipe-length.markdown:
First came a note from a short pipe, then one from a long pipe. The second note sounded much lower. Ian peered down the pipes. All he could see inside was air. The two pipes at the exhibit had nearly the same width, both had two open ends, and each was playing its lowest resonant note.

Air itself can vibrate. As sound waves travel back and forth inside a pipe, vibrations at certain frequencies reinforce each other. This is called resonance. In a pipe open at both ends, the wavelength of the lowest resonant note is about twice the length of the pipe. The longer pipe has a longer wavelength for that note. Its frequency is lower, and so is the pitch Ian hears.

In the next row of the exhibit, the pipes had one end closed. That changed the way the air could vibrate. Ian now looked at the ends before he compared lengths. Two pipes of much the same length can have different lowest notes if their ends are different.

ns-physics-musical-sound-guitar-box.title: A Guitar's Body Vibrates, Too
ns-physics-musical-sound-guitar-box.markdown:
A single string stretched across a frame made such a faint sound that Willa had to listen closely from the back row. The guide switched to an acoustic guitar and plucked a note about as high. From the very same seat, she heard the beginning of the note clearly and could follow it as it died away.

A thin string on its own moves very little air. On a wooden guitar the string is attached to a bridge. When the string vibrates, the bridge carries its vibration to a much larger surface, the soundboard. The moving soundboard pushes more air, and the air inside the hollow body vibrates, too. Sound from the string reaches the room much more effectively.

The same soundboard and body respond more strongly to some frequencies than to others. Certain parts of a note stand out. Together they give the guitar its own recognizable sound. Willa looked again at the little bridge. She had found the place where the vibrating string set the body in motion.

ns-physics-musical-sound-timbre.title: The Same Note on Two Instruments
ns-physics-musical-sound-timbre.markdown:
A violin played over the classroom speakers. Next came a flute. The teacher had chosen notes of the same pitch that sounded about equally loud. Joel closed his eyes. Almost as soon as the second note began, he could tell the instrument had changed.

A single musical note often sets the air vibrating at several frequencies at once. The lowest one, called the fundamental, usually tells us the pitch. Other parts of the sound ring along with it, some more strongly than others. A flute and a violin playing the same note produce different mixtures of these sounds. How a note begins and how it dies away also give the ear clues.

Joel asked to hear just the beginning again. He caught the sound of the bow first touching the violin string. Listening to the whole recording, he could also recognize the flute's long, steady note. Musicians use the word timbre for qualities like these that give an instrument its own sound.

ns-physics-musical-sound-sound-beats.title: Two Steady Notes That Seem to Pulse
ns-physics-musical-sound-sound-beats.markdown:
One button played a long, steady note. The other played a steady note just a little higher. Taylor turned on both and listened from the same spot. The sound grew louder, then softer, over and over. Both volume knobs were sitting still.

Where the two sounds reach an ear, their vibrations add together. At times they keep pace, squeezing the air together or letting it spread out together. Their combined vibration then grows stronger. At other times one wave squeezes while the other lets up, and the combined vibration grows weaker. When the frequencies are close but slightly different, the waves slip out of step and back into step again. Those regular swells in loudness are called beats.

Taylor adjusted the notes until their frequencies were even closer. There was a longer wait from one loud swell to the next. The smaller the difference between the frequencies, the longer it took for the vibrations to come back into step.

ns-physics-electromagnetism-static-paper.title: How Can a Comb Pick Up Paper?
ns-physics-electromagnetism-static-paper.markdown:
A corner of the paper lifted while there was still a gap between it and the comb. Avery had just run the plastic comb through his hair. He moved it a little closer. The thin scrap jumped up and stuck to the back of the comb.

As hair and plastic touch and rub together, tiny particles called electrons can move from one to the other. This can leave the comb electrically charged. The paper starts out with its positive and negative charges balanced overall. As the charged comb approaches, the charges in the paper shift apart a little. Charge opposite to the comb's ends up slightly closer to it. The attraction over that shorter distance is stronger, so the paper feels a pull toward the comb. A strong enough pull lifts the light scrap.

Avery thought of the magnet on the message board. For this event, he wrote a different set of clues in his notebook. There was the plastic comb he had run through his hair, the scrap on the desk, and the pull of static electricity between them.

ns-physics-electromagnetism-switch.title: The Switch Inside a Flashlight
ns-physics-electromagnetism-switch.markdown:
Click. A circle of light appeared on the wall. Click again, and it disappeared. Through the side of a model in a display case, Tilly could see the switch. Two little metal contacts behind the button came together or moved apart each time it was pressed.

A battery has two terminals. In a flashlight with a charged battery, a working lamp, and good wires, closing the switch completes a loop between the terminals through the lamp. Electric charges can keep moving along this connected path. That flow is an electric current, and the lamp lights up. Opening the switch leaves a gap. The current stops and the light goes out.

Tilly traced a circuit diagram on paper. Her finger went from one battery terminal through the lamp and the closed switch, all the way to the other terminal. She drew a gap at the switch. That was where her finger's path came to an end.

ns-physics-electromagnetism-branches.title: One Light Goes Out. What Happens to the Other?
ns-physics-electromagnetism-branches.markdown:
Each of two model houses had two lights on. The guide opened a switch beside one light in the first house. Both went dark. In the second house, opening a switch beside one light left the other one shining. Rowan set the two circuit diagrams side by side under the light.

In the first diagram, the two lamps lay one after the other along a single path. This arrangement is called a series circuit. Opening the switch broke the path for both lamps. In the second diagram the path split in two, with one lamp on each branch. The ends of both branches joined the same two connection points. This arrangement is called a parallel circuit. When one branch opened, the other lamp still had a complete path connecting the two battery terminals.

Rowan spotted a stretch of wire between the battery and the place where the path split. Both branches shared it. A break there would disconnect them both. To figure out which lights will keep shining, Rowan first needed to find exactly where the switch was.

ns-physics-electromagnetism-compass-curr.title: A Compass Needle Turns When Current Flows
ns-physics-electromagnetism-compass-curr.markdown:
On the exhibit table, a compass needle pointed roughly north. The guide pressed a button, and the needle swung to one side. When she let go, it wobbled and gradually turned back. The wire beside the compass had stayed in the same place the whole time.

The little magnetic needle can turn in a horizontal plane, like a hand on a clock laid flat. With no other magnets or strong currents nearby, it usually settles along the horizontal direction of Earth's magnetic field. When the guide pressed the button, current flowed through the wire and created another magnetic field around it. At the needle, the two fields combined. The needle turned to line up with the new horizontal direction.

The guide reversed the current once. The magnetic field made by the wire reversed, too. With the wire and compass arranged as they were in this exhibit, the needle now swung to the other side of its original direction. The button was released, the current stopped, and the needle returned.

ns-physics-electromagnetism-motor.title: What Makes a Fan Blade Turn?
ns-physics-electromagnetism-motor.markdown:
The blades of the little fan were fastened to a shaft. Through a clear cover, Sam could see that the shaft in the teacher's model DC motor was attached to a coil of wire. A magnet stood on each side, fixed in place. The coil turned between them.

When electric current passed through the coil, it ran in opposite directions along the two sides. In the magnetic field of this model, the wires on those sides felt forces in opposite directions. A push one way on one side and the other way on the other side turned the coil around its shaft. At the right point in the turn, a device in the model reversed the current in the coil so the turning push could continue.

As the shaft turned, the blades fixed to it turned, too. They pushed air forward. Sam traced the moving air back to the blades, along the shaft, and all the way to the spinning coil inside the cover.

ns-physics-electromagnetism-generator.title: What Lights the Bulb When the Crank Turns?
ns-physics-electromagnetism-generator.markdown:
A turn of the handle lit the little bulb on the exhibit. A slower turn gave a dimmer light. Lee looked through the clear cover. The handle turned a coil of wire between two magnets, and the coil was connected to the lamp circuit.

Picture a thin sheet of paper stretched across the opening in the coil. When the sheet faces straight into the magnetic field, a larger amount of field passes through that area. Turn the sheet edge-on, and much less passes through. The measure of the magnetic field passing through a surface is called magnetic flux. A change in flux over time produces a voltage in the coil. When the circuit is closed, current can flow through the bulb.

The energy for the lamp came from the hand turning the handle. Some of the mechanical energy became electrical energy. The bulb gave off light and warmed its surroundings. When Lee stopped the handle, the coil and the magnets were at rest relative to each other. The little lamp in this model went out.

ns-physics-energy-ball-ramp.title: Starting the Ball a Little Higher
ns-physics-energy-ball-ramp.markdown:
Near the bottom of a toy ramp, Parker made two marks close together. They marked off a short stretch where the ball could be timed. On the first run, Parker let the ball go from low on the ramp. On the second, the same ball started a little higher. Both times it rolled down on its own. It took less time to pass between the marks on the second run.

Use the bottom of the ramp as the starting point for comparing heights. A ball set higher up has more gravitational potential energy because of its position relative to Earth. As it rolls down and loses height, some of that energy changes into kinetic energy, the energy of motion. Both the ball's forward motion and its spinning motion carry kinetic energy. A real ball and ramp also change shape slightly as the ball rolls, turning some mechanical energy into internal energy.

Parker wrote the two times beside the marks. They showed how fast the ball covered the same short stretch at the bottom. The two starting points were different distances up the ramp. Timing the whole trip from release to the bottom would answer a different question.

ns-physics-energy-pendulum.title: What Makes a Pendulum Swing Back?
ns-physics-energy-pendulum.markdown:
The pendulum ball swung out to the right. It seemed to pause in midair, then swung back to the left. Alex watched in slow motion. Near the right-hand end, the ball's positions in one frame and the next were very close together. At the instant it changed direction, its speed was zero.

As the ball swung down, it lost height and gravitational potential energy changed into kinetic energy. It moved fastest at the lowest point. Climbing the other side, it slowed as kinetic energy changed back into gravitational potential energy. At the rightmost point its speed reached zero for an instant. Part of gravity's pull still acted along the curved path toward the bottom, so the ball immediately began speeding up that way.

Alex marked the rightmost point on several swings. Each mark was a little lower than the one before. Air resistance and friction at the pivot turned some of the pendulum's mechanical energy into internal energy. With less mechanical energy, it couldn't swing back quite as high.

ns-physics-energy-spring.title: A Spring Pushes Back
ns-physics-energy-spring.markdown:
Inside a clear cover, a spring lay on its side. Its right end was attached to a pointer that could slide left and right. A staff member used a handle to push the pointer left, squeezing the spring shorter. When she let go, the pointer slid right, passed the middle, and sprang back.

A hand compressing a spring exerts a force and pushes one end through a distance. That means the hand does work. Some of that work is stored as energy in the spring's changed shape. It is called elastic potential energy. Released, the spring tends to return to its original length. It pushes the pointer to the right, turning stored energy into the kinetic energy of the moving parts.

The pointer slid back and forth a few times. Each trip was shorter than the one before. Friction changed some of the mechanical energy into internal energy. Eventually the pointer stopped near the middle. The effect of that first push could be followed through every slide of the pointer.

ns-physics-energy-rebound.title: Why Does Each Bounce Get Lower?
ns-physics-energy-rebound.markdown:
Thump, thump, thump. A soft ball dropped from a low height onto a mat and bounced a little lower each time. Reese froze the slow-motion video at the first contact. The ball looked a bit flat, and the mat had a little dent.

As the ball fell, gravitational potential energy turned into kinetic energy. On impact, the ball and the mat squeezed against each other. Their changed shapes temporarily stored some of the energy. As they sprang back, they returned part of that energy to the ball moving upward. Some energy became internal energy in the mat and the ball, and a small part traveled away with the sound of the thump.

Reese read the highest point of the second bounce on a scale beside the mat. With less mechanical energy to carry the ball up, its peak was lower than the last one. The ball looked round again, but the different heights on the scale kept a record of the bounces.

ns-physics-energy-palms.title: How Does Rubbing Your Hands Warm Them?
ns-physics-energy-palms.markdown:
Tara gently pressed her palms together and counted to five. She rested a while, then put her hands together again. This time she rubbed her palms back and forth as she counted to five. They felt warmer than before.

When one palm slides against the other, there is friction between the skin surfaces. Muscles in the hands and arms keep doing work to maintain that motion. Through friction, some of the energy supplied by the body becomes internal energy in the skin and nearby tissue. The palms can warm up. Simply holding two hands together also changes how they lose heat to their surroundings.

The second count took about as long as the first. What Tara had added was the sliding motion. She wrote down how her palms felt when she just held them together and how they felt after rubbing. To say exactly how many degrees Celsius their temperature had risen, she would need suitable temperature measurements.

ns-physics-energy-power.title: Lifting a Box of Books in Half the Time
ns-physics-energy-power.markdown:
A display at the library showed two people taking turns lifting the same box of books from the floor to a table half a meter high. One person took two seconds and the other took four. Each started with the box at rest and brought it to rest on the table. The box gained the same gravitational potential energy both times.

If we ignore air resistance, the hands also did the same work on the box. Suppose the box weighs 10 newtons. Lifting it half a meter takes 5 joules of work. In two seconds, that averages 2.5 joules per second. In four seconds, it averages 1.25 joules per second. Divide work by time to find average power. Power is measured in watts. One watt is one joule per second.

For the same 5 joules, the first person's average power in lifting the box was 2.5 watts. The second person's was half as much. Those numbers describe how quickly each person did the lifting work. To tell who worked up more of a sweat, you'd need information beyond the display.

ns-g1-weather-signs.title: A Look at the Sky Before School
ns-g1-weather-signs.markdown:
Before leaving home, Hugh put a slip of paper on the shoe cabinet. He folded it into three panels, one for each look at the weather outside. Before breakfast, gray clouds filled the sky. The ground was still dry. All he drew in the first panel was cloud.

During breakfast, something went pitter-patter outside the window. Raindrops were making little rings in a puddle. Hugh added raindrops to his second panel. Dad set an umbrella beside the schoolbag, so Hugh drew that, too.

By afternoon the rain had stopped. A patch of blue sky showed through a gap in the clouds, and the leaves were still stirring. Hugh finished his third drawing and unfolded the paper for Grandma. Her finger went from gray clouds to raindrops to blue sky. “So when I came to pick you up,” she said, “we were already in the third picture!”

ns-earth-wind-ribbon.title: Which Way Is the Flag Blowing?
ns-earth-wind-ribbon.markdown:
The flag hung against its pole. Then, with a snap, it spread out. From his classroom window, Logan could see the loose corner pointing toward the reading corner. On the school map, the reading corner was west of the flagpole.

The flag streamed west because moving air was pushing it west. To name a wind, though, we say where the air comes from. Air moving from east to west makes an east wind. On his map, Logan drew an arrow with its tail in the east and its point in the west.

A little later the flag drooped again. Leaves behind another building were still moving gently. Buildings and trees can shelter places from wind and change the direction of the air flowing nearby. Logan added “by the flagpole, in the afternoon” to his notes. Anyone reading them could now place that particular gust.

ns-g3-weather-log.title: Three Temperature Readings in One Day
ns-g3-weather-log.markdown:
At 8 a.m., Natalie recorded 18 degrees Celsius. At noon, she recorded 24 degrees Celsius. At 5 p.m., it was 22 degrees Celsius. She used the same thermometer each time and waited for the reading to settle. All day it stayed at the same height in a shady spot on campus where air could flow freely.

Why choose the spot so carefully? Natalie wanted to measure the temperature of the air. Direct sunlight could heat the instrument itself and affect its reading. Using the same method all day made the morning, midday, and late-afternoon numbers easier to compare.

Noon was 6 degrees Celsius warmer than morning. By late afternoon the temperature had fallen 2 degrees Celsius from the noon reading. Her desk partner asked when the day had been warmest. Natalie looked at the blank stretch from noon to five. “Of the three times we measured, noon was warmest,” she said. “To answer your question, we'd need more readings from the afternoon.”

ns-earth-cloud-rain.title: How Do Clouds Make Rain?
ns-earth-cloud-rain.markdown:
Daisy had just one ribbon left to tie on a bookmark. Gray clouds already covered the sky above the roof, but the ground outside the hallway was dry. By the time she tied the knot, drops had made dark spots on the paving bricks. The clouds had been there all along. Why had the rain taken a while?

Moist air often cools as it rises. When conditions are right, water vapor condenses into tiny drops. Cold clouds can also contain ice crystals. A cloud is made of many such droplets or ice crystals. Tiny drops fall very slowly, and rising air can help keep them aloft.

Inside a cloud, some drops bump together and join to make larger drops. Sometimes ice crystals grow and fall, then melt into raindrops as they pass through warmer air. Rain can also evaporate on the way down. Only the drops that reached the ground left spots on the bricks. Daisy could see those spots from the hallway. She had learned about the part inside the cloud from a science diagram.

ns-earth-fog-visibility.title: Where Did the Distant Rooftop Go?
ns-earth-fog-visibility.markdown:
From one window, Clara could usually pick out a low wall, the branches of a Chinese parasol tree, and a building farther away. This morning the wall was clear. The branches looked like faint pencil lines. The faraway rooftop had almost disappeared in the fog.

Fog contains many tiny drops of water hanging in the air. On some clear nights the ground cools, and the damp air touching it cools, too. Water vapor can then condense into little drops. As light passes through fog, the drops scatter it in many directions. Light from the distant roof has to travel through more fog. The difference in brightness between the building and the sky fades, and its outline gets harder to see.

Later that morning the branches appeared more clearly. After a while the rooftop came into view. Warming air near the ground can let fog droplets evaporate again. Wind can also carry fog away. With her familiar window for a lookout, Clara could tell just when the roof reappeared.

ns-earth-weather-climate.title: Does It Often Rain Here in the Fall?
ns-earth-weather-climate.markdown:
“Does it rain a lot where you live in October?” Charlie's cousin wrote after receiving a photograph of a rainy morning. Charlie opened his weather notebook. It covered eight days, three rainy and five sunny. The photo matched one of the little raindrops on his page.

That particular fall shower was weather. To find out how much rain usually falls there in October, Charlie would need the local weather station's October records for many years. The long-term patterns in the weather, including which seasons are rainy and how much years vary, describe a place's climate. Weather agencies often use 30 consecutive years of data to calculate standard climate averages.

Charlie tucked a fresh sheet into his reply. On one line he wrote, “It rained that morning.” He saved another line for the local average October rainfall over many years. He already had the date for his first line. For the second, he needed the first and last years the station had used in its average.

ns-earth-zhangjiajie-pillars.title: Tracing the Stone Pillars of Zhangjiajie
ns-earth-zhangjiajie-pillars.markdown:
From a distance, the mountains in a photograph of Zhangjiajie looked like stands of tall, straight bamboo. Mason leaned in. Real trees were growing on top of those giant “bamboo tips”! So many tall, narrow rock pillars stood together that people call the landscape a forest of peaks.

Many of these pillars are made of quartz sandstone. Long ago, some of the rock masses that now stand apart were joined together. Cracks already ran through the rock. As the land rose and running water wore it away, water gradually cut valleys along the cracks. Some chunks of rock also broke away from the cliffs. The rock left standing between the valleys forms today's tall peaks.

Mason traced two of the peaks on paper. His pencil went from one summit down into a deep valley, then up the side of the next peak. He left a little white space at the valley floor. Anyone looking at the drawing could see how deep the gap between the pillars was.

ns-g5-loess.title: How Did the Loess Plateau Get Its Gullies?
ns-g5-loess.markdown:
Toby was drawing China's Loess Plateau. Just as he finished the top of a slope, he noticed a gully cutting across it in the photograph. Two smaller channels joined a wider one. The paths taken by rainwater helped explain those cuts in the land.

Some rain soaks into the soil on a hillside. Some flows downhill over the surface. This flowing water is called runoff. It can loosen soil particles and carry them away. Small streams of water meet in low spots. When water scours the same spot again and again, a shallow groove can grow wider and deeper. Water has been wearing away many of the plateau's gullies for a very long time.

In a classroom tray, two little slopes had been made from the same soil at nearly the same angle. The teacher let a little water flow slowly over just one of them and left the other slope dry for comparison. A shallow groove appeared there, and a small pile of sediment collected at the foot. Toby could see soil being carried away and then deposited. How deep a real gully grows also depends on the slope, plant cover, soil, and the rains that fall over time.

ns-earth-yellow-river-sediment.title: Where Does the Yellow River's Mud Go?
ns-earth-yellow-river-sediment.markdown:
The same cup appeared in two photographs. In the first, the water was muddy from top to bottom. In the second, a layer of mud lined the bottom. Blake turned the pictures over. The first had been taken just after stirring. The second showed the cup after it had stood still for a while.

Water carries particles of mud and sand called sediment. When the water slows down, some particles settle. Among particles of similar material and shape, coarser ones usually settle faster. Finer ones can stay suspended longer. The layer on the bottom of the cup had once been mixed throughout the water.

The Yellow River carries sediment all the way to its mouth in Shandong, where it enters the Bohai Sea. Some settles there. Years of deposits can build stretches of land out into the sea. Tides and waves can move the sediment again. One part of the coast can build up while another erodes and retreats. Settling was easy to see in the cup. Satellite images taken at different times show where the shoreline itself has changed.

ns-earth-dunhuang-dunes.title: A Grain of Sand on a Dunhuang Dune
ns-earth-dunhuang-dunes.markdown:
In a photograph of Mingsha Mountain near Dunhuang, Gavin spotted little ripples on a dune and a curved ridge along its top. He picked an imaginary grain of sand and tried to sketch a route it might have taken.

A strong enough wind can roll loose grains along the ground. It can also lift grains into short, low hops. When a hopping grain lands, it may knock other grains into motion. Where the wind can no longer carry as much sand, some gets left behind. Many grains can gradually build up into a dune.

With the wind coming from the right direction, a grain can move up the gentler slope facing the wind, cross the ridge, and settle on the sheltered side. If the pile gets too steep, some sand slides down. The wind around Mingsha Mountain changes direction. Gavin labeled his arrow “a possible path in one gust.” To measure how far the ridge had moved in a year, he'd need pictures of the same place taken at different times.

ns-earth-guilin-karst.title: Waterways Inside Guilin's Limestone Hills
ns-earth-guilin-karst.markdown:
Several stone peaks rose from fairly flat land in a photograph of Guilin. Grace opened a cutaway drawing, too. Under some of the hills, it showed caves. How could thin cracks at the surface connect with passages underground?

Much of the area is limestone. As rainwater passes through the air and soil, some carbon dioxide dissolves in it, making the water slightly acidic. Flowing through limestone, that water can dissolve some of the rock's minerals and carry them away. Over a long time, water passing through cracks can widen them. Some cracks join up to form underground channels or even caves. As the rock at the surface is slowly worn away by dissolving and other processes, tall limestone peaks can remain. A landscape shaped by dissolving rock is called karst.

Grace set the Guilin photograph beside a picture of Zhangjiajie's peaks. One caption said limestone. The other said quartz sandstone. She could trace the outline of either peak from a photograph. To learn how it formed, she also needed clues from the kind of rock and the traces water left behind.

ns-earth-tianshan-glacier.title: A Glacier on the Move in the Tianshan Mountains
ns-earth-tianshan-glacier.markdown:
High in the Tianshan Mountains of Xinjiang, the tongue of Urumqi Glacier No. 1 reaches down a valley at the head of the Urumqi River. A television camera lingered on the ice. Skyler could hardly see it move. One way scientists track a glacier is to measure the positions of the same set of markers again after some time has passed.

Snow that builds up over many years high in the mountains gradually packs into ice. When the ice grows thick enough, gravity can make it slowly change shape and flow. In some places it also slides along its bed. Comparing the markers' positions reveals how far the ice has flowed. The position of the very tip also depends on new snow and on ice loss. Even when melting makes the tip retreat, the ice can still be flowing down the valley.

Moving ice carries broken rocks that scrape the valley floor and walls. Some valleys shaped this way have a broad floor and steep walls. A slice across one looks like the letter U. Scratches on the rock and piles of debris left by the ice give more clues to a glacier's past. Skyler looked from the ice on television to the measurements. With a long enough interval, its slow progress could be measured after all.

ns-g2-moon-draw.title: Three Drawings of the Moon
ns-g2-moon-draw.markdown:
On Monday evening, Rachel saw a crescent Moon from inside her home. She drew the bright curve and wrote the date beside it. Thick clouds covered the sky on Thursday. She wrote a four-character note in Chinese that meant “Cloudy. No Moon seen.”

By Saturday, she could see the Moon again. Its bright part was wider, almost a semicircle. A few days later she saw it for the third time. Now the bright part bulged beyond a semicircle. She lined up the three dated drawings. Her finger could follow the thin crescent filling out from one picture to the next.

Her brother asked what the Moon had looked like on the day in between. Rachel opened the notebook to Thursday. Clouds had covered that part of the sky, so clouds were all she had drawn. The three Moon pictures on the table came from three evenings when she had seen it for herself. The cloud page told her about the cloudy evening between sightings, too.

ns-earth-moon-crater.title: Are Those Circles on the Moon Little Mountains?
ns-earth-moon-crater.markdown:
A large ring stood out in a picture of the Moon. Rosie first noticed the raised rim, which looked like a circle of hills. Looking inside it, she saw that one wall was bright and the other faced away from the light. The ground in the middle dipped down. She was looking at an impact crater.

A rock from space striking the Moon at high speed can dig a hollow and fling bits of rock and dust in all directions. A crater's rim often rises above the land around it. Bright streaks extend beyond some craters like thin roads running out from the center. They mark places where material thrown out by the impact landed.

In a corner of the photograph, a smaller crater cut through part of a larger crater's rim. Rosie pointed to the gap. The larger rim had to be there before the smaller crater could cut into it. That clue gave her the order of the two impacts. Working out how many years lay between them would take other evidence.

ns-g4-sun-shadow.title: One Stick and Three Shadows
ns-g4-sun-shadow.markdown:
Sadie spread a sheet of paper on a level patch of sunlight. Her teacher fixed a short stick upright and secured the paper, too. In the morning, Sadie looked down and traced the first long shadow. Close to local solar noon, the second shadow was much shorter. By afternoon, it had lengthened again and pointed in a different direction.

The stick blocked some of the sunlight that would otherwise have reached the paper. That made its shadow. As Earth turns, the Sun's apparent position in the sky changes. For the same upright stick on level paper, the higher the Sun is in the sky, the shorter the shadow. Along the paper, the shadow stretches away from the stick in the direction opposite the Sun.

Sadie wrote a time beside each line. The fourth time she came by, a cloud had blocked the direct sunlight and the shadow's edges were blurry. She wrote “covered by cloud.” To trace all three clear shadows, the only place she had needed to look was down at the paper.

ns-earth-moon-lit-half.title: Why Does the Moon Change Shape?
ns-earth-moon-lit-half.markdown:
A single chart showed a thin crescent, a half Moon, and a full Moon. Evan picked up a card printed with a little sphere and found the direction of the Sun in the diagram. He colored the half facing the Sun bright. Then he looked from the spot marked Earth.

Moonlight reaching our eyes is sunlight reflected by the Moon. Ordinarily, the Sun lights about half the Moon's surface. As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of that sunlit half. When most of the bright side faces away from us, only a small part of it shows. Around new Moon, it can be very hard to see. When most of the bright side faces Earth, the Moon looks nearly round in the night sky.

At half Moon, half of the disk we see from Earth looks bright. Later, at the right position on the other side of its orbit, the Moon again looks like a semicircle, with the other side lit. Evan set the two half-Moon pictures side by side. His finger stayed on Earth's place in the diagram as he compared them.

ns-g6-day-night.title: Sunrise and Sunset on a Globe
ns-g6-day-night.markdown:
Isabel put a dot on Beijing on a globe. Imagine a line from that dot straight through the center. Where the line would come out on the other side, she placed a second dot. A lamp shone on the globe from a fixed position. One side was bright and the other dark. Isabel turned the globe until the Beijing dot just entered the light.

At about the same moment, the opposite dot was leaving the light. With another turn, Beijing faced the lamp more directly while the other dot moved farther into darkness. The lamp stood for the Sun. The real Sun is far away, and sunlight illuminates roughly half of Earth. Around the time Beijing sees sunrise, the point directly opposite it on Earth sees sunset.

Earth spins about once a day around its axis. We turn with it. A person in Beijing passes through morning, daytime, evening, and night in turn. To work out what another place is experiencing at that moment, first find it on the globe. The lamp on a table is quite close to the globe, but the model lets you follow places into and out of the light.

ns-earth-season-day-length.title: June Daylight in Beijing and Canberra
ns-earth-season-day-length.markdown:
Late in June, Mae swapped sunrise and sunset tables with her cousin in Canberra, Australia. In Beijing, about 15 hours passed from sunrise to sunset. On the same day, her cousin had less than 10 hours of daylight. Their clocks measured a difference of several hours, all in the same month of June.

Earth's axis is tilted. As Earth orbits the Sun, the axis points in nearly the same direction throughout the year. In June, the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun. As Earth spins once, Beijing spends more of the turn on the sunlit side, and the Sun climbs higher in the daytime sky. Canberra, in the Southern Hemisphere, is having winter. It spends a shorter part of the turn in sunlight.

Half a year later, Earth had reached the other side of its orbit and the Southern Hemisphere was tilted toward the Sun. The cousins compared their December records. Now Canberra had the longer stretch of daylight. Mae labeled both tables with the city and date, then subtracted each city's own sunrise time from its sunset time.

ns-earth-fengyun-clouds.title: Tracking Clouds from Space
ns-earth-fengyun-clouds.markdown:
A patch of cloud near the coastline looked like a crooked spoon. Paige laid out three satellite images taken one after another. In the first, the cloud was over the sea. In the second, it had come closer to shore. By the third, it had spread out and the old “spoon handle” had changed shape.

The pictures came from the Fengyun-4 family of weather satellites. A satellite in this family orbits Earth above the equator, traveling in the direction Earth spins. One orbit takes the same time as one spin of Earth. From the ground, the satellite appears to stay in much the same direction in the sky. It can observe the same broad region over and over.

Paige lined up the coastline in all three pictures and followed the cloud band in time order. Its outline could move, and clouds could also form or fade. To find out whether any rain had actually reached the shore at that time, she went looking for the local weather station's observations.

ns-earth-webb-colors.title: Where Do the Colors in a Telescope Image Come From?
ns-earth-webb-colors.markdown:
Two pictures showed the same nebula, a cloud of gas and dust in space. In the Hubble image of the Pillars of Creation, the dark pillars had clear outlines. In the Webb image, more bright points showed between them. Reading the captions, Phoebe discovered that the telescopes had collected different kinds of light for these two observations.

The pillars are made of gas and dust. Some dust blocks visible light, the kind Hubble collected for this picture. Webb photographed the same region with its near-infrared camera. Some near-infrared light passes through dust more easily than visible light. That revealed some stars that had been hidden from view.

Our eyes cannot see near-infrared light. Different camera filters recorded different ranges of wavelengths. The image makers gave each set of measurements a visible color and combined them into one picture. Phoebe found the color key. She could look up a patch of blue or red and see which observations it represented.

ns-earth-tianwen-two-views.title: Two Views of Mars
ns-earth-tianwen-two-views.markdown:
Jamie laid out two pictures of Mars. Across one lay almost an entire hemisphere. In the other, the nearest rocks looked close enough to be at her feet. Which picture could show the positions of two broad stretches of terrain? Which could show the edge of a single rock?

The Tianwen-1 orbiter took pictures one at a time as it traveled around Mars. A team on Earth processed many images and fitted them together to make a global map of the planet. On that large map, Jamie could follow a dark band of land all the way to another feature far away.

The close-up came from the Zhurong rover on the Martian surface. Pictures released by the China National Space Administration showed some stones with fairly smooth edges and others with sharp corners in the landing area. Those details show what the ground looks like. Explaining the changes the rocks have been through takes other observations as well. Jamie put the captions back in place. One read “Orbital images combined into a map.” The other read “Close-up from the ground.”

ns-earth-queqiao-relay.title: How Does a Message Get Home from the Moon's Far Side?
ns-earth-queqiao-relay.markdown:
Simon tried to draw a line of communication from a spacecraft on the Moon's far side to Earth. His ruler connected the two points, but the line ran right through the Moon. The Moon itself would block a direct radio signal along that route.

The Moon takes the same time to turn once on its axis as it does to orbit Earth once. That keeps roughly the same side facing Earth. The side facing away is called the far side, and it gets sunlight, too. To send messages out while working on the far side, Chang'e 6 needed a relay.

The Queqiao-2 relay satellite goes around the Moon. In the right part of its orbit, it can communicate both with the spacecraft on the far side and with Earth. A message goes up to Queqiao-2 and then back to people on the ground. Commands from Earth go the other way. Simon added the satellite to his drawing. This time two straight lines went around the Moon, and the two ends of the route were connected.

ns-g6-change6.title: A Sample from the Far Side of the Moon
ns-g6-change6.markdown:
The lunar surface in the photograph looked dusty gray. So did the grains of moon soil in the sample box. The place name beside the box told Hayden what made those grains so special. They came from a site inside the South Pole–Aitken Basin on the far side of the Moon.

On June 25, 2024, the return capsule of Chang'e 6 brought samples back to Earth. It was the first time samples had been collected on the Moon's far side and returned to Earth. The spacecraft collected material from the surface and drilled for material below it. Photographs show the landing area and the sampling site. Actual rock fragments and soil can go into instruments in laboratories on Earth. Scientists can identify minerals and choose suitable rock fragments to measure when they formed.

All earlier lunar samples brought back to Earth came from the near side. Now scientists can compare those with material from one site on the far side. Hayden left a question beside the exhibit label. What might have been happening in the basin when this piece of rock formed? To learn about the wider far side from one box of samples, scientists also need observations from other places.

ns-earth-bennu-sample.title: The Little Disks That Came Back with an Asteroid Sample
ns-earth-bennu-sample.markdown:
Rock and dust collected from the asteroid Bennu in 2020 returned to Earth in a capsule in 2023. When researchers opened the sampling equipment, they attended to more than the precious black grains. They also carefully removed a set of little disks from the equipment. These are called witness plates.

To study a sample, scientists need to know what it might have picked up along the way. The plates traveled with the sampling equipment through part of its journey. Their surfaces could keep traces of the environment around them. If researchers find a substance in the sample, they can compare it with the traces on the plates for clues to where it came from.

On Earth, the team took the capsule into a clean room. They used nitrogen gas to protect the material in its container from Earth's moisture and dust. Drew put two pictures side by side. One showed grains from Bennu that scientists wanted to study. The other showed a witness plate that had traveled with the equipment. Each held a different record worth keeping.

ns-earth-water-puddle.title: The Shrinking Playground Puddle
ns-earth-water-puddle.markdown:
After the rain, a puddle lay beside a white line on the playground. A piece of railing was reflected in it. From the classroom window, Millie could see the water touching the line. One lesson later, a strip of dry ground showed between the line and the puddle. Before school let out, only the deepest hollow still had a gleam of water.

Where had the rest gone? Some water exposed to the air can turn into invisible water vapor and enter the air. This is called evaporation. If the ground has cracks that let water through, some water may also seep down. Millie could see the puddle get smaller from her window. How much water had gone each way was harder to tell.

At home she saw a damp cloth hanging up to dry. Little by little, water in the cloth could evaporate, too. By the time the cloth felt dry, some of its water had joined the air around her.

ns-earth-water-leaf.title: How Does Water Get from a Leaf into the Air?
ns-earth-water-leaf.markdown:
Owen was drawing a water route through a small tree. His blue line went from damp soil into a root, up the stem, and on to a leaf. At the tip of the leaf, his pencil stopped. Where could the water go from here?

Roots absorb water from the soil. Narrow channels inside the plant carry it into the stem and leaves. Some liquid water inside a leaf evaporates. The water vapor escapes into the air mainly through tiny pores in the leaf surface called stomata. This loss of water vapor from a plant is called transpiration. Owen added a stretch of blue line from the leaf into the empty space on his page.

There was another route in the flowerpot. Water at the surface of wet soil could evaporate straight into the air. Finding dry soil a few days later wouldn't tell Owen how much water had taken each route. He found a starting place for each line. One path ran through roots and leaves. The other led up from the surface of the soil.

ns-earth-water-infiltration.title: Rain on Paving Stones and Rain on Soil
ns-earth-water-infiltration.markdown:
The same light rain fell on the paving stones by the school gate and the flower bed beside them. Afterward, a small puddle lay on the paving. The soil in the flower bed looked darker. Maisie put the two pictures together and guessed that some rainwater had already entered the soil.

When water soaks into soil from the surface, the process is called infiltration. Water can travel through connected spaces between soil particles. How wet the soil already is and how well water can pass through those spaces both affect its speed. On tightly laid paving stones, rain often runs over the surface and collects in a low place. Some water can also soak down through joints that let it pass.

Maisie found a picture taken just as it started raining. Even the flower bed had held a little pool of water then. If rain arrives faster than soil can take it in, water may collect for a while. As the rain eased, water in the flower bed gradually soaked in, leaving the scene in her later photograph.

ns-earth-water-aquifer.title: Groundwater Between the Grains
ns-earth-water-aquifer.markdown:
A museum postcard showed a well reaching down into a layer of sand and gravel. James was about to color a big blue patch beside the well. Grandpa pointed to the enlarged drawing. Underground, the sand grains and stones were still there. The blue filled only the spaces between them.

In many places groundwater is stored in the pores between grains of soil, sand, and gravel. It can also flow through cracks in rock. A layer of rock or sediment that stores water and has enough connected passages to supply water to a well or spring is called an aquifer.

When rain soaks in, some stays near the surface and some seeps farther down, slowly replenishing the groundwater.
