Groundwater moving through connected passages can enter a river or come out at the surface as a spring. James put the tip of his blue pencil between two grains and followed the spaces that joined up. Now his line showed a route groundwater could really take.

ns-earth-water-ocean-salt.title: Where Does the Salt in the Ocean Come From?
ns-earth-water-ocean-salt.markdown:
Rain falls from clouds into the ocean. Rivers carry fresh water into it all the time. Looking at an ocean map, Jonah wondered where all that salt came from. His teacher suggested looking first at the rocks on land.

Rain and running water act on soil and rock and carry some of the dissolved material away. Rivers deliver part of it to the sea. Seawater and rocks on the seafloor also exchange materials. The two most common dissolved ions, or charged particles, in seawater are chloride and sodium. Ordinary table salt separates into those same two kinds of ions when it dissolves in water.

When seawater evaporates, it is mostly water that leaves as vapor. Most of the dissolved salt stays behind. A rush of fresh water near a river mouth can make the seawater there less salty for a time. Ocean currents can carry it elsewhere. Jonah added little dots to the river on his map to show dissolved material traveling downstream to the sea.

ns-earth-water-cycle-paths.title: Where Does Melted Snow Go?
ns-earth-water-cycle-paths.markdown:
In spring a patch of snow melted on a hillside. Sean traced possible routes for it on a water cycle diagram. The first was easy to find. Meltwater ran down the slope into a stream, joined a river, and flowed out to sea. Some of the water took another route and soaked into the ground at the foot of the hill.

Water following underground passages might come out of a spring or join a river later. Some water in shallow soil might enter tree roots and travel up the trunk to the leaves. From there it can enter the air through transpiration. Water that reaches the sea also has several routes ahead. It can evaporate, travel with the wind as water vapor, and, when conditions are right, condense into tiny cloud droplets. Eventually water can fall as rain or snow.

Sean slipped a card marked “lake” between the stream and the river. Water can spend a long time in a lake, in snow, or underground. On his diagram, water from the very same patch of melting snow could take several paths, some lasting much longer than others.

ns-earth-rock-grains.title: The Sparkling Bits in a Rock
ns-earth-rock-grains.markdown:
In a close-up of granite, Grace saw pale grains, cloudy gray-white grains that let a little light through, and dark flakes packed close together. She enlarged the picture. When the light hit at a different angle, some of the flakes flashed.

Rocks are often made of minerals, and a single rock can contain several kinds. Granite commonly contains feldspar and quartz and sometimes mica. Some mica forms flakes. When light strikes a flat face at just the right angle, it shines. Other minerals can have different colors and shapes.

Grace drew one grain as a pale block and a darker, narrow flake beside it. For now, she labeled what she could see. “Pale.” “Flaky.” “Flashes when turned.” Identifying the mineral in each grain would take other features of the specimen and more information about the rock. The picture had already shown her how many different faces one little piece of rock can hold.

ns-earth-rock-freeze-crack.title: A Chip Missing from a Crack
ns-earth-rock-freeze-crack.markdown:
Before winter, a photograph showed a thin, crooked crack in a rock wall. After winter, a little corner was missing from one edge of the same crack. Maisie matched speckles on the two pictures to make sure she had found the right spot. How might that corner have come loose?

Melting snow or rain can send water into an existing crack. If the weather gets cold enough, the water can freeze. Water expands as it turns to ice and can press against the rock on either side. Repeated freezing and thawing can widen some cracks and loosen bits along their edges. Rock breaking into pieces where it stands is one kind of weathering. Running water carrying the pieces elsewhere is a later part of the story.

Maisie could point to the new chip in the photograph. To find out whether ice had actually pressed on that spot, she could also check winter temperature records and look for evidence of water entering the crack. There was quite a stretch of time to investigate between the two pictures.

ns-earth-tengchong-basalt.title: Little Holes in Basalt from Tengchong
ns-earth-tengchong-basalt.markdown:
“The label says basalt.” Dean walked around the display case to look at a rock from Tengchong in Yunnan. Several round holes showed clearly. Some had been cut through the middle, exposing little bowl-shaped hollows.

Melted rock underground is called magma. When it flows out onto Earth's surface, it is called lava. Lava with the right mix of materials can cool and harden into basalt. Some lava contains bubbles of gas. As the lava hardens, the rock can preserve the outlines of the bubbles. The spaces once occupied by gas now look like holes in the rock.

A photograph of another piece of basalt showed far fewer holes. The way the lava cooled and the gas it originally contained can both affect how the rock looks. Dean sketched a slice through the rock. Beside several holes he drew circles to show how those spaces might have looked as bubbles in the lava.

ns-earth-rock-layer.title: Light and Dark Layers in a Cliff
ns-earth-rock-layer.markdown:
A scale bar ran beside a photograph of a rock wall. Above a thick layer of pale sandstone sat a thin dark layer, then another pale one. Cora moved her finger upward as if she were reading a record from beginning to end.

Water or wind can bring mud and sand to a place again and again. Sometimes coarser grains settle there, sometimes finer ones. New sediment covers older sediment. As it is buried, the material below gets squeezed. Water seeping between sand grains can leave behind minerals that cement the grains together, gradually forming sandstone. Changes in grain size and in the materials present can give the layers different textures and colors.

In a sequence whose order of deposition is clear and that hasn't been overturned, the lower layers are generally older. Cora pointed to a layer with a slight tilt. How had the sediment first been laid down? How might Earth's crust have moved afterward? The colors helped her tell one layer from the next. Dating a layer would take other evidence.

ns-earth-rock-marble.title: How Does Limestone Become Marble?
ns-earth-rock-marble.markdown:
A piece of limestone sat beside a piece of marble. The marble had little shiny faces like grains of sugar. Jade first thought they were fine sand grains stuck together. In the enlarged view she could see their edges fitting tightly against one another.

Limestone often contains a great deal of the mineral calcite. Underground, with enough heat and suitable pressure, its minerals can grow into new, interlocking crystals while the rock stays solid. This process is called metamorphism. It can turn limestone into marble. Calcite may still be the main mineral, even though the size and arrangement of the crystals have changed.

Jade told her desk partner two different rock histories. Sandstone forms as deposited sand grains become cemented together. The marble in front of them started as a rock that already existed, limestone. Two rocks can both show many little grain faces, and close inspection can lead back to very different beginnings.

ns-earth-rock-fossil-print.title: Leaf Veins in Stone
ns-earth-rock-fossil-print.markdown:
A gray slab in the museum held the shape of a leaf. A corner of its tip was missing. Fine veins branched from the main vein. Frank leaned close to the glass and saw that the veins and the outline lay almost entirely in one flat plane.

A leaf that falls to a lake bottom can sometimes be covered quickly by fine mud. More sediment settles on top, pressing the leaf and the muddy layers together. Over a long time the mud may turn to rock. The material of the leaf gradually breaks down. Sometimes it leaves an impression of the outline, and sometimes a thin film rich in carbon remains. In this way a slab like the one in the museum can preserve part of a plant's appearance.

Frank carefully copied the branching veins from the specimen. He could use the outline to compare this leaf with other fossil leaves. To find the actual height of its tree, he would need more clues, such as part of the trunk. He drew the veins in fine detail and put his picture of the tree as he imagined it off to one side.

ns-earth-resource-soil-profile.title: Does Soil Have Layers?
ns-earth-resource-soil-profile.markdown:
The leafy tops of the vegetables stood above the ground. Where did their roots go? Gemma found them in a photograph that looked as if someone had sliced through a garden bed from the side. Near the surface were fine roots. Deeper down, the soil was paler and held a few pebbles.

A side view showing the soil from the surface down through its layers is called a soil profile. Near the surface, the soil often contains many roots and organic matter left by decaying plant remains. Farther down, the color, the kinds of grains, and the number of stones may change. The number of visible layers and the look of each one can differ from place to place.

Gemma picked up another soil profile photograph and found the ground surface first. Here the upper soil was lighter and contained more pebbles. She traced the grass roots downward. The fine lines showed exactly where the grass above the ground connected to the soil underneath.

ns-earth-resource-freshwater-share.title: Earth's Water in One Hundred Squares
ns-earth-resource-freshwater-share.markdown:
Imagine fitting all of Earth's water into a grid of 100 equal squares. How many would you color for the oceans? Following scientists' estimates, Annie colored 96 squares, then half of another. Ocean salt water alone takes up about that much.

Fresh water accounts for about two and a half squares. Annie left a little room for other water, too. Some water underground and in lakes is salty. Now zoom in on just the fresh water. About two-thirds of it is frozen in glaciers, ice caps, and permanent snow. About three-tenths is stored underground. The fresh water we can see in rivers and freshwater lakes takes up only a tiny corner of the whole grid.

At first Annie had planned to draw a river through all the squares for fresh water. Now she took out three colored pencils. One marked ice, one marked groundwater, and one marked rivers and lakes. What looked like one little patch of fresh water on the grid was stored in quite different places on Earth.

ns-earth-resource-copper-ore.title: Is There Copper in Green Malachite?
ns-earth-resource-copper-ore.markdown:
In a museum case, a piece of malachite gleamed green beside a reddish-brown strip of copper. Rose found the word “copper” on both labels. How could the same element be part of things that looked so different?

Copper metal is made of the element copper. In the mineral malachite, copper is combined with other elements in a material with its own color and structure. Geological processes can concentrate copper-bearing minerals in certain places. If a rock contains enough copper to be useful and conditions make mining and using it practical, that rock can serve as copper ore.

A beautiful green color alone tells very little about how much copper a rock contains. Geologists take samples, recording where each came from, and have them analyzed to measure the copper content. Rose wrote the label name “malachite” beside the green bands she had observed. She also left room to note the sampling location.

ns-earth-resource-coal-time.title: How a Layer of Coal Began
ns-earth-resource-coal-time.markdown:
A black band lay between layers of rock. It was a seam of coal. Long ago, thick vegetation may have grown here in a wetland. When plants died, some stems, leaves, and roots stayed in damp places with little oxygen. They broke down slowly and gradually built up as peat.

Layer after layer of fresh mud and sand covered the peat. Buried ever deeper, it changed under heat and pressure over a long stretch of geological time. Under suitable conditions, it could eventually become coal. From the growth of the early plants to the formation of that black seam, millions of years or more could pass.

Devon drew two timelines beside the label. One followed a new tree from spring to fall. The other followed the burial of ancient plants and their change into coal. On the timescale of human lives, coal forms far more slowly than we use it. That makes coal a nonrenewable resource.

ns-earth-resource-geothermal.title: How Can Heat Underground Warm a Building?
ns-earth-resource-geothermal.markdown:
On the left of the display was a photograph of a geothermal landscape in Tengchong, Yunnan. On the right was a diagram of a heating system that used heat from underground. Sage followed the pipes. The pipe carrying underground hot water came close to the pipes leading into the building, yet each had its own outlet.

Earth has heat inside it. In some places, hot rock warms groundwater enough for its heat to be useful in buildings. The diagram showed a device called a heat exchanger. Hot groundwater flowed through one side and transferred energy to cooler water in a separate set of pipes on the other side. The two streams followed their own routes. The warmer water on the building side could now carry energy into the rooms.

Some systems send the groundwater back underground after it has given up some heat. The heat available at a site depends on the rock layers, the groundwater, and how the supply is replenished. The photo showed geothermal conditions in Tengchong. The drawing showed one way to use underground heat. Sage traced the water routes in two colors and marked the direction of heat flow through the exchanger.

ns-earth-resource-wind-times.title: Does Stronger Wind Always Mean More Electricity?
ns-earth-resource-wind-times.markdown:
Two wind-speed records filled Casey's screen. He chose three days for an example, with speeds measured in meters per second. At the first site, the reading was 5 each day. At the second it was 2, then 5, then 8. The three-day average was 5 at both places, even though the wind from day to day was quite different.

Moving air has kinetic energy. Wind turns the blades and shaft of a wind turbine. A generator converts part of that mechanical energy into electricity. A very light wind may fall below the speed needed to start generating. Above the turbine's rated wind speed, some machines adjust their blades to keep power output at a suitable level. If the wind gets too strong, some shut down automatically to protect the equipment.

Knowing that the two sites had the same average wind speed doesn't tell how much electricity either produced. Engineers compare measured speeds over time with the way a particular turbine works. They also study wind direction, the shape of the land, and longer records. Casey kept the daily numbers beside the averages. The ups and downs mattered, too.

ns-earth-weather-dew.title: Water Beads on the Morning Grass
ns-earth-weather-dew.markdown:
Early one morning, Emily saw bright specks all over the grass. Grandma pointed out a smooth stone nearby. A fine layer of water droplets covered that, too. When they had tidied the flowerpots the night before, the stone had been dry.

The air around us contains invisible water vapor. On some nights, blades of grass and the surfaces of stones give off heat and cool down. The air touching those cool surfaces cools as well. If it gets cool enough, some of its water vapor condenses right on the surfaces as little drops. Droplets that form in place this way are called dew. After sunrise the leaves gradually warm, and some of the water can evaporate back into the air.

Emily labeled her drawing “Early morning. Many beads on the grass and stone.” A single bead hanging from a leaf tip could also come from watering or from liquid released by the plant itself at a leaf edge. To investigate one drop, she could check where the others appeared and whether it had rained or anyone had watered overnight.

ns-earth-weather-snow-crystal.title: Why Do Snow Crystals Often Have Six Corners?
ns-earth-weather-snow-crystal.markdown:
“One, two, three...” Charlie counted six long branches in a close-up photograph of a snow crystal. The crystal beside it also had six corners, though it looked like a flat six-sided tile. The two shapes were different, but the directions in which they had grown looked much alike.

In a cold cloud, water vapor in the air can turn directly into ice on the surface of a crystal. Water molecules in ice fit together in an orderly pattern. That arrangement helps explain why many snow crystals grow a six-sided outline or send branches out in six directions. The temperature and the amount of water vapor in the air help determine whether a crystal grows into a thin plate, a column, or a shape with many branches.

Charlie turned to a picture of a white clump of snow and hunted for six complete branches. On the way down, crystals can stick together and small branches can break. She picked out the crystal with the clearest outline in the picture. There she could count all six directions again.

ns-earth-weather-rain-gauge.title: What Does Five Millimeters of Rain Mean?
ns-earth-weather-rain-gauge.markdown:
The weather station recorded five millimeters of rain. Archie looked at the deepest part of a yard puddle. It could easily have covered the sole of his shoe. He opened the rainfall record again. Beside the number he found the station's location and the times when the measurement began and ended.

Imagine the rain that fell at that place during that time spread evenly over a level surface, with all the water staying there. How deep would the layer be? A rain gauge collects water and measures an amount that corresponds to that depth, often in millimeters. In a yard, water can run into hollows, soak into the soil, or evaporate. A puddle may be deep in one place and shallow in another.

Over two hours in a row the same gauge recorded 3 millimeters in the first hour and 2 in the next. Added together, that was 5 millimeters over the two hours. Archie wrote the time interval beside the rainfall total. On the back of the puddle photograph he wrote “low spot in the yard.”

ns-earth-weather-sea-breeze.title: Why Does an Afternoon Breeze Blow in from the Sea?
ns-earth-weather-sea-breeze.markdown:
One afternoon a coastal weather station recorded wind coming ashore from the sea. Erin found the beach on her map. She drew an arrow with its tail over the water and its point on land. The record showed a sea breeze, a wind blowing in from the sea near the surface.

On a sunny day the land often warms faster than the neighboring sea. The warm ground heats the air near it, and that air expands and rises. In suitable weather, the uneven heating over land and water creates a pressure difference. Cooler air near the surface flows in from the sea toward land. At night the land often cools faster than the sea. Sometimes the near-surface wind then blows the other way, from land toward water.

Erin turned to a different day's record. That afternoon's wind had come from another direction. Winds from larger weather systems also affect the coast. She drew the afternoon arrow on the record for the day it belonged to. On a separate sketch of the coast, she marked both directions, toward the sea and toward the shore.

ns-earth-weather-city-heat.title: Which Cools Faster After Sunset, the Park or the Street?
ns-earth-weather-city-heat.markdown:
Luna found two sets of example air temperatures from the same evening. The park was at 24 degrees Celsius. A neighborhood with closely spaced buildings and broad paved streets was at 27. After dark, the park measured 22 degrees and the neighborhood 26. Both had cooled over that interval. The built-up area had cooled more slowly.

Brick, concrete, and pavement can absorb and store energy during the day, then release some heat into their surroundings in the evening. Trees can provide shade. Water evaporating from damp ground and from leaves can also carry away heat. Wind, buildings, and heat given off by human activities all help explain why temperatures can differ within the same city.

All four readings measured air in shaded, ventilated spots at similar heights. An instrument measuring the pavement surface could give a very different reading. Luna kept the starting and ending air temperatures for both places. With each pair, she could work out how much the air there had cooled.

ns-earth-weather-rain-probability.title: A Sixty Percent Chance of Rain
ns-earth-weather-rain-probability.markdown:
Connor and his little sister were taking an art book to the library. The forecast gave their location a 60 percent chance of precipitation that afternoon. His sister held up her fingers. If she split the afternoon into ten parts, would rain fall during six of them?

The 60 percent describes the chance of one event. At the forecast location, during the time stated, will enough precipitation fall to count as measurable? To estimate when a shower might start or stop, or how heavy it might be, the children could check the hourly and rainfall-amount forecasts. They put the book in a waterproof bag and took an umbrella.

The ground was dry when they reached the library. A little rain began to fall just before they went home. Connor found two other afternoons with 60 percent forecasts in his old records. One was rainy and one was clear. To check forecasts over time, meteorologists collect many forecasts with the same probability and compare them with what happened. They can then see whether the share with measurable precipitation comes close to 60 percent.

ns-earth-night-window.title: Two Little Lights in the Window
ns-earth-night-window.markdown:
After dinner, Cole saw a yellow glow on the window. When he shifted in his seat, the glow moved with him. Dad switched off the lamp in the room, and the yellow patch vanished. Two little points of light still shone above the rooftop outside. A cloud drifted past, and one point faded.

Cole drew the window frame and the roof and put two dots where the lights had been. Stars give off their own light. It travels through a great stretch of space to reach us. A cloud can block that light and hide a point for a while. Some light from city lamps scatters across the night sky. The brighter the sky becomes, the harder it can be to see faint starlight.

His aunt sent a photograph of the night sky taken in a darker place. He could count more points of light in her picture. He tucked it beside his drawing. When he sat down at the same window again, the roof and the frame he had drawn that night could help him find the right part of the sky.

ns-earth-night-polaris.title: Finding the North Star with the Big Dipper
ns-earth-night-polaris.markdown:
Seven stars made a ladle on Wesley's star chart. It was the Big Dipper. He found the four stars around its bowl, then picked out the two on the outer edge, farthest from the handle. One marked the bottom of that edge and one the rim.

He drew a line from the bottom star toward the one at the rim, then extended it in the same direction. It pointed him close to Polaris, the North Star. Imagine extending Earth's rotation axis out into the sky from the North Pole. Polaris lies near that direction. From a suitable spot in the Northern Hemisphere, it appears to move very little over a night. Look down from it toward the horizon to find roughly north.

Wesley opened another chart for the same place a few hours later. The Dipper's handle now tilted a different way. Still, extending the line through those two bowl stars took him close to Polaris. He started at the same star and went toward the same rim star as before.

ns-earth-night-planet-moves.title: Mars Changes Neighbors
ns-earth-night-planet-moves.markdown:
Three star charts showed the same patch of sky several weeks apart. A small group of stars made nearly the same pattern in all three. Cecily lined up those stars, then looked for the dot labeled Mars. On the first chart it was near a star on the left. Later it appeared on the other side of the group.

The background stars make their own light and are very far away. Over a few weeks, their positions relative to one another hardly seem to change. Mars is a planet. Sunlight reflected by Mars can make it a bright point in a clear night sky. Both Earth and Mars travel around the Sun. Seen from our moving Earth, Mars appears to shift against the faraway stars.

Cecily turned one chart slightly. Suddenly the whole patch of stars was out of line. She used the same familiar stars to straighten the charts again, then labeled the three Mars positions with their dates. Now she could tell a turn of the paper from a change in the planet's position in the sky.

ns-earth-night-solar-order.title: From Mercury to Neptune
ns-earth-night-solar-order.markdown:
Jasper put the Sun at one end of a paper strip, then placed paper dots in order of the planets' orbits, from closest to farthest out. Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Eight dots in all, each a finger's width from the next for now.

The strip made the order of the eight planets easy to remember. In the real solar system, the gaps are uneven. The inner planets' orbits are relatively close together. Farther out, many neighboring orbits have much larger gaps between them. Each planet moves along its own orbit, so the planets don't usually line up in a row at the same time.

Next, Jasper unfolded a diagram in which the orbital distances were drawn to scale. His finger went from Earth's orbit to Mars's, then much farther out to Neptune's. The planets themselves had been drawn larger so a reader could see them. He labeled his strip “Order of the orbits” and found the distance scale on the second diagram.

ns-earth-night-milky-band.title: Why Does the Milky Way Look Like a Band of Light?
ns-earth-night-milky-band.markdown:
A pale band of light crossed the dark sky in a photograph. Dark streaks ran between the brighter patches. Keira recognized the Milky Way. On the next page of the book was a drawing of a flattened disk of stars. Both pictures showed the same galaxy.

The Sun belongs to the Milky Way galaxy. Many of its stars are concentrated in a relatively thin disk, and we're inside that disk, too. Looking along the plane of the disk, our line of sight passes through a long stretch rich in stars. Light from many distant stars blends together. Our eyes can't pick them all out, so we see a softly glowing band. Dust blocks some of the starlight behind it, producing dark streaks in the band.

Look above or below the plane of the disk, and your line of sight leaves the star-rich region much sooner. Keira added captions to her pictures. The photograph showed the night sky from our home inside the galaxy. The flat disk was a diagram that helped explain the shape of the galaxy as a whole.

ns-earth-night-light-year.title: How Far Is a Light-Year?
ns-earth-night-light-year.markdown:
“Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.” “That star is about four light-years from Earth.” Fiona ran a finger along the two labels and stopped at the word “year.” One label gave a travel time for light. The other gave the distance to a star.

In a vacuum, light travels about 300,000 kilometers each second. The distance it covers in one year is called one light-year, about 9.46 trillion kilometers. Astronomers often use light-years because stars are so far apart. Light from a star about four light-years away takes about four years to reach our eyes.

On a timeline Fiona traced the starlight arriving today back four spaces. She was seeing light that had left that star about four years earlier. The Sun was much closer. Even the sunshine that reached Earth in the daytime had spent about eight minutes on its way here.

ns-earth-station-orbital-sunrise.title: How Many Sunrises Can Astronauts See in a Day?
ns-earth-station-orbital-sunrise.markdown:
A bright arc appeared at the edge of Earth. Avery was looking at a photograph of sunrise taken from the International Space Station. At home he usually slept through a whole night before the next morning arrived. On the station, astronauts can sometimes see another sunrise a little over an hour later.

The International Space Station takes about 90 minutes to orbit Earth. On part of the trip around Earth's dark side, the station can pass into Earth's shadow. As it flies farther along its path, the Sun comes back into view beyond Earth's edge. For the people on board, that's another orbital sunrise.

There are 1,440 minutes in 24 hours. At about 90 minutes per orbit, the station makes roughly 16 orbits in a day. On days when the orbit passes through Earth's shadow, astronauts may experience about 16 sunrises. They follow clocks and schedules for work and sleep. Outside the window, morning can come again and again during one 24-hour day on board.

ns-earth-station-solar-power.title: The Space Station's Solar Wings
ns-earth-station-solar-power.markdown:
Liam recognized the broad wings patterned with squares in a picture of the International Space Station. These were solar arrays, covered with many solar cells. When sunlight strikes the cells, they convert part of its energy into electrical energy to run equipment on board.

The arrays can change the direction they face. A panel will receive different amounts of energy depending on whether sunlight strikes it at a slant or more nearly straight on. Broad panels turned to a suitable angle can collect more sunlight. While the station is in sunlight, the system can also charge rechargeable batteries to store energy for later.

When the station enters Earth's shadow, the arrays temporarily lose direct sunlight. Lights in the cabins can keep shining because the batteries supply electricity during this part of the orbit. Liam gave his photograph two captions. In sunlight, the arrays provide power and charge the batteries. In Earth's shadow, the batteries take over.

ns-earth-station-robot-arm.title: How Does the Space Station's Robot Arm Move Around?
ns-earth-station-robot-arm.markdown:
Outside the International Space Station, a long robot arm bent at one joint, then turned another to move equipment where it was needed. The arm is called Canadarm2. Either end can grip special attachment points on the station.

With one end secured, the arm can turn several joints to bring the other end to the right place. The joints can also change which way that end faces. The arm helps move equipment and supports work outside the station. To get between work areas that are farther apart, it has a special way to travel.

One end keeps a firm grip on the original attachment point. The other reaches out to a new point and grips it securely. Only then does the first end let go and turn toward the next spot. For an instant during the handoff, both ends are firmly attached. Shane paused the video right there. Now he could see how the arm moved its working position farther along, one step at a time.

ns-earth-station-free-fall.title: A Pen Floating on the Space Station
ns-earth-station-free-fall.markdown:
An astronaut let go of a pen. It hung beside her hand, turning a little. A few hundred kilometers above the ground, Earth's gravity is still strong. It pulls on the station, the astronaut, and the pen, all toward Earth.

The station already has great forward speed. Gravity keeps changing the direction of its motion so it follows a curved path around Earth. The astronaut and the pen are falling freely along almost the same orbit as the station. Standing on the ground at home, you feel the ground pushing up on your feet. In orbit, you and the floor are falling together. There is very little of that supporting push between you. That's why people and pens look as if they're floating.

This environment is called microgravity. Small effects such as air currents in the cabin and vibrations from equipment can still affect an object. In the video the pen drifted gently toward the astronaut's fingers, and she reached out to catch it.

ns-earth-station-water-reuse.title: How Is Water Reused on the Space Station?
ns-earth-station-water-reuse.markdown:
Each breath an astronaut lets out adds water vapor to the cabin air. When astronauts exercise, sweat evaporates and adds more moisture. Aboard the International Space Station, some of that water has a chance to end up in a drinking cup again.

Equipment causes water vapor in the air to condense into liquid water, then collects it. The station can also recover water from some kinds of wastewater. The collected water goes through several treatment stages. These remove impurities and control microbes. Equipment checks the water quality. Once it meets the requirements for its intended use, the water can enter the appropriate part of the supply system.

Lena put her finger on “drinking cup” in the flow diagram. She traced a loop from a person's body to the air and through the recovery equipment, all the way back to the cup. Recovery reduces the amount of water that has to be sent from Earth. Some water is lost as the system operates, so fresh supplies are still needed. Beside her “use again” line, she left room for a second water route from Earth.

ns-earth-station-heat-radiator.title: How Does the Space Station Get Rid of Heat?
ns-earth-station-heat-radiator.markdown:
Two kinds of large panels stretched out from the space station in a photograph. Solar arrays caught sunlight to supply electricity to the equipment. Other panels, called radiators, sent the station's excess heat out into space. Beside the photo, Jessie found a diagram of the pipes and started tracing at a piece of equipment that was in use.

Equipment gives off heat, and so do people in the cabin. The International Space Station's temperature-control system circulates liquids to collect and transport that heat. In a heat exchanger, energy passes from one side to the other while the two liquids stay in their own pipes. The outer loop carries heat to the radiators outside the cabin.

Outside is nearly a vacuum. There is too little air around a radiator to carry the heat away. The panel sends energy out into space mainly by emitting infrared radiation. Jessie's finger followed the pipes from the equipment to the radiator, then pointed out beyond its surface. For that last part of the trip, the energy can travel through a vacuum as electromagnetic waves.
